News.title: Huge fire breaks out after explosion at Quaker Oats factory as ‘dynamic’ blaze shatters windows and sparks evacuations
News.content:
Next

A HUGE explosion has ripped through a Quaker Oats factory – sparking a massive blaze which sent flames smashing through glass windows.

Dramatic footage shows a “dynamic” inferno moving through the top of the building as thick plumes of smoke billow over the facility in Iowa.



Emergency services rushed to the scene in Cedar Rapids at 4.45pm local time on Saturday.

They found what appeared to be “evidence of an explosion and subsequent fire”.



Images show firefighters tackling the savage blaze as a fireball rips apart the sprawling factory.

All plant workers were forced to evacuate but were all accounted for just 45 minutes after the fire started.

READ MORE US NEWS MANHUNT ON Five victims confirmed in university shooting as persons of interest pictured

Local authorities told the Daily Mail the situation was “dynamic and ongoing”.

It is currently unclear what caused the explosion.



Witnesses told local media that they heard a blast go off.

They also reported seeing thick plumes of black smoke billowing from the site of the explosion.

A spokesperson for PepsiCo Foods US, which owns Quaker Oats, told the outlet they could confirm the fire took place.

They said: “First responders are on-site working to ensure the fire is controlled and quickly put out.

“Details of how the fire started will be investigated.”



Iowa Senator Chuck Grassley said he was “praying for the safety of those in or near the building and for the first responders on the scene”.

In 2021, a train in Iowa derailed and exploded after a bridge collapsed, causing evacuations in the area after 47 carriages piled up.

The train was carrying fertilizer and ammonium nitrate – highly flammable substances.

A Hazmat team was called in to assist as those within a five-mile radius of the explosion were ordered to evacuate.

News.title: Two members of the public injured after police dogs escape handler’s home and run onto streets barking before attack
News.content:
DOG HORROR Two members of the public injured after police dogs escape handler’s home and run onto streets barking before attack







Next

TWO members of the public have been attacked by police dogs after they escaped from their handler’s garden.

The hounds – one working dog and the other retired – are believed to have bitten a man and woman after breaking free as cops launch an investigation.



The two dogs, who appear to be German shepherds, were seen barking in the street in Sileby, Leicestershire.

A woman approached them to see if they were okay before a man driving nearby pulled over in an effort to also help.



The man claims he was suddenly bitten on the ankle “within moments” of getting out of his car.

He told LeicestershireLive: “As a professional dog handler myself, I stopped to offer assistance.

“Within moments of exiting my vehicle, the operational police dog bit my ankle, breaking the skin on both sides.

“Fortunately, my protective work boots prevented what could have been a much more serious injury.”

He emphasised that he did not want the dogs to be put down or attached any blame to them over the attack.

He did warn: “Had a child, an elderly person or someone unable to retreat quickly encountered these dogs, the consequences could potentially have been much worse.”



The two dogs were found by their owner and taken back to their home shortly after.

A spokesperson for the local police force said: “This incident will understandably cause some concern and during the last few days the force has carried out a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding what happened.

“The force has deemed that the correct security arrangements are usually in place, and this was an isolated incident.

“The dog handler has been spoken to regarding the importance of ensuring the gate of the property is always secure.

“The dog handler and police dog will also be undergoing a safety assessment to ensure operational standards continue to be met.



“All other dog handlers in the team have also been spoken to regarding the importance of ensuring the dogs are kept in a secure premises when not on duty.

“The two members of the public have been updated and the force has apologised to them.”

News.title: Heartbroken friends of student murdered by depraved stepdad pay tribute to ‘girl in the strawberry pyjamas’
News.content:
Next

HEARTBROKEN pals of the student murdered by her depraved stepdad have paid a touching tribute to “the girl in the strawberry pyjamas”.

Carla Georgescu, 19, was discovered dead on what would have been her 20th birthday at the University of Lancashire campus in Preston.



Her stepdad Nathan Owens, 34, had driven 100 miles from the family home to strangle Carla to death after becoming “consumed by jealousy”.

Preston Crown Court heard how Owens had become “sexually fixated” with his stepdaughter and made a life-size effigy of her to fulfil his sexual fantasy.



He had also manipulated innocent selfies of Carla into sexual images and had filmed himself having sex with her anime dolls and a stuffed cat she had bought him.

Owens has now been jailed for life with a minimum of 35 years after he was convicted of murder.

Following his sentencing, Carla’s flatmates Jen Kirkham and Imogen Flowers have paid a heartfelt tribute.

Jen said she will always remember Carla as “the girl in the strawberry pyjamas with the smile.”

She added: “You would see her walking round campus, she always knew what she was doing.

“She wanted to help people who went through similar situations as she did – she felt she wasn’t heard a lot as a child and wanted to help people in difficult situations particularly young children to make sure they didn’t go through what she did.”



Jen said she had been in class when she was told cops were in her flat on February 5.

When she returned to the halls of residence she was stopped by security who took her to the student centre and told her Carla had died.

Jen said: “It hurts to know that she was a year older than me, but I’m 19 now and she will be forever 20. It’s unfair to think that she went through all that.

“An hour and a half it lasted, while I was sleeping and I’ve heard people and I’ve seen people online asking how could the roommates not hear anything and I apologise that I don’t wear my hearing aids to sleep.”

Jen also described Owens, calling him “narcissistic”.



She said: “Every time I saw him he was smiling or looking bored.

“He laughed when they gave the guilty verdict. He actually laughed to himself like it was some inside joke. The rage I felt.

“He was supposed to look after her. He stood up to take the role of a father and he didn’t because for some reason his sick twisted desires were more important.

“I will never understand the cruelty and the twisted nature of someone who could do something like that.”

Imogen said she had been inspired by Carla, who had written and illustrated a book about Romanian life in the 1990s.



She added that Carla was always smartly dressed, wearing kitten heels.

DI Pete Macdonald, of Lancashire Police‘s Force Major Investigation Team said: “Carla had her whole life ahead of her, which was ripped away by someone she should have been able to trust.

“Owens has taken Carla’s life, but he has also changed her mum’s completely. He has torn apart the family he was trusted to love.

“As Carla’s stepfather, he had the unique responsibility of being welcomed into a family.

“He should have respected and loved Carla as his own child. He completely abused that trust, harbouring a perverted infatuation with her, before ultimately killing her.



“Owens’s offending ended with the worst possible outcome – the loss of Carla’s life, but the way it began is equally as disturbing.

“He took innocent childhood photos and made them indecent images. Because of this, Carla’s mum has not only lost her daughter but has had some of her memories of Carla’s childhood, before she met Owens, destroyed too.

“Carla was a young woman, a dedicated student who had the rest of her life to look forward to.

“She was happy and healthy and living a life reflective of many other 19-year-old women.

“What she didn’t know is that Owens had a disgusting sexual obsession with her, which led him to believe that if he couldn’t have her, no one could.



“He knew Carla was moving forward with her life, and he knew as part of that she was travelling to meet her new boyfriend, so he travelled to her halls, a place she should have felt safe, and brutally assaulted her before killing her.

“He is truly despicable.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Nothing will bring Carla back to her mum and all those who loved her, but I hope they can take some comfort in knowing that Owens has been convicted and given a life sentence.

“He will rightly remain in prison for a long time.”

News.title: Huge fire breaks out as residents forced to evacuate after ‘blast blows roof off building’
News.content:
Next

A MAJOR fire has broken out at an industrial unit as nearby residents were urgently evacuated after a “large explosion”.

Ten fire engines were sent to a farm in Sittingbourne, Kent, after the blaze broke out yesterday at around 3.30pm.



Thick black smoke could be seen for miles with the fire reportedly starting inside a metal barn.

Within minutes of the blaze igniting, the barn’s roof blew off, according to witnesses.



Videos show the rising flames engulfing Tonge Corner Farm, believed to house at least five businesses.

Firefighters were forced to turn to foam to put out the flames after water failed to extinguish the inferno.

It is also understood the local power grid has been switched off over fears of a larger explosion should it catch light.

At least 10 properties currently have no access to any power as firefighters were concerned the flames could reach the nearby electricity pylons.



Four fire trucks remained at the scene overnight.

Locals have been quick to express their concerns over the blaze, with many reporting seeing a rush of ambulances and fire engines.

One person said: “Flames are well above the houses from where I can see.”

Another said: “There’s loads of black smoke.”

A third said: “I hope nobody is seriously hurt.”



A spokesperson for Kent Fire and Rescue Service said: “Firefighters are currently at the scene of a barn fire at Tonge Corner Road in Tonge, Sittingbourne.

“At the height of the incident, ten fire engines, a height vehicle and a bulk water carrier were sent to the scene.

“Crews have made good progress extinguishing the fire, and the incident is now being scaled down to four fire engines. The firefighting robot is also being used to reach parts of the building that firefighters cannot safely access.

“The KFRS Volunteer Response Team is also in attendance, carrying out welfare checks on nearby residents who have lost power.”

News.title: Ukraine lands direct hit on Putin’s war factory producing components for deadly ballistic warheads
News.content:
Next

UKRAINE hit a Russian war factory yesterday using British-made Storm Shadow missiles.

The key complex in Oryol produced components for the deadly ballistic warheads unleashed on Kyiv this week.



The strike on the Proton-Electrotex facility caused a massive fireball and comes after the UK agreed to send more bunker-busters to Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Kyiv’s access to Elon Musk‘s Starlink and Starshield satellite internet network have been fully restored.



Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky said speed restrictions imposed on drones using the votal SpaceX technology had been lifted.

Mr Zelensky said: “Now we have the speed we need.

“This is very important; it is significant for our frontline logistics and for protecting Ukraine from jet-powered Shahed drones.”

It comes after US First Lady Melania Trump brokered a temporary ceasefire deal to open up evacuation routes for residents trapped in an occupied Ukrainian city.



She led round-the-clock negotiations to secure a localised truce after harrowing reports of a major humanitarian crisis in Oleshky.

Up to 6,000 residents, including hundreds of kids, have been left on the brink of starvation after months without food deliveries.

There is next to no electricity, gas or running water and some have been forced to eat grass and garden weeds.

Medical supplies have run out and hospitals are barely functioning amid daily shelling, drone threats and heavily mined roads.

The ceasefire is due to begin on Tuesday at 4am local time. It is unclear how long it will last.

News.title: Ed Miliband faction in Labour Party ‘waging war with Home Secretary’ after refusing to back immigration reforms
News.content:
Next

THE Ed Miliband faction in the Labour Party is waging war with Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, insiders claim.

Ally Miatta Fahnbulleh sparked anger this week for refusing to back Labour’s immigration reforms.



The Energy Secretary eventually caved in by tweeting her support for the Home Secretary, but only after No10 told her to.

Weeks earlier, Foreign Secretary Mr Miliband appeared to cast doubt on the decision to ban Palestine Action.



One frontbencher said: “Miatta is seen as a loose cannon — and not a very good politician.”

A government insider said: “She’s only been an MP for two years but acts like she’s untouchable because she is close to Ed Miliband.



“It’s the Ed Miliband tendency. And it’ll only get worse.

“Ed and Miatta are wading into Home Office matters. He’s pushing for some kind of climbdown on proscribing [Palestine Action] as a terror group.”

Another senior Labour insider said: “Shabana is furious and a lot of the Cabinet are furious.

“Miatta’s veering all over the place. What has the Home Office got to do with her?”



In interviews, Ms Fahnbulleh failed to back Home Office plans to extend the time it takes an immigrant to get indefinite leave to remain.

Her spokesman declined to comment but pointed to her tweet, which read: “I fully support our Home Secretary and the Government’s position on migration reform.”

Asked about the Palestine Action comments, a source close to Mr Miliband said: “This is a matter for the Home Office, and the Foreign Secretary supports the Home Secretary in it.”

News.title: Twenty students aged five or below suspended from schools over sexual misconduct as shock figures hit record high in UK
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

EDUCATION CRISIS Twenty students aged five or below suspended from schools over sexual misconduct as shock figures hit record high in UK







Next

TWENTY pupils aged five or below have been suspended from UK schools due to sexual misconduct, as shocking figures hit a record high.

A concerning 7,278 students were suspended in the 2024-2025 school year, figures from the Department for Education show.



It’s the highest total since the current recording method started in 2020.

Nineteen of the 20 children suspended were in the reception year.



Five kids in the infant years were expelled outright with no conditional return.

Primary schools accounted for 759 of all suspensions.

Suspensions due to sexual misconduct can cover sexual assaults, abuse, harassment and lewd behaviour.

This can be aimed at either other pupils or staff.

The latest figures show cases have risen by 12 per cent, from 6,479 in the previous school year.

The rise comes while the total number of suspensions for all other issues is dropping.



Ofsted, which inspects schools, found sexual harassment was normalised among schoolchildren.

Teachers’ leaders have warned that misogynist online influencers, such as Andrew Tate, are shaping how boys treat girls in schools.

Pupils aged 13 and 14 were the most frequent offenders, accounting for 1,564 suspensions.

Schools can record up to three reasons for each suspension.

Amongst the worst cases, 143 pupils were permanently excluded from school last year.



Christopher McGovern, chairman of the Campaign for Real Education, said: “These shocking figures represent only the tip of the iceberg of misogyny in schools.

“Most cases go unreported.

“Schools are no longer safe places for girls and for female teachers.

“The Government needs to greatly expand the option of single-sex schooling rather than allowing it to largely disappear.”

Soma Sara, chief executive of the charity Everyone’s Invited, said: “We hope that schools are now more conscious of the reality of sexual harassment and abuse among children and young people, and are better equipped to identify it and intervene when it happens.



“For too long, the harm children were experiencing was not always being recognised or understood by the adults around them.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A government spokesman said: “As part of our strategy to halve violence against women and girls, we have pledged to make sure all young people are taught about healthy relationships and consent from an early age.

“We have also forced tech companies to tackle harmful content and protect young people online through the Online Safety Act.”

News.title: Three brothers face extradition to Poland over killing after fleeing to Britain before trial
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

KILLERS FACE BOOT Three brothers face extradition to Poland over killing after fleeing to Britain before trial







Next

THREE brothers face extradition in a British legal first after being jailed in their absence for a killing in their homeland.

The Polish trio were among thugs who battered and stomped on two men in the city of Radomsko in 2020.



One victim died days later after suffering a brain haemorrhage.

Dariusz Paczkowski, 30, Dawid Paczkowski, 29, and Hubert Paczkowski, 27, were charged with “participation in a beating resulting in the death of a person”.



They fled to Britain before a trial in Lodz last October, where each got five years.

Polish authorities issued arrest warrants and warehouse packer Dariusz, of Romford, Essex, and Hubert, of Southend, were nicked in June by National Extradition Unit officers.



Dawid was picked up in Southend last month.

The trio are now all in custody while facing extradition proceedings at Westminster Magistrates Court.



They are next due to appear on 30 October.

It is understood to be the first time in British legal history that three siblings have faced removal from the UK for crimes committed overseas.

The Crown Prosecution Service was unable to provide a record of any other similar case.

News.title: Storm Boelo amber warnings kick in as parts of UK brace for 80mph gusts
News.content:
It has emerged that an oil tanker sailing 350 nautical miles off the Isle of Mull with 21 people on board issued a distress alert to the HM Coastguard because of "large swells" on Saturday afternoon.

"A Royal Air Force (RAF) aircraft was sent to investigate and established communications with the vessel," a spokesperson for the UK's Coastal & Maritime Agency said in a statement, without detailing from which country the ship was flagged.

The statement continued: "It was determined that there was no need for assistance, and that the vessel would continue with onwards passage."

Events across the country planned for the weekend have been cancelled due to the weather, and a number of travel disruptions have been reported.

In Merseyside, a River of Light event was called off for the second day in a row, and Knowsley Safari Park has announced that it will close on Sunday due to "high winds".

Several markets across the North West have also been cancelled due to the weather, including Quayside Makers Market in Salford and Macclesfield Treacle Market in Cheshire.

Dublin Airport in Ireland has cancelled several outbound and inbound flights and ferry providers such as StenaLine, Irish Ferries and P&O Ferries have cancelled a number of ferry crossings in the Irish Sea.

Jason Kelly, the Met Office's chief forecaster, said: "People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies. Secure loose items outside, plan ahead if you are travelling and keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings for your area."

News.title: Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls, the BBC understands.

Sources close to the duchess said Meghan warned Thomas Markle in a letter that he would never meet his grandchildren.

It is understood the letter was sent to Markle, 82, while he was in hospital in the Philippines after having his leg amputated.

It has been reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle had been found in his former home in the Philippines and UK police in 2019 told Meghan about claims of abuse against him. Markle, who is based in the US, denies all such allegations.

Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. He pulled out of his daughter's royal wedding that year, citing ill health.

The letter sent in 2025 appears to be the end of what has been a troubled relationship between father and daughter.

It is understood details of the letter, first reported in the Sun on Sunday, external, include Meghan telling Markle that he would never meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lillibet, with Meghan making it clear she would never contact her father again.

She also apparently told her father that authorities were aware of the claims made against him.

Philippines officials have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father, telling the BBC on Friday that its anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force was investigating the matter.

Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured Thomas Markle's computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.

Meanwhile, Thomas Markle has given an interview to the Mail on Sunday, external in which he acknowledged paying for sex in the Philippines on past visits but denies sleeping with underage girls and ever possessing child abuse images.

News.title: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
News.content:
The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.

Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said he wants pursue a new type of relationship with Brussels, potentially including full EU membership or joining the single market, which would require free movement.

"I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he told the newspaper.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said there could be "no return" to free movement after the 2016 EU referendum, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the prime minister's comments were a betrayal of voters who supported Brexit.

Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

He has said that any fundamental changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the "leave" campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

But the prime minister suggested the type of migration experienced during the years of EU membership was "different" from the challenges faced now.

"It was generally younger people, not always, but spending a few years, then going back," he said in his told the Sunday Times., external

"And obviously the ease of that worked for British people as well."

He acknowledged that freedom of movement "had very significant challenges associated with it".

"Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said.

"The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."

Burnham's willingness to re-open some of the most sensitive debates in British politics has been a feature of his first months in power.

In an interview with the BBC in September, Burnham said Britain could go "all the way" towards rejoining the European Union.

However, in his latest remarks, the prime minister stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."

The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. While the UK did not previously abandon the pound while it was an EU member, the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the single currency.

The remarks were made ahead of his meeting with EU chiefs at a summit on 20 November in Brussels, where he is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations with the bloc.

The shadow home secretary said EU free movement would amount to "handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe".

Philp said: "The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it."

Burnham won the Greater Manchester seat of Makerfield at a by-election in June, ahead of him becoming prime minister the following month. The constituency voted to leave the European Union in 2016.

As a candidate in the by-election, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".

In response to the Sunday Times interview, Farage said: "This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch".

"He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty," the Reform UK leader added.

News.title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
News.content:
We're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.

That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing.

Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around Â£24bn to as low as Â£11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors.

The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track.

At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance.

Increasing taxes on capital gains or extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources.

BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor to raise some more money, external on Wednesday.

News.title: Ukraine depends on Starlink - can Europe plug the gap?
News.content:
Ukraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet.

Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network.

There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation.

France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared with Starlink's 10,000-plus.

The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, IrisÂ², however it won't be up and running until 2029.

For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death.

"God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line."

For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones.

That vulnerability was highlighted by Musk himself on Saturday when he accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by using it for "drone strikes to kill people".

Saying that loophole was closed last week, he wrote on X: "Violation of those terms will result in end of service."

He added: "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately".

News.title: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates
News.content:
All West Bank land crossings will be closed during Tuesday's election in Israel, the country's military says, and Palestinian workers will be barred from entering all settlements.

The restrictions come amid a crackdown in the occupied West Bank after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the territory.

The Israel Defense Forces announced a "ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings" on Tuesday.

It said most workers would also be barred from settlements from Sunday, with the exception of industrial zones and a limited number of other areas.

Before the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, more than 100,000 Palestinian workers were permitted to enter Israel. Since then only a small fraction have had their permits restored.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a major operation on Friday in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.

The Israeli military have been demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron, with hundreds of families having been displaced.

News.title: Voters in Brazil to choose between Lula and Bolsonaro's son
News.content:
Never before has a candidate who trailed after the first round managed to overturn the deficit and win in the second round.

Bolsonaro's supporters were jubilant at his final campaign rallies, confident that he would bring change to Brazil through his promised tough crackdown on organised crime, as well as tax and public spending cuts.

He campaigned on the eve of polls in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, which has been a must-win state for any presidential hopeful since the 1980s.

"The time is almost here," Bolsonaro told supporters in a social media video.

"There are only a few hours left before we shape the future of our nation for the next 30 or 40 years."

He has also pledged to release his father, who is currently serving his sentence under house arrest due to ill health.

In Barra de Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro, where Jair Bolsonaro has a home, Bolsonaro supporters rallied in support of him dressed in the national colours.

"Brazil needs change, and FlÃ¡vio is the person that represents that today, after so many years of the Left destroying the economy and the country," one told BBC News.

Another said that what she most liked about FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro was his promise to "end violence in Brazil, end terrorism, narco-trafficking, and to reduce interest rates".

News.title: Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm
News.content:
When we landed by helicopter at Rosebank, this oil field was at the centre of a political storm - and set to be in the path of a real one.

We arrived on Wednesday morning, just a few hours after the UK government had granted consent for the production of gas from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea.

But already attention was shifting to this wild and windy patch of the North Atlantic â the next big decision for Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Rosebank is bigger than Jackdaw, it would generate higher greenhouse gas emissions, and it could be far more lucrative for its owners, Adura and Ithaca.

News.title: Budget to include £1bn for social and affordable housing
News.content:
Under the plans for the regions, an initial Â£285m in transitional seed funding will be allocated by the government next year to support mayors and local leaders - and reduce reliance on "fragmented bidding pots" in Whitehall, the Treasury said.

The government will also confirm that it will work with mayors to design a new Â£1.5bn borrowing facility from 2028, which would allow them to access capital needed to support local priorities.

The Treasury said this could be put towards new homes, bringing high streets back to life, or improving transport links.

Healey said: "Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas."

Areas across the country which are not yet strategic authorities will be able to access a share of the Â£285m funding to "unlock projects which will contribute to growth in their areas".

The prime minister said: "I'm calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country."

Claire Ward, chairwoman of the UK Mayors Network and Labour's East Midlands mayor, said that having the "right powers and resources through increased devolution" would help turn "ambitious plans into reality and deliver real, lasting change" for communities.

Lord Sadiq Khan, Labour's mayor of London, said greater ability to invest could "help unlock transformational infrastructure projects" including the West London Orbital route, the extension of the Bakerloo Underground line and Docklands Light Railway, and the development of Stratford International station.

However, Healey's Budget preparations suffered a blow when the Treasury's entrepreneurship adviser, Alex Depledge, announced she was resigning from the role. She will leave on Thursday, the day after the Budget.

Start-ups, she told the Sunday Times, external, were being treated as a "sideshow" and should not be pushed to the "margins of economic policy".

"Keeping scale-ups on the fringes underestimates the contribution of our greatest companies, and we need to support and develop them on British shores at all costs," she said.

Leading up to the Budget, defence has also remained a key talking point. Healey resigned in June from his role as defence secretary in the previous government over the defence investment plan, which he claimed fell "well short" of what was needed to fund the armed forces.

He had called for defence spending to rise to 3% of the country's GDP by 2030, on the way to reaching a Nato target of 3.5% in 2035.

But urging him to commit to setting out plans to spend 3% of GDP on defence, the shadow chancellor said: "We are living in an era of extraordinary threats, and yet the chancellor is dithering over finding the money to pay the country's insurance premium... you cannot have a strong economy without a strong defence".

Responding to Andrew Griffith's comments, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Conservatives were to blame for failing to invest in the military while in office.

Streeting said the prime minister had made it clear that his government was "determined to give our armed forces the investment needed to keep us safe".

News.title: Why the King's Caribbean tour could be 'biggest risk of his reign'
News.content:
The King will make three significant speeches during the Caribbean trip and will follow government advice not to issue an official apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade.

A senior royal aide said that the King would "not shy away from the darkest days of our past" but stressed that decisions over apologies and reparations were matters for government.

The current Burnham administration, like those before it, will not pay reparations.

Buckingham Palace says that acknowledging the wrongs of the past will be built into the King's programme in all three countries.

But apologies, reparations, and republicanism are rich pickings for campaigners and protests are likely.

This is the reality for the King and Buckingham Palace, and they are accepting of it.

Those who've worked on the planning of the trip view protests as part of the open debate in the region and security preparations include their possibility.

Lurking in the back of Royal Household minds will also be memories of the last tour by senior royals to the Caribbean in the early part of 2022.

Then, as the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, William and Catherine found themselves facing criticism over the optics of the trip - images of the royal couple reaching out to touch the outstretched hands of Jamaican children through a wire fence looked clumsy. Engagements designed as tributes to past royal visits appeared outdated. And protests also caused the cancellation of a small part of the schedule.

Everything will have been done to avoid those kinds of missteps on the 2026 Caribbean tour.

News.title: Murder charge after body found in wheelie bin
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder after a body was found partially within a wheelie bin, police have said.

Devon and Cornwall Police said Mohamed Abotaka, 36, of Grand Parade, Plymouth, was charged with the murder of 52-year-old Ali Barzai. The force said Abotaka was due to appear in court on Monday.

Police said Barzai's body was found in a service lane off Grand Parade at about 06:40 BST on Wednesday.

Det Insp Chris Lithgow urged people not to speculate and said a heightened police presence would remain in the area in the coming days.

News.title: Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget
News.content:
The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work.

It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how different cities could share the games, how communities could benefit.

Crucially it will also examine how much it could cost as well as assess the chances of a bid succeeding. The Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government said in 2013 it estimated hosting in London had cost Â£8.9bn.

A report in 2013 by the UK Trade and Investment, which has since been replaced by the Department for International Trade, said it had sparked a Â£9.9bn boost to the economy through new contracts, sales and foreign investments.

But the estimated amount was queried by some, including the Federation of Small Businesses and the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR).

Conservative shadow sports minister Louie French said that while hosting an Olympic Games would "likely provide a positive boost for the country", the cost of proposals would require "careful scrutiny".

He said the chancellor should use the Budget to bring down everyday costs before looking to "spend millions in taxpayer cash on reheated announcements made by his predecessor".

French added: "The irony is that Labour's new tourism tax will create a cost barrier for sports fans wanting to visit the North of England for an Olympic Games."

The new feasibility study for the Northern Games will be done by government, UK Sport, the Northern Mayors and include the British Olympic and Paralympic associations.

Healey said: "Olympic legacy lasts way beyond the celebration of sport over the summer. The North hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable.

"Britain's experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I'm picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious games. It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost."

News of the funding for the study was welcomed by the British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport.

"We welcome the government's continued support for exploring the potential of a future bid for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the UK in the 2040s," they said in a joint statement.

"Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements."

News.title: Thousands of people gather in support of Drumcree Orangemen
News.content:
The first part of the parade was followed by a series of speeches, mainly from members of the Orange Order.

This was very much an Orange Order event and not a political rally but inevitably there was a political tone to many of the comments.

There was explicit criticism of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher, the secretary of state and the first minister, but also implicit criticism of the leaders of the two biggest unionist parties - the DUP and Ulster Unionist Party.

Traditional Unionist Voice leader Jim Allister was applauded but by far the loudest cheers were for the Orange Order's legal adviser Jamie Bryson and the local MP Lockhart.

She was invited on to the stage and presented with a special gift for her support of the Orangemen.

Lockhart was the only politician to take to the stage, where she repeated her challenge to the DUP leadership: "Profound consequences must mean profound consequences. Michelle O'Neill must go.

"That's where I stand, and this lady is not for turning."

Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson warned politicians that they could face consequences at the next election over the Drumcree dispute.

"Politicians need to remember that we put them into office and we can take them out of office," he said.

He added that the Orange Order had won the right "to return home via our traditional route and Portadown District intends to exercise that right on a date and time of our choosing, and if necessary, without further recourse".

Orange Order Deputy District Master Alistair Power said Drumcree must not be allowed to divide unionism.

"It should not be used by parties to attack each other publicly over differences of opinion," he added. "We need to stand united."

News.content:
More than Â£1m is to be spent on nature recovery projects, including the restoration of habitats destroyed by a fire which ripped through a huge area of hillside in the Cairngorms.

News.title: Reward offered over murder in flat used as brothel
News.content:
A Â£20,000 reward is being offered by Crimestoppers in connection with the murder of a man who was found dead in a Birmingham flat in 2022.

Jinming Zhang had been stabbed multiple times before he was found in the property, which police said was being used as a brothel, in Moseley Street in Digbeth.

West Midlands Police previously released CCTV of a suspect, while a DNA sample from the suspected killer found at the scene did not produce a match on the national database.

The case was featured in the BBC series of Forensics: The Real CSI last year, which revealed police believed the murder suspect may have sustained a hand injury in the frenzied attack.

Jenny Birch, who has been overseeing the investigation, urged anyone with information "no matter how small" to contact police.

"Someone out there knows something, and we won't give up until we have answers," she said.

News.title: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of tour
News.content:
Sam Fender has called out the price of gig tickets ahead of his next tour, promising to lower the cost.

The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027.

While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices.

The Geordie musician also said standing would not be split into a front and back tier and he had "no idea how this was normalised at gigs".

Tickets are due to go on general sale at 09:30 GMT on Friday, with a pre-sale at the same time on Wednesday.

But Fender said he was "not happy" with the reported prices.

"They're getting changed," he said on Instagram.

"It got inflated well more than I'd had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on."

The North Shields singer also said he did not want there to be an option for fans to pay more money to be closer to the front.

"The standing will not be split as well, I had no idea about it," Fender said.

"I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs... it won't be happening on this tour."

He is not the first musician to raise concerns over ticket pricing.

Zara Larsson agreed with fans earlier this year that her tickets were too expensive.

The Swedish singer said while she did not have control over the prices, she hoped she would in the future.

At least 12 people were injured, including six children, in a shooting Saturday near a football stadium in Tallahassee on homecoming weekend for Florida A&M University, authorities said.

Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell told reporters that no arrests had been made.

In a statement, police said the preliminary investigation indicates that a fight broke out prior to the shooting. It followed a football game in a crowded area.

News.title: Protesters clash with police in Paris as demonstrations turn hostile across France
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Mass rallies drew hundreds of thousands of protesters across France on Saturday, with predominantly peaceful demonstrations giving way to evening skirmishes in Paris and Marseille despite an extensive security strategy deployed to head off a repeat of the previous week's unrest.

According to the interior ministry, 410,000 individuals joined demonstrations nationwide, though trade unions claimed the actual turnout was double that figure.

The main demonstration happened on the southeastern fringes of Paris, where at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality.

open image in gallery Several tens of thousands of secondary school pupils and university students, trade unionists and professionals demonstrated in Toulouse, in the Haute-Garonne department in the south of France, ( AFP/Getty )

Nearly 1,000 people were arrested as officers faced "an extremely elevated level of violence" from black-clad "ultra-left" people, interior minister Laurent Nunez claimed.

Two people were “seriously” injured, Mr Nunez said, with one man injured in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off, and another person in Clermont-Ferrand. He did not give details of either case.

The protests began in mid-September, when secondary school pupils took to the streets over staff shortages, deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms. The movement has since grown into a broader challenge to Emmanuel Macron’s government, drawing in teachers, parents and trade unions.

Conditions turned hostile following the conclusion of the rally on Saturday. Riot police deployed tear gas and water cannon against a crowd of roughly 500 masked youths, who eventually dispersed in the cold, wet conditions.

In Marseille, France's second city, young protesters set fire to rubbish bins to obstruct roads and threw stones and bottles at security officers. Police reported that several businesses, including two jewellery shops, were looted.

Confrontations were also reported in Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse.

open image in gallery Several tens of thousands of secondary school pupils and university students, trade unionists and professionals demonstrated in Toulouse, in the Haute-Garonne department in the south of France ( AFP/Getty )

"In almost every march we saw the formation of these high-risk groups. They broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence," said Mr Nunez, who blamed far-left activists and organised criminal groups for provoking the unrest.

Mr Nunez said 135 people had been arrested before the main marches began, with police seizing an assortment of weapons, including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, improvised weapons, a katana sword and airsoft guns. Paris police later reported that 65 people had been arrested in the capital.

The demonstrations come as Macron approaches the final months of his presidency, with the growing movement exposing wider anger over living costs, public services and the government's handling of dissent.

Security measures in the capital

A total of 70,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed by authorities – 10,000 more than the preceding week – after officials admitted they had underestimated the extent of the unrest on 17 October.

open image in gallery Protesters hold a French flag amid clashes during demonstration organised by labour unions in Paris ( Reuters )

Mr Nunez stated to reporters that the violence was less severe than the previous week, when vandals and looters engaged in widespread destruction. "What changed was anticipation," he said.

He added that far-right activists had attempted to confront leftist groups in the southern cities of Nice and Montpellier, creating a potential new dimension to the disorder.

Large parts of central Paris resembled a city under lockdown, with business owners shuttering premises, museums closing and more than 20 metro stations suspended.

open image in gallery Protesters dressed as Spider-Man attend a demonstration against rising living costs in Rennes, France, Saturday, 24 October 2026 ( AP )

Trade associations urged shopkeepers to keep their doors closed following damage or looting at thousands of commercial premises across France the previous weekend.

"There are hardly any customers, so it's not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris.

A number of the capital's prominent cultural locations, such as the Louvre, the Musee d'Orsay and the Paris Opera, opted to close as a preventative measure, leaving visitors disappointed.

"Everything's boarded up and we're not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans.

Protest movement spreads

The countrywide movement originated from minor student demonstrations in the Paris suburbs last month over school conditions. It quickly expanded into broader opposition to government economic policies, prompting similar rallies in neighbouring European nations.

open image in gallery Belgian police used pepper spray and tear gas during confrontations in Brussels with anti-government protesters on Saturday ( AFP/Getty )

Belgian police used pepper spray and tear gas during confrontations in Brussels with anti-government protesters on Saturday, while demonstrations also took place across several Italian cities for a second consecutive weekend, as well as in Albania.

Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who attended the Paris demonstration, suggested that rallies would persist until President Emmanuel Macron, whose term ends next year, addresses social discontent in France, one of the world's wealthiest nations.

"Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door," Melenchon told reporters.

Far-right event underway

Numerous protesters accused the administration of an excessive response to the prior week's disruption, noting that military personnel were assigned to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a famous boulevard featuring high-end shops and restaurants.

"We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.

open image in gallery A protester throws a teargas canister to police after a demonstration against rising living costs in Rennes, France, Saturday, 24 October 2026 ( AP )

"My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added.

The day's initial approved march proceeded without incident in Orléans, roughly 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where marchers gathered to oppose Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally as it held a party congress in the city.

Tensions were heightened by a shooting west of Paris on Friday, in which a gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one individual and injured four others, including a 12-year-old girl.

"We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon's France Unbowed party.

News.title: As the US and China form AI blocs, countries are increasingly torn between them
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

With the two leading AI powers, the United States and China, forming their own AI blocs, other countries are maneuvering to harness the strengths of both groupings and avoid losing out.

As the rivalry intensifies, experts say the window for countries to be able to choose freely between the two AI superpowers may be narrowing, forcing them to at one point pick between the U.S.-led Pax Silica and the China-inspired World AI Cooperation Organization.

That could put many countries in a dilemma: Do they go with the U.S.’s most advanced chips and AI technologies, or join China’s more affordable, open-source AI systems?

Kazakhstan, a Central Asia nation of about 21 million people, is a rare example of a country that has sought to bridge that gap.

Just three weeks after its AI minister Zhaslan Madiyev visited Washington in June to join the U.S. group working to strengthen AI supply chains, he headed to Shanghai for a signing ceremony making the Central Asian country a founding member of China's initiative to shape the global AI agenda.

Being in Pax Silica means more technological partnerships, high-tech manufacturing jobs and a place in global AI supply chains. At the same time, as part of China’s World AI Cooperation Organization alongside 28 other initial founding countries including Pakistan and Russia, Kazakhstan hopes to also have a voice in setting regional and global AI standards.

“Everyone is hedging,” said Dana Masalimova, a former Kazakhstan diplomat and independent scholar and center associate at the Kathryn W. and Shelby Cullom Davis Center for Russian and Eurasian Studies at Harvard University.

“We don’t want this binary choice,” Masalimova said.

Kazakhstan among countries hoping to harness the best of both blocs

Kazakhstan is benefiting from both U.S. and Chinese investments, but is in a “very precarious spot,” she said,

It has rich critical mineral resources essential to AI development and has cheap electricity to power data centers, which have become politically fraught in the U.S.

Earlier this year, Kazakhstan's government signed an investment deal worth up to $10 billion involving Nvidia to build a “data center valley” in the country.

Meanwhile, more Chinese companies are investing in Kazakhstan. Local officials say Chinese foreign direct investment in Kazakhstan reached a record $2.8 billion in 2025. Chinese leader Xi Jinping met with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in July to expand cooperation under China’s global infrastructure building Belt and Road initiative.

Washington’s pressure campaign versus Beijing’s courtship

Both China and the U.S. are leveraging access to AI to increase their global influence.

President Donald Trump insisted last month that “whoever wins AI, wins.” U.S. officials and AI companies have accused China of large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American models.

Beijing has rejected those claims and says the U.S. is pursuing an AI monopoly while restricting China’s access to some of the world’s most cutting-edge AI chips and chipmaking machinery.

Washington has signaled that Pax Silica — with China as its implicit target — is only for the trusted.

“Countries can’t be trusted partners in Pax Silica while substantively engaging in initiatives that advance a competing vision for super intelligence,” the U.S. State Department said, using the Trump administration’s new preferred term for AI.

For its part, Beijing touts the openness and inclusiveness of its World AI Cooperation Organization. “As both major countries in AI, China and the United States should leverage respective strengths in AI rather than guarding against each other,” the Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement. “AI should not be owned by major countries.”

The two AI powers have different messaging largely because Beijing needs to court third countries in its bid to build an alternative coalition, whereas Washington already has a powerful network of allies, said Kyle Chan, a fellow at The Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center.

That lends power to what he described as “swing countries.”

Indonesia, Singapore may also be caught between China and the US

Like Kazakhstan, Indonesia has resources vital for AI and other technologies, such as nickel and copper. It's also seeking to make the most of both AI powers, having joined China's World AI Cooperation Organization.

Indonesia wants to benefit from both, Mari Pangestu, Indonesian National Economic Council's vice chair, told reporters at a University of Hong Kong Business School event. “We should be able to be part of both, put it that way. And choose the best system.”

U.S. AI firms are bringing investments to other countries like Singapore, where Anthropic is setting up its latest Asia office. The city-state says it is also considering joining China’s AI organization.

In Saudi Arabia, the AI startup Humain unveiled in September a platform built on an open model by a Chinese AI company. The kingdom also has a deal with Nvidia to expand AI computing with its advanced chips.

France, one of the most ambitious AI developers aside from the U.S. and China, is attempting to go its own way with its startup Mistral, whose new model released this month outperforms some advanced Chinese models.

Japan is closely aligned with the U.S. on strategic and security issues, including advanced semiconductors, trusted AI and standards. But it will not reject the more affordable Chinese AI models for “lower-risk applications,” said Takahiro Tsuchiya, a professor at Kyoto's University of Foreign Studies.

Difficult to challenge the two leading powers

For countries like the U.K. and Germany which have substantial economic and military capacity but no self-developed powerful frontier AI models of their own, aligning with the U.S. may be vital for their access to data centers and chip deals with U.S. companies, said Anton Leicht and Sam Winter-Levy at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Essentially, their access to advanced AI systems “depends on the whims of policymakers in Washington and Beijing,” they said, while those countries may have limited influence over AI’s future.

China, meanwhile, has been closing the technology gap with the U.S. when it comes to chipmaking and advanced AI capabilities, but it still trails top U.S. technological capabilities, at least for now.

Also, Beijing's open-source approach allows countries to be less reliant on the U.S., and China has been providing funding for developing countries to develop their own AI ecosystems, said Alberto Lemma, a research fellow at the think tank ODI Global.

To date, China has provided official sector grants and loans for project and activities that use or enable AI technologies in at least 77 low- and middle-income countries, according to the AidData research lab at William & Mary, a public university in Virginia. Some top recipients include Nigeria, Zambia, Ghana, Bangladesh, Senegal, Cameroon, and Kenya. Public perceptions are also changing. Recent study results from Pew Research Center have shown that people in middle-income countries are becoming more positive and trusting of China when it comes to AI and the technology’s regulation.

All things considered, many countries “don’t want to pick a side ... because there are advantages and disadvantages to each technology stack,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Most countries may eventually lack a good option since they cannot compete on building AI frontier models, but “every country in the world in some way or another is thinking about AI sovereignty," he said. After all, “maybe no other country than the U.S. and China can really build these very large, powerful models.”

___

Tang reported from Washington.

Sal Frelick tied the score with his first home run in three months, Cooper Pratt hit a go-ahead single in the seventh inning and the Milwaukee Brewers stunned the Tampa Bay Rays 5-4 on Saturday night for a 2-0 World Series lead by overcoming a four-run deficit for the second time in the postseason.

Tampa Bay, which won the AL pennant by forcing opponents into mistakes, committed one error, made two other misplays that could have been charged as errors and had a runner thrown out at the plate.

Down 4-0 in the first inning, Milwaukee rallied for its seventh comeback win of this postseason. The Brewers also rebounded from a 4-0 deficit to beat the Los Angeles Dodgers 6-4 in Game 4 of the NL Championship Series, completing a four-game sweep.

After losing Friday’s opener 3-2, the Rays burst ahead against rookie Logan Henderson but the Brewers started to claw back with two runs in the bottom half against Tampa Bay ace Drew Rasmussen.
