World.title: APC Campaign Flag Off: Tinubu shuts down Kaduna
World.content:
Kaduna metropolis was filled to the brim as from Friday when party supporters and government officials converged on the former capital of Northern Nigeria, for the flag-off of the 2027 APC presidential campaign on Saturday.

The Township stadium burst at the seams as people spilled out of the campaign venue onto Independence way and adjourning boulevards around the arena.

As early as 6am on Saturday, party members massed at the event’s venue, wearing T-shirts with party colors and logos, as well as apparels of various designs, bearing President Bola Tinubu’s picture or broken shackles symbol.

APC-led State Governors, Ministers of the Federal Government of Nigeria, members of the National Assembly, APC National Working Committee members, federal and state appointees were at the stadium.

Musicians kept the party faithful entertained as they waited for the event to kick off while supporters chanted the praises of their various Governors and President Tinubu.

Arriving in a coaster bus with Vice President Kashim Shettima, Governor Uba Sani and other dignitaries, the crowd greeted President Tinubu with a chorus of “Baba Oyoyo.”

Speaking during the flag off, President Bola Tinubu urged Nigerians to support his re-election, promising to sustain efforts towards economic recovery, prosperity and a better future for the youth.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Tinubu, who thanked Kaduna residents for their support during the 2023 presidential election, said he had returned to seek another mandate to continue his administration’s policies and programmes.

The president dismissed criticisms of hunger and poverty bedevilling the nation, accusing previous administrations of creating the problems he is working to address.

Commending his administration for paying salaries regularly, President Tinubu praised APC governors for their efforts to develop their respective states.

He urged supporters to mobilise voters ahead of the January 16, 2027 election, calling on them to vote for APC candidates at the presidential, governorship, National Assembly and state assembly levels.

“Your prosperity is here. Your future is in your hands. Your fingerprints on the ballot will determine it,” he said, warning supporters against misinformation and attempts to mislead voters.

Earlier, Governor Uba Sani thanked the president for significant federal government interventions in transportation, education, healthcare, agriculture, security and human capital development.

The interventions has brought renewed hope to Kaduna State and other parts of Northern Nigeria, he said, adding that residents should support continuity in the 2027 election.

Governor Uba Sani highlighted the reconstruction of the Kaduna-Birnin Gwari 123 km road, saying N178bn has been released for the project, which had been abandoned for more than 40 years.

He recalled that Tinubu visited Birnin Gwari during the 2023 presidential campaign despite security concerns, where promised to improve security along the corridor.

The Governor told the gathering that ‘’today, you can travel to Birnin Gwari without a police escort. That is progress, Mr President, and we thank you for it.’’

He added that more than 300 schools and over 150 primary healthcare centres that had been closed because of insecurity in Kaduna State have been reopened.

He also thanked the president for the ongoing reconstruction of the Zaria-Soba-Kambuwa road and the proposed Kaduna metropolitan light rail project.

According to him, $865m had been approved for the rail project, while the contractor, China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation have been mobilised with $300m.

On education, Sani said the North-West had received N84bn through the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), supporting about 414,000 students across the region.

Also speaking, Senator AbdulAzeez Yari, Director-General of the Tinubu presidential campaign, said Kaduna was deliberately selected to host the campaign flag-off because of its political importance in Northern Nigeria.

Yari commended Governor Uba Sani and other APC leaders for their preparations, saying the turnout reflects the collective efforts of party members across the country.

He dismissed claims that the federal government is working against farmers, as about two million have indicated their commitment to support Tinubu in the 2027 election because the administration has taken steps to improve their livelihoods.

The campaign director-general also defended the administration’s economic policies, arguing that the country’s foreign reserves have increased from about $33.9bn when Tinubu assumed office to approximately $54.7bn.

Yari called on traditional rulers, Islamic scholars, imams and other community leaders to mobilise support for the president, saying continuity is necessary for national development and peace.

“By God’s grace, Northern Nigeria is 101 per cent behind you, Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu, and we are determined to deliver our promise in the 2027 general election,” he said.

Speaking at the event, Vice President Kashim Shettima said the APC had demonstrated its commitment to national unity and development through cooperation with state governments.

Shettima said the party won the 2023 election because Nigerians believed the alternative would have been disastrous for the country.

He also praised Kaduna residents for electing Governor Sani, saying his administration had helped promote unity across the state.

According to him, Kaduna has become a state where residents from different communities could regard one another as brothers and sisters, with the benefits of democracy extending beyond the metropolitan area.

Shettima said the federal government had supported educational development in Kaduna through the establishment of the Federal University of Applied Sciences in Kachia and the transition of the Federal College of Education, Zaria, into the University of Education.

The vice president said the administration had continued projects initiated by previous governments, including the Ajaokuta-Kaduna-Kano gas pipeline, the Kano-Maradi railway, the Lagos-Kano rail corridor and the Abuja-Kaduna-Kano Expressway.

Shettima also defended Tinubu’s political relationship with Northern Nigeria, citing his past support for northern political leaders seeking the presidency, recalling his support for former Vice President Atiku Abubakar after he left the PDP.

According to him, the president had consistently demonstrated political goodwill towards the North and urged the region to reciprocate by supporting his re-election bid.

World.title: Enugu Forest Guard reaffirms commitment to safe forests, strengthens inter-agency cooperation
World.content:
The Enugu State Forest Guard Command has reaffirmed its commitment to securing forests and rural communities across the state following the successful completion of a week-long training programme designed to enhance personnel professionalism, operational readiness and inter-agency cooperation.

In a press statement issued in Enugu on Saturday by the Commander of the National Forest Guard, Enugu Command, Dr Akinbayo Olasoji, the training, which concluded on 23 October 2026, equipped personnel with enhanced professional competencies, including sophisticated techniques for handling assorted rifles, alongside other operational skills required for responsible security duties and the protection of forest environments.

The programme also focused on joint military guard operations, intelligence analysis, leadership, human rights, crime-scene preservation, emergency coordination and professional report writing.

Olasoji said the initiative was part of its sustained efforts to ensure that Enugu’s forests remain safe for farmers, residents, travellers and rural community dwellers, while protecting wildlife, natural resources and critical infrastructure from criminal activities.

A major highlight was the lecture on joint military guard operations delivered by Lieutenant Colonel Solomon Kure Shekarau of the Nigerian Army, 82 Division Garrison, Enugu which emphasised effective command coordination, clearly defined responsibilities and cooperation among security agencies during forest deployments.

Similarly, senior police officers, including ACP Suraju Kehinde Oyewole and ACP Oliver Odimega, trained participants on intelligence gathering, incident documentation, crime-scene preservation, first-response procedures and the appropriate referral of suspected criminal cases to the police.

The programme further addressed the protection of critical national assets, with Nwatu Emmanuel Amechi of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps highlighting vigilance, incident-scene safety and emergency coordination.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

On legal compliance, the Command’s Legal Officer, Amaka Mandy, reinforced the importance of operating within the provisions of the Enugu State Forest Guard Law, 2020, and respecting the fundamental rights of citizens.

The training also stressed emotional discipline, accountability and respectful engagement with members of the public, underscoring the principle that effective security operations must be supported by professionalism and public trust.

Speaking on the development, Olasoji, reaffirmed the Command’s determination to discharge its responsibilities diligently, lawfully and professionally.

He emphasised that sustainable forest security requires continuous training and collaboration among the government, security agencies, traditional institutions, community leaders and residents.

He further disclosed that another week of training was planned for November 2026, alongside a proposed 30-day improvement framework to strengthen personnel performance, reporting standards and accountability.

Reiterating the resolve to translate the knowledge acquired into effective field operations, the Commander said he would ensure that forests and surrounding communities across Enugu State remain protected, secure and accessible for legitimate economic and social activities.

He also commended Governor Peter Mbah for his unwavering support, encouragement and commitment to strengthening the operational capacity of the Forest Guard in the state, noting that the Governor’s support had continued to inspire the Command’s determination to discharge its responsibilities effectively, enhance forest security and protect farmers, travellers, rural communities and other residents from security threats.

World.title: Winners emerge in NCDMB Essay Competition
World.content:
Winners of the 10th Edition of the NCDMB Annual National Undergraduate Essay Competition 2026 were on Thursday unveiled at a colourful ceremony at the NCDMB Conference Centre, Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, with the Management of the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB) underscoring the strategic importance of youth development and local manufacturing in promoting sustainable local content and building a resilient economy.

The coveted prize of N1 million, a brand-new laptop and a plaque was won by Mr Wisdom David Fabunmi, a 200-level Physiotherapy student of the University of Ilorin, Kwara State, who emerged as overall winner, while the second prize of N700,000, laptop and plaque was won by Ms. Joy Oghogho Enogieru, a 100-level Doctor of Optometry student of the University of Benin, the first runner-up. The third prize of N500,000, laptop and a plaque was won by Mr. Ahmadu Kodan Yusuf, a 100-level Law student of Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria.

There were some 5,000 entries in the Essay Competition from 52 universities across the six geopolitical zones of the country, with consolation prizes going to the 4th to 9th place winners.

The competition, which the Board notes has become an important platform for promoting research, analytical thinking, effective communication and intellectual engagement among undergraduates, had this year’s focus on, “Promoting Manufacturing for Sustainable Local Content Development.”

Representing the Executive Secretary of the NCDMB, Felix Omatsola Ogbe, at the Grand Finale of the Award and Prize-giving Ceremony, the General Manager, Corporate Communications Division (CCD), Dr. Obinna Ezeobi, stated that the competition is particularly important to the Board because it contributes to the realisation of its mandate, which centres on development of human and material capacity and monitoring of compliance by players in the oil and gas industry.

He explained that the Board discharges its capacity building mandate through various programmes such as Direct Intervention trainings for graduates and artisans in technical and non-technical skills as well as project-based human capital development, which entails on-the-job trainings on live projects as required by the Nigerian Oil and Gas Industry Content Development (NOGICD) Act, 2010.

Ezeobi pointed out that universities are institutions where ideas should be developed, problems examined, innovations encouraged and solutions created for the advancement of the society, hence the Board undertook to engage students and encourage them to think critically and write about Nigerian Content. The ideas, commitment and ingenuity of youths, he noted, were crucial to the future of Nigerian Content.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the Annual Undergraduate Essay Competition is connected to several other interventions the Board has for youths in higher institutions, such as the Research Centres of Excellence in Federal University of Technology, Owerri; Federal University of Technology, Minna; Niger Delta University, Wilberforce Island, Bayelsa State; University of Port Harcourt, Choba; University of Ibadan, Ibadan, and Modibbo Adama University of Technology, Yola.

He also listed the Nigerian Engineering Olympiad (NEO), to inspire innovation among engineering students, with the maiden edition concluded in July 2026.

Other initiatives of the Board targeted at youths include specialised training programmes like Nigerian Oil and Gas Readiness Training, where 10,000 young Nigerians are being trained in the 10 top skills needed in the emerging new projects being developed by the industry, and the Catch-the-Researcher-Young Programme (CRYP), a digital research capacity development initiative designed to equip undergraduate students with modern technology skills, advanced research methods, and industry-relevant digital competencies.

Ezeobi noted that the focus of this year’s essay competition on promoting manufacturing for sustainable local content development is intended to challenge participants to examine how Nigeria can strengthen its productive capacity and create greater economic value.

Manufacturing, he emphasised, is “the bedrock of sustainable local content development,” and that the NCDMB established the Nigerian Oil and Gas Parks Scheme (NOGaPS) “to incubate the manufacturing of components used by the oil and gas industry.”

According to him, “It is also the reason we implement a policy known as Nigerian Content Equipment Commitment (NCEC), which compels companies to show proof that they manufacture components and have capacity to execute key activities” before they get contract opportunities in the oil and gas industry.

Earlier in a welcome address, the programme consultant, Mr Eyinimi Omorozi, Chief Executive Officer of Mahogany 21st Century Concepts Limited, said the Award and Prize-giving Ceremony was a celebration of “a decade of investment in ideas by the NCDMB.” He expressed satisfaction with the output of the participants in the competition, stating, “From the essays of these young men and women, you can just tell that the future is very bright.”

In regard to the sponsors, he declared, “NCDMB is not just building facilities and monitoring compliance, it is also building minds.”

In his opening remarks, the Chairman of the occasion, Professor Promise Mebine, Vice Chancellor, Federal University, Otuoke, congratulated the NCDMB on its successful hosting and sponsorship of the competition and for staying faithful to the vision.

“Year after year, you have proven that building Nigerian Content is not only about pipelines and platforms, but about building people, particularly our youths, the leaders of tomorrow,” he stated.

To the winners, his word was, “Your prize today is well-deserved, but the real prize is not the cheque or the plaque. The real prize is that NCDMB has now opened a door for you. Walk through it!” To the other contestants, he said, “you are not losers; every essay you submitted is a seed. You have trained your mind to think. You have trained your hand to write. Keep writing; keep researching; keep believing in Nigeria; Next year, the podium may be yours.”

In a goodwill message, the Director, Monitoring and Evaluation Directorate (MED) Mr. Esueme Dan Kikile, Esq. commended the Executive Secretary, the Corporate Communications Division and the programme consultant for all the effort toward sustenance of the competition, which he noted has been immensely beneficial to the Board and participants.

World.title: Enugu jingles competition: Pincode wins ₦2m as 20 entries emerge winners
World.content:
Chunwike Ukuta, popularly known as Pincode, has emerged overall winner of the 2026 Enugu Good Governance Jingles Competition organised by the Office of the Senior Special Assistant to the Governor on Mainstream Media, in partnership with the Tomorrow Is Here Movement (TIH), winning the top prize of ₦2 million with his entry, Ife Ọma Melụ Na B’anyi.

The competition attracted 157 entries from musicians, songwriters, vocalists, music producers and other creative talents, with 20 entries selected for cash prizes following an assessment by a panel of judges.

Princess Ndidiamaka Okafor came second with Peter Mbah Bụ Agụ, winning ₦1 million, while Kelechi Obeta, popularly known as Kelycool, placed third with Ndi Enugu Onye Ka Unu Ge-eso Na’azụ?, winning ₦750,000.

Ejike Okonu took fourth position with Aafụm Onye Kwerụm Nkwa Merụ Mee, winning ₦600,000, while Solomon Chukwuebuka Ojobor came fifth with It’s Time for Us to Reward Our Governor Peter Mbah, winning ₦500,000.

The next five winners, each to receive ₦250,000, are Blessing Okolo Ogadimma, whose Enugu Na Ihe Ọma Abia placed sixth; Ijeoma Agbo, with Ndi Enugu Kunie Nụ, Nke Ọchiri Achi Dụ Anyi Mma, in seventh position; Chizoba Okorie, whose Ndụ B’anyi N’Oruwo placed eighth; Hon. Esther Ugwuefi, with Onyeze, in ninth position; and Maduekwe MaryJane Chinasa, popularly known as Jane C, whose Okwute Ndigbo Binie placed tenth.

Ten additional entries were selected for consolation prizes of ₦100,000 each. They are APC – Ebe Esere Aziza by Ejike Okonu; Peter Mbah Chant by Shepherdman Iyioku; Peter Mbah Chirụ Gaba by Patience Nnamani; Peter Mbah Makwarụ Ụzọ by Princess Chinwe Nnamoko; Peter Mbah Bụ Onye Nke Anyi, Omeru K’Okwuru by Ijeoma Agbo; Ogbom Eze Kam Kamanụ Gu Oo by Mrs. Martha Chidiebere Ugwu; Peter Mbah Carry Go by Mokwe Kingsley Chidiebere; Onye Ge-eme Enugu State Ka Ọdi Mma Ọzọ? by Stanley Ugwu; Governor Peter Mbah Is Good to Go by Destiny Wonder Kids; and APC, Ebe Esere Aziza, Ka Anyi Zapụ Ụbiam N’Enugu by Hon. Sunday Chinemeze Ezugwu.

The competition, announced in July, was designed to discover and promote home-grown musical talents and encourage creative expressions of the achievements, vision and developmental programmes of the Enugu State Governor, Dr. Peter Ndubuisi Mbah, while mobilising support for his re-election in the February 6, 2027 governorship election.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The entries were assessed on originality, creativity, lyrical content, musical quality, memorability and overall campaign appeal.

The organisers commended all participants for their creativity and enthusiasm, noting that the selected jingles could be deployed for publicity, campaign and mobilisation activities by the organisers and other authorised pro-Peter Mbah and pro-APC support groups, in accordance with the published competition rules.

The competition was jointly coordinated by Dan Nwomeh, Senior Special Assistant to the Governor on Mainstream Media, and Hon. Tony Okonkwo, State Coordinator of the Tomorrow Is Here Movement.

The organisers said the date of the award ceremony would be communicated to all the winners.

World.title: Six players secure scholarships as Ajayi Elebire basketball camp ends
World.content:
The fifth edition of the Ajayi Elebire Elite Basketball Camp ended in Ado Ekiti, Ekiti State, on Friday, with six players securing scholarships and the state’s Commissioner of Police, Michael Falade, praising the organisers for providing opportunities for young people.

The four-day camp, which began with trials in Lagos, brought together more than 40 players selected from across Nigeria to compete for scholarship opportunities and improve their skills under the guidance of coaches from Nigeria and the United States.

The programme ended with an All-Star game at the Ekitikete Pavilion in Ado Ekiti.

Mr Falade, who attended the closing activities, said the initiative could help keep young people away from crime by engaging them in productive activities.

“If you look at the rate of people that are involved in crime, they are youths, and for engaging them in this sport like this, at least you have taken them off the streets,” he said.

“And when somebody is engaged, you can never do otherwise; you have to do the right thing. Secondly, this is providing work because when you have the foundation, then there is no way you can miss it.”

Coaches praise players

Scott Adubato, one of the American coaches invited for the programme and a former coach of the camp organiser, Olalekan Ajayi, said the event gave talented players an opportunity to improve their game.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the coaching team worked with the players throughout the camp, introducing them to different principles of basketball and preparing them for the final game.

“The players were prepared every day. We worked on the training. We did everything we needed to teach them different principles of the game. They were very receptive. They played hard to the last game. And I think they earned everything that they earned, especially the MVP and the All-Star players. So, a thumbs up to the organisers,” he said.

Ajayi recounts journey

Mr Ajayi said the camp was organised in honour of his father, Ajayi Elebire, adding that his own basketball journey began with a similar camp through which he was discovered.

He thanked those who supported the initiative and said it was designed to help talented Nigerian players access opportunities that might otherwise be difficult to find locally.

“Every year we come here, we impact the lives of these Nigerian kids. We have, you know, a lot of talented players; we have five scholarships guaranteed. The sky is the limit. And this is a record call. The NBBF refused to do what they’re supposed to do to get the house in order and do what is good for Nigerians.

“People like me and the rest of them, we’re going to keep coming from America and get these players out of this country. To give them an opportunity that they refuse to provide for them.”

Six players secured automatic scholarships at this year’s camp. They are Ejirinade Neuman, Igwe Ikechukwu, Muiz Salami, Felix Jackson, Destiny Eze and Lucky Anyaorah.

The scholarships are expected to give the selected players opportunities to further develop their basketball careers.

World.title: NDC says 80% of its candidates couldn’t afford nomination forms, blames APC
World.content:
The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has said 80 per cent of its 2027 candidates could not afford the party’s expression of interest forms.

The NDC spokesperson, Osa Director, in a statement on Saturday said the candidates could not afford the party’s forms due to the high level of hunger and poverty in Nigeria.

Mr Director suggested that the inability of the candidates to buy the expression of interest forms affected the NDC’s finances.

He blamed the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) for the hunger and poverty in the country.

“Our finances would have been more robust.

“However, contrary to speculations in the public domain, and due to the level of poverty, hunger and deprivation in the country occasioned by the rudderless APC and its amorphous economic policies, about 80% of our candidates could not afford the Expression of Interest forms,” he said.

“The party had to issue forms to such candidates free of charge.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The spokesperson, however, did not identify the NDC candidates who were given the forms “free of charge.”

Presentation of NDC account

Mr Director said the NDC’s National Treasurer, John Odey, would release and present the party’s statement of account on Monday.

“This is in deference to our avowed commitment to the principles of transparency and accountability.

“In this regard, we challenge other political parties, especially the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), to emulate this level of openness and transparency in the management of their finances,” he said.

The spokesperson said the statement of account would be presented during the NDC’s Third National Executive Committee (NEC) meeting in Abuja.

He said the NDC would use the opportunity of the NEC meeting to unveil its National Campaign Council (NCC).

“As a party of innovation, our NCC is all-encompassing. It covers the Presidential, National Assembly, Governorship, and State Houses of Assembly Campaign Councils.

“Our various candidates will be presented with Certificates of Return for their respective offices,” he said.

“The NDC is turbo-charged and ready to give Nigerians the altruistic leadership the nation deserves.”

APC silent

Felix Morka, the national APC spokesperson, did not respond to calls and a text message seeking his response to the allegations that the party was responsible for hunger and poverty in Nigeria.

World.title: Tinubu blames opposition for hunger, poverty in Nigeria, Atiku kicks, says president delusional
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has accused opposition politicians of causing the hunger and poverty Nigerians are experiencing, insisting that his administration is working to address the problems as he formally launched his 2027 presidential campaign in Kaduna on Saturday.

Mr Tinubu made the remarks at the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign flag-off at Ranchers Bees Stadium (also known as Kaduna Township Stadium), ahead of the 2027 general elections.

“I have heard the opposition talking about hunger and poverty. Who caused them? They did! They caused hunger and poverty. We are trying to eliminate them,” the president said.

He also urged his supporters to be wary of statements from the opposition, particularly criticism of his decision to remove the petrol subsidy, insisting that the country would not return to the previous system.

“Be careful; watch them. Don’t let them lie to you. What is past is in the past.

“Fuel subsidy is in our past: no more corruption, no more falsification of invoices, no more lies, no more smuggling of fuel,” Mr Tinubu told supporters at the rally.

The president’s remarks come amid persistent public concerns over high food prices, inflation and declining purchasing power, issues expected to feature prominently in political debates ahead of the 2027 elections.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In a swift reaction to the president’s remarks, the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, described President Tinubu’s claim “as a delusional, shameless attempt to dodge responsibility for the misery his own government has inflicted on Nigerians.”

He said a president cannot light the fire of hardship with his own policies, then blame the neighbours for the smoke.

Tinubu defends petrol subsidy removal

Since assuming office in May 2023, the Tinubu administration has implemented major economic reforms, including the removal of the petrol subsidy and changes to the foreign exchange regime.

The government has defended the measures as necessary to reduce public expenditure, tackle alleged corruption associated with the subsidy system and establish the foundations for sustainable economic growth.

While Mr Tinubu insists that the removal of the subsidy is irreversible, critics continue to demand evidence that the savings and additional revenue generated by the reforms are translating into improved living conditions for ordinary Nigerians.

At the rally, the president also said salaries were being paid on time and praised APC governors for their development projects.

Tinubu thanks Kaduna residents

At the rally, Mr Tinubu thanked the people of Kaduna State for supporting him in the 2023 presidential election, saying their backing contributed to his victory.

“You gave me the joy of remembering the victory you gave me to become president. I have returned to thank you once again,” he said.

He urged Nigerians to give him another opportunity in 2027, promising to continue pursuing his agenda of prosperity, development and national growth.

Tinubu has a long history of supporting the North – VP Shettima

Vice President Kashim Shettima defended Mr Tinubu’s political relationship with northern Nigeria, saying the president had supported politicians from the region for years, including those who contested the presidency in previous elections.

Mr Shettima cited Mr Tinubu’s political relationships with former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and the late President Muhammadu Buhari to argue that the president had consistently supported northern political figures.

“President Bola Tinubu is one person who has fiercely identified with the North over the years. It is pertinent to mention that when former Vice President Atiku Abubakar was harassed and chased off the PDP with his tail between his legs, he ran to the Lion of Bourdillon, who gave him political succour, support and a platform to contest for the presidency of this country in 2007.

“In 2011, Asiwaju supported another northerner, Nuhu Ribadu, and in 2015 and 2019, he supported our late President Muhammadu Buhari,” Mr Shettima said.

The expression, “Lion of Bourdillon,” refers to Mr Tinubu, whose residence on Bourdillon Road in Lagos has become associated with his political influence.

Atiku contested the presidency under the Action Congress (AC) in 2007 after leaving the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), with support from Mr Tinubu and other party leaders.

In 2011, Mr Ribadu contested the presidency under the Action Congress of Nigeria (ACN), a party led by Mr Tinubu. In 2015 and 2019, Mr Tinubu supported Mr Buhari’s presidential bids under the APC.

However, Mr Tinubu and Atiku subsequently became political opponents, particularly during the 2019 and 2023 presidential elections, when the former vice president contested under the PDP while Mr Tinubu was in the APC.

Mr Shettima’s remarks were part of the APC’s effort to highlight Mr Tinubu’s history of political alliances and support for politicians from Northern Nigeria as the party seeks another presidential term for him in 2027.

Top government officials attend the rally

The event attracted senior federal government officials, APC governors and party leaders from different parts of the country.

Those in attendance included Vice President Kashim Shettima and Kaduna State Governor Uba Sani, who received Mr Tinubu upon his arrival in the state.

Secretary to the Government of the Federation George Akume was also among the senior officials at the event. Other attendees included ministers, senators, members of the House of Representatives, APC governors and prominent party figures.

APC National Chairman Nentawe Yilwatda and Abdulaziz Yari, director-general of the party’s presidential campaign council, were among the party leaders involved in preparations for the rally and efforts to mobilise support for Mr Tinubu’s re-election.

The event marked the official launch of the APC’s presidential campaign, as the party seeks to consolidate its support base ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Controversy over the cost of the rally

Meanwhile, the APC campaign rally took place amid controversy over its alleged cost after a letter circulated on social media claimed that the Kaduna State Government had allocated and released ₦2.3 trillion to organise the event.

The state government rejected the allegation, describing the purported letter, said to have been written by Governor Sani to Mr Yari, the director-general of the Tinubu presidential campaign council, as fake.

The Kaduna State Commissioner for Information and Culture, Ahmed Maiyaki, said the governor did not write the letter and had not authorised the alleged release of funds.

The government also pointed out that Kaduna State’s 2026 budget stood at ₦985.92 billion, substantially below the ₦2.3 trillion allegedly spent on the rally.

The APC Presidential Campaign Council also dismissed the allegation, describing it as fabricated information intended to discredit Mr Tinubu, Governor Sani and other party leaders.

Dele Alake, a spokesperson for the campaign council, accused Atiku and the ADC of being involved in the circulation of what he described as false information; an allegation the ADC denied.

Atiku says Tinubu’s claim delusional, shameless

Meanwhile, in a statement by the Director of Strategic Communication, ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Phrank Shaibu, Atiku described President Tinubu’s claim that the opposition created hunger and poverty “as a delusional, shameless attempt to dodge responsibility for the misery his own government has inflicted on Nigerians.”

The former VP said a president cannot light the fire of hardship with his own policies, then blame the neighbours for the smoke.

“Mr President, blaming the opposition for hunger is either delusion or a staggering case of political amnesia. The APC governed Nigeria for eight years before you took office. You have added another three and a half years. Nigerians know who has been in power, and hardship did not begin when the opposition started talking about it. Stop insulting their intelligence and answer for your record.

“The hardship your administration has brought upon Nigerians is real. You cannot deny it by blaming others.”

Atiku listed some of the policies of the Tinubu administration that he said have impoverished Nigerians.

“Which administration removed the petrol subsidy and watched the naira fall from about ₦471 to ₦1,329 to the dollar?

“Which administration has presided over a rise in poverty that led the World Bank to estimate that 63 per cent of Nigerians will be below the national poverty line in 2026? Which administration extended the 2024 budget into 2025 while also operating a separate 2025 budget?

“Which administration recorded ₦7.13 trillion under ‘energy security’ in 2024 and faces questions over ₦11.2 trillion in NNPC pipeline related spending? Nigerians deserve to know who received these sums and what was delivered.

“Which administration must explain the $12.4 billion gap flagged in Nigeria’s external accounts for the first half of 2026? Which administration paid $22.5 million in ‘other charges’ on the Abu Dhabi financing facility?

“Which administration is responsible for the killings, kidnappings and displacement that continue to terrorise communities? These are the questions Nigerians are asking while your government blames the opposition.

“You cannot govern for three years, make life harder, and then blame others for describing the hardship. You asked who created the hunger. Nigerians are asking what you have done to end it.

“The people will judge your government by the lives they are living, not by the excuses you offer at campaign rallies.

The ADC flagbearer said the decision of the president to commission the unfinished Abuja-Kaduna Expressway from the venue of the APC campaign rally showed how far he had been removed from reality.

“Your decision to commission the unfinished Abuja to Kaduna Expressway from inside a stadium shows how far removed you are from the daily reality of Nigerians. A road cannot be completed with a speech or a ribbon cutting ceremony,” he said.

Atiku stated that the 16 January election would be a referendum on President Tinubu’s record.

“The 2027 presidential election will be a referendum on your record. Nigerians have felt the cost of your leadership in their homes, markets and communities. Their verdict is already clear: they have rejected your administration,” Mr Shaibu wrote.

World.title: Fasoranti’s Death: Why reconciliation in Afenifere will be difficult — Okurounmu, ex-Secretary
World.content:
•Group’s future uncertain —Mogaji Adejumo

By Dapo Akinrefon

Tongues across the country are wagging over a possible leadership crisis within the once formidable pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, Afenifere, especially with the demise of its leader, Pa Reuben Fasoranti.

Fasoranti died on Tuesday at the age of 100 years.

Before his death, the Yoruba group had been engulfed in leadership crisis.

It is instructive to note that Afenifere hinges on a traditional, non-competitive succession process to choose its next leader.

However, the body faces the critical task of unifying its historically fractured factions.

While the old guards like Chief Olu Falae express hope that a new leader will emerge seamlessly through ancestral custom, key insiders paint a much bleaker picture of the group’s future.

How division set in

In 2023, its then Acting Leader, late Pa Ayo Adebanjo, rocked the boat by suspending two of its officials, the National Publicity Secretary, Jare Ajayi and National Organising Committee, Abagun Kole Omololu.

The suspension, however, led to a split and worsened the crisis.

Both officials were removed from office and subsequently suspended for alleged uncouth activities and issuance of unauthorised statements, as well as constant denigration of the organisation.

Recall that in November 2022, the late Afenifere leader, Pa Fasoranti, insisted that he remained the leader of the group.

This was after he had named his deputy, late Pa Ayo Adebanjo, as the leader of the organization.

Pa Adebanjo, who was taken aback over Fasoranti’s suddenly change of mind, had alleged that there was an attempt to split the organisation.

Observers of events in the polity were of the view that he was not far from the truth.

The split, however became a reality.

It was as a result of the fact that during the 2023 electioneering campaign, then candidate of the All Progressives Congress, APC, Asiwaju Bola Tinubu had visited Pa Fasoranti in Akure, where the former Lagos State governor was endorsed.

The decision did not sit well with the Adebanjo group.

How Fasoranti stepped down in 2021

It will be recalled that in March 2021, Pa Fasoranti stepped down as Afenifere leader, citing old age.

While Adebanjo had endorsed Peter Obi, who was presidential candidate of the Labour Party, LP, the Fasoranti group, threw its weight behind Tinubu.

Fasoranti had named the deputy leader, Chief Ayo Adebanjo, as the acting national leader of the group, while the former financial secretary, Oba Oladipo Olaitan, the Alaago of Kajola Ago in Atakumosa East Council Area, Ilesa, Osun State, was named the group’s deputy leader.

Fasoranti had said: “The development became necessary as the group needs, more than ever before, to have an improved organisation with a more effective approach to combat the monstrous invasion of our culture and pride as a people.

“Only a more alike and active leadership can achieve this. At 95 I am hardly able to provide such and so it is time for me to step aside.

“At this junction, I am proud to announce Chief Ayo Adebanjo, a politician of the Awolowo school of thought, as Acting leader of Afenifere and Oba Oladipo Olaitan, the Alaago of Kajola Ago in Atakumosa East Local Government Area, as the Deputy Leader.”

The late Afenifere leader, in a viral video had claimed: “I am still the leader of Afenifere. Afenifere has not endorsed Obi, we are endorsing Jagaban (Bola Tinubu) for the presidency.

“You can see the trend, the approval and the acceptability. You could see what happened when Tinubu came to meet me in Akure. The media carried the whole thing.

“Adebanjo cannot warn me not to welcome Tinubu. Can he do that successfully?

“What happened was that Adebanjo took a stand and I took a stand. I didn’t call him and he didn’t call me. We never spoke about the visit.

“As you can see, Jagaban is accepted and we approve of him. Obi has no stand in our mind at all.”

Adebanjo counters Fasoranti

But in a swift reaction, Ayo Adebanjo, known to be a staunch Awoist, faulted Tinubu’s visit to Pa Fasoranti, saying the comments trailing it were aimed at dividing the group.

Adebanjo, who earlier endorsed Peter Obi, said: “Nothing is going on other than an attempt to split Afenifere to which I will not be a party.

“It is a sort of conspiracy among those who want to see Afenifere divided. They have been on this plan for over a month ago and my members came to me to alert me about it and I said, ‘Don’t talk about it. It would be a diversion. All we want now is an election on issues.”

He said Pa Fasoranti had called to inform him about Tinubu’s planned visit adding that the former Afenifere leader was initially not open to receiving the APC candidate but he persuaded him to do so.

Adebanjo had said: “I will tell you the story and I won’t go further. Pa Fasoranti phoned me on Friday that Tinubu had phoned him and that he wanted to come and see him and he wanted to say no. I said no, don’t do that, you are an elder statesman. If he wanted to see you, why not?

“As far as he is concerned, Obi’s endorsement is based on the principles of equity as the South-East has not produced a president since the return of democracy in 1999. Since the South-West and South-South have produced the president, he said it is the turn of the South-East.

“South-South has had its own and I said it is remaining the South-East.”

Adebanjo died and the once formidable Yoruba body became polarized.

But with Fasoranti’s death, both camps are still laying claim to the leadership of the group.

Falae speaks

However, a former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, SGF, Chief Olu Falae, dismissed concerns about a possible succession struggle in Afenifere, saying the pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation has a tradition of producing leaders without contests or internal fights.

Falae, who is now a monarch, rules out the possible division within the Yoruba fold.

He said Afenifere was a self-perpetuating and self-regulating organisation in which leadership emerged through an established process rather than through competition for positions.

“Leadership chooses itself. A new leader will emerge without any struggle.

“It is obvious who the next leader will be, and I hope and pray it will be so this time,” he said.

Is reconciliation a tall order?

Vanguard was reliably informed that before Fasoranti’s death, there was underground moves to bring all Afenifere member under one roof.

For instance, it Chief Sola Ebiseni, who was the General Secretary of the Adebanjo camp, had crossed over the Fasoranti camp.

A senior Afenifere leader had confided in Vanguard that the reconciliation was to be unveiled immediately after the 2027 general elections.

However, with Fasoranti’s demise, this may be turn out to be difficult to achieve.

‘No light at the end of tunnel’

Providing his perspective on the crisis and possible reconciliation, a former National Secretary of the Yoruba body, Senator Femi Okurounmu, said he does not see light at the end of the tunnel as far as reconciliation in Afenifere is concerned.

Okurounmu, a former Senator from 1999-2003, said though it was too early to talk or reuniting the group, the two factions cannot be reconciled.

In a chat with Vanguard, the former lawmaker said: “You see, it is difficult. Things are difficult. It is very difficult to unite the two groups. The Akure group supports Tinubu. You cannot criticise Tinubu in the presence of the Akure group.”

Speaking further, he said: “Everything Tinubu does must be supported. That is the philosophy of the Akure group.

“The Adebanjo group is very critical of Tinubu. That is an irreconcilable difference, and that is why the two groups cannot be reconciled.”

Origin of crisis – Adejumo

Giving his perspective on the crisis in Afenifere, Mogaji Gboyega Adejumo, a former Public Relations Officer of the body, traces the origin of the crisis.

Adejumo, who is also the Gbonka Aare-Ona Kakanfo, said Afenifere’s future remains uncertain.

Tracing the origin of the crisis within the fold, he said: “What happens to Afenifere after the departure of Pa Fasoranti? All I can say is that Afenifere lost its glory some time back. Perhaps it is as long ago as 2008, and I will explain. The momentum of the Afenifere as at the moment that the June 12 episode became a national movement, which Afenifere spearheaded by forming NADECO, the ascendancy of Afenifere was assured.

“So it wasn’t in any way surprised that in 1999 Afenifere formed the Alliance for Democracy, AD, and the AD was able to sweep at least, all the southwest states. But that momentum faltered in 2003 due to so many reasons.

“However, in 2008, when Pa Abraham Adesanya, who was not only Afenifere leader, but the leader of the Yoruba, that was proclaimed by every Yoruba group, apart from the fact that Afenifere leaders have always been known as Yoruba leaders, but Pa Adesanya enjoyed that, which was the spoken word of every other group appointing him as Yoruba leader.

“So Pa Adesanya had suffered a stroke, and he felt it was time to anoint a new leader. As at that time, the foremost leaders were Pa Ayo Adebanjo, who actually started with them in 1951, and then there was Sir Olaniyun Ajayi, and the whole idea was Pa Adesanya asking the two of them to choose one among themselves.

“So that he can then proclaim the choice of the two of them as the new leader. But Pa Adebanjo felt that, as at that time, Pa Adesanya, who was an Ijebu kan, who took over from Pa Adekunle Ajasin, who was from Owo in Ondo

“And it just happened, there was nothing like Ijebu mafia, it just happened that Pa Ajasin and Pa Adesanya, and the mightier than the image of just a knighted man, somebody that was well loved, that is Sir Olaniyun Ajayi, they were all Ijebu; at least to that effect we could say that Pa Olaniyun Ajayi too, from Remo, is Ijebu.”

How Fasoranti took over from Adesanya

Mogaji Adejumo also spoke on how Fasoranti emerged of Afenifere and how the late Adebanjo convinced Adesanya to make him (Fasoranti) the leader of the group.

He said: “So Pa Adesanya felt another Ijebu man to succeed Pa Adesanya might look like a reality, perhaps an accentuation of the idea that there was an Ijebu mafia. So he now suggested that Papa Fasoranti should be the new leader. Pa Adesanya didn’t quite even remember who Papa Fasoranti was.

“Papa Fasoranti was the Commissioner for Finance during the time of Papa Ajasin as Governor of Ondo State, but he was not a member of the caucus of the Afenifere, and neither was he a participant in the struggle that followed after the June 12 1993 election, in which case Papa Fasoranti was not part of the Afenifere that fought for this democracy. He had more or less like retired from politics. So it was hard for Papa Adesanya to even remember him, let alone see him as the right kind of person.

“But Papa Adebanjo went on to convince him that he is a very cool-headed man, and after all that happened between 2003 and 2008, quite a lot happened, because the Governor of Ondo State then, who campaigned on the platform of the AD in 2023, broke away and the Afenifere went into some serious crisis. It started from 2001 when Uncle Bola Ige died, mysteriously and unexpectedly. So what Papa Adesanya felt was that we needed a user-friendly leader, very cool and unassuming, somebody who will be able to pull everybody together, and they will support him.

“And besides, he was older, joined the Afenifere in 1953 as what they called the Action Group Mosquito. As at that time, he was a student in the university, so he was recruited by Papa Adesanya himself. Anyway, that was how Papa Fasoranti was made the leader of the Afenifere, which eked Asiwaju Bola Tinubu, who was not even part of the Afenifere at that time, but had some influence here and there. There was even this Afenifere Renewal that had his signature all over it, but yet he was still interested in the leadership of the Afenifere.

So, he went ahead and announced the late Senator Ayo Fasanmi as the leader, as against Papa Fasoranti.

“And all of that happened. Papa Fasoranti, for about a year or more, was not even holding the Afenifere meeting at Akure.

“In the tradition of the Afenifere, the leader becomes the rallying point, and meetings would be held in the leader’s house, and which means everybody should go to Akure.

“Well, they started even at Ijebu Igbo for a while, and moved to the home of Sir Olaniyun Ajayi.

“So it was, I should think, I should think, Professor Bolaji Akinyemi, who even suggested that, look, the leader is Papa Fashononji, and his home is Akure, why should we be having the meeting here? So somehow, that sank in, and then the meetings now moved to Akure. But in the true sense of it, Afenifere leadership has always been very energetic, very eloquent, and ready to engage anyone intellectually and forcefully to work on principles. And Papa Ajayi too was like that.

“He gave late Sani Abacha some serious trouble, and even when he died, Abacha wouldn’t just have someone to come and preach. So it was Papa Ajayi who formed NADECO. And then Papa Adesanya, oh, well, a lawyer of note, he represented Papa Obafemi Awolowo everywhere.

“And then, of course, he was a Senator in the Second Republic. He was yet in the same mould of the kind of leaders Afenifere have been able to produce. So he was just like Obafemi Awolowo and Papa Ajayi.

“But by nature, his passion was not that kind of a Afenifere ready to fight, ready to carry the placard, ready to engage any one kind of leader. So that, again, would make the Afenifer to be a bit vulnerable and not to be as forceful, as pushful as Afenifere has been known to be. And sometime in 2015, Papa Ajayi actually wrote a letter and said he was resigning.

“He didn’t want to carry on again as the leader of Afenifere. He was overwhelmed, really. The opposition came from everywhere and just couldn’t handle it.

“And you won’t blame him because some are made very strong, some are mild-mannered. And he’s one of those mild-mannered, never-really-wanting-to-cause-any-trouble kind of gentlemen. So, but it was Pa Ayo Adebanjo again who said, no, you can’t just leave.

“You won’t just succumb to pressure. Those who want Afenifere to die will really be happy if you suddenly just up and left. So he convinced him to stay on.”

Afenifere’s rebirth under Fasoranti

“And, yes, Afenifere went through some rebirth under Papa Fasoranti. He started to attract new members, too, and started to evolve as yet an offshoot of the original Action Group. They became involved in the 2019 elections.

“From the 2015 elections, when Afenifere fully supported former President Goodluck Jonathan. Don’t forget that in 2014, there was the CONFAB organised by the Jonathan administration, which Afenifere had every signature of theirs in the preparation, the setting up, and even the exercise of having a conference of that nature happen.

“Afenifere was there. It was well put together. That is, the framework was put together by Dr. Femi Okurounmu of Afenifere.

“And co-chaired, well, Professor Bolaji Akinyemi was once a very active Afenifere member, was one of the co-chairs. So Afenifere rebirth, or let me say renewal and renaissance took place even at that time. Because when Afenifere had all the governors, yes, Afenifere was very solid.

“But from 2005 to 2013, those were very trying years for Afenifere. But Afenifere was good to come together again. And in 2017, Baba Adebanjo called everybody and said, everything we said would happen with Buhari have started to manifest.

“So what do we do? So Afenifere, by our tradition and principles and all that, is seen as a national movement. But then national movement with a particular principle, the Awolowo principle, which is so difficult for just anyone to pick up. So we decided we’ll pull in other Yoruba groups.

“And many groups showed up, maybe about 70 or so, but 42 were chosen. And then we launched the Yoruba Summit Group. And that was how we came by the Yoruba Declaration of 2017.

“I was made the National Policy Secretary of the Yoruba Summit Group. And that was when we even invited every other group in the Middle Belt Forum from the Southeast, the Ohanaeze Ndigbo, and from the South-South, the PANDEF. And we came together and formed the Southern Middle Belt Leaders Forum, SMBLF.

“So all of this happened during the time Baba Fasoranti himself was thinking of, well, resigning. But he was buoyed, he was kept on by Baba Adebanjo and a few others, Chief Supo Shonibare and the rest, that, no, you go on. We will continue to fight.

So all of this happened during Baba Fasoranti’s time. And in 2021, that was when the, would I say it was just some kind of innuendo, some, well, I wouldn’t know where it came from, that Baba was going senile.

“And he moved against those who wanted to take an advantage of what they felt would make Anthony Ferry’s leadership come their way. So that was when Baba Fasoranti now decided, look, it’s time for me to truly bow out. And he made Baba Adebanjo the acting leader.

“I wouldn’t know what exactly that meant. And then see Oba Oladipo as the deputy leader.”

Vanguard News

World.title: Oil Spill in Delta: When environment is destroyed from within and without – black tide ‘swallows 216 communities’
World.content:
By Egufe Yafugborhi

The water at Odidi struggles to flow. It sits, thick, black, and dead. For seven months, the 28-inch Trans-Forcados Pipeline at the Kantu-Odidi axis, Warri South-West LGA has bled crude and associated gas into the creeks.

What was sighted February 19, 2026 as a single rupture has become a black tide that has swallowed over 216 communities, according to their leaders.

This is no longer just an oil spill. It is a war of narratives about who is destroying the Niger Delta — from within, or from without?

On one side, the Joint Investigation Visit, JIV, of February 20-21, 2026, conducted by the National Oil Spill Detection and Response Agency, NOSDRA, officials and community representatives, gave a technical verdict: Corrosion and equipment failure. No sabotage.

On the other side, voices from inside the Niger Delta say the truth is more uncomfortable.

That Odidi has been a hub of illegal bunkering for 25 years and that hot-taps have turned the pipeline into Swiss cheese.

Between those two truths, the environment dies.

Seven months of nothing

Odidi Federated Community is angry because containment has been a theatre.

Comrade Justin Gbenekama, Chairman of the community, narrated: “This spill occurred on the 19th of February 2026, and up to this moment as we speak, the operator, Heritage Energy Operational Services, HEOSL, has not done anything properly to contain the spill.

“As you can see within the environment, even their recovery activities is not effective.”

He measured the scale of tidal spill: “And so six hours flow from this point, you get to Escravos area. And where we are standing is just five minutes drive to Forcados River, 10 minutes to the Escravos Bar. So the spill has spread very far.”

For the people, the consequences are immediate.

Drinking water is contaminated with hydrocarbons.

Fishing and farming are dead.

Cooking is a risk.

Gbenekama added: “And most importantly, there is no medical attention to any of the affected communities. And even relief materials that were brought were not adequate.”

He called the recovery method futile: “They will scoop, take it (spilled crude) back to their station in Isoko and inject it back to the same line, and the oil here will still come out in this point. That is an exercise in futility.”

His demand: “There should be immediate shutdown of the Trans-Forcados Pipeline and carry out the complete repair before operation will commence.”

It is a demand backed by law. Because the JIV ruled out third-party interference, HEOSL bears absolute liability under Nigerian environmental law.

The operator must fund 100 percent of clean-up and compensation.

And the Federal High Court in Port Harcourt, in Suit No. FHC/PH/CS/132/2026, HRM Udogri Isaac I v. Heritage Energy & NOSDRA, ordered a mandatory injunction to cease discharge and clean up all impacted ecosystems.

No more business as usual

Ijaw Youth Council, IYC, says it has had enough. Its President, Dr. Doubra Collins Okotete, led youths to threaten total shutdown of OML 42, OML 30 and the Forcados Terminal.

“Today we are here not for jokes, but to shut down the operations of the Heritage Oil and Gas Services. This spill has been on for over seven months. The operators of Heritage are heartless, wicked,” Okotete declared.

He dismissed the sabotage argument: “This is not sabotage. This is pure equipment failure. And we all know this oil activity has been going on for a very long time.

“And this pipeline has been damaged for over six, seven months, yet no tangible has been done.”

He alleged: “All they do is to employ contractors to come and curtail oil, yet the contractors they have employed could not contain this oil because, what as the community chairman said, they come here scoop the oil, take it back to their station, inject it back to the same Trans-Forcados Pipeline, and this oil keep popping out, destroying our ecosystem, creating health hazard for our people.”

Okotete linked Odidi to the wider Niger Delta crisis, including Bille in Rivers State:

“The same thing is happening to Alakiri, Rivers State, same thing that happening to Bille, Rivers State, and other communities across the Ijaw nation that are being threatened, that today life expectancy has dropped.”

His message to Abuja was blunt: “President Tinubu, you are the President and Commander-in-Chief of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. The Minister, Senator Heineken Lokpobiri, this is under your watch and today our river has been bastardized.”

And to the companies: “If they are tired of exploiting our oil, they should leave our environment.”

Uncomfortable truth from within

But long-time environmental monitor and Coordinator, Niger Delta Peace Coalition (NDPC), Zik Gbemre, offers a counter-punch that many in the creeks do not want to hear.

He said Odidi’s black tide is also self-inflicted.

“The Odidi axis in OML 42 has served as an active hub for illegal bunkering for over 25 years. What is happening there today is not a new development”, Gbemre said.

“The ongoing environmental degradation is largely artificial and directly tied to pipeline sabotage.

“Even after comprehensive cleaning and proper remediation, fresh spills reoccur within days because the root cause remains unchecked.”

According to him, the pipeline is being killed by repeated hot-taps: “What is unfolding across the Odidi and Egwa fields is the direct impact of illegal bunkering operations.

“Repeatedly placing hot taps on the same pipeline segments severely compromises structural integrity over time.

“Even when damaged points are clamped and repaired, the weakened metal around the hot taps continues to deteriorate, making future leaks inevitable.”

Gbemre, who has flown with Shell’s spill team over Odidi, said complicity is local:

“A total stranger cannot enter a community, transport heavy equipment, and place hot taps on high-pressure pipelines without the knowledge, authorization, or passive approval of host community leaders and influential actors.”

He listed it clearly: “Illegal bunkerers: Physical installation of hot taps, line breaching, and crude siphoning. Host Community leaders: Granting access, and providing cover.”

His warning is moral: “You cannot destroy infrastructure, profit from illegal trade, and present yourself purely as an innocent victim.

“You cannot demand millions in cleanup funds while harboring the very individuals who will re-break the pipes tomorrow.”

He also punctured the IYC claim that surveillance by Tantita and others has ended vandalism:

“It’s funny to hear the IYC boss claiming ‘no more vandalism in the operations space because TANTITA and other surveillance contractors are securing the space.

“That is joke of the year and media gymnastics to justify sustenance of the multi-thrillion naira surveillance contracts. Oil theft still thrives.”

Both sides in order

Media consultant and Coordinator, Journalists for Just Development of the Niger Delta, Austine Aghomi, says both narratives must be held together to understand the ticking bomb.

“Yes, NOSDRA is bound to do its work without bias when there are eventualities, just as oil and gas operators need to take responsibility on routine maintenance of their assets, particularly ageing pipeline from failure,” Aghomi said.

He added: “What is equally concerning, however, is the realisation that unrestrained assets vandalism, particularly tapping into oil wellheads, flowlines and pipelines to steal crude oil now helps to hasten the ageing of pipelines beyond manufacturers’ set lifespan.

“The lines suffer repeated cuts from oil thieves. Over time, assets operators get overwhelmed by repeated repairs and ultimately forced replacement earlier than normal.”

Heritage Energy, through its Community Relations Manager Jeremiah Oharisi, told protesting women: “Heritage is more than willing to do the right thing.” But trust is gone.

The pipeline is 50, its life was 25

The hard fact remains. Most trunklines in the Niger Delta, including Trans-Forcados, were laid in the 1970s with a 20-25-year design life. They have done double that, battered by corrosion outside and hot-taps inside.

Whether the cause is rust or bunkering, the effect is the same: Odidi is dying. And if Odidi is not clamped permanently, if Bille’s gas leaks are not stopped, if the Trans-Forcados is not replaced, the black tide will come to the next community.

The environment is being destroyed from without by ageing assets and corporate negligence. And it is being destroyed from within by an illegal economy that feeds on the same pipes.

Until both are stopped, no clean-up will be final.

World.title: Ebola in Nigeria: Fears contacts could test positive mount
World.content:
Ali Pate, coordinating minister of health and social welfare

•Prof Tomori asks authorities to prepare •Nigeria’s real test is inside its hospitals •Can health workers count on running water, sanitizer, protective equipment?

By Chioma Obinna

The tap is there. But is there water? The sanitiser dispenser is mounted on the wall. But is it filled? And if a patient walks into a hospital with symptoms that raise suspicion of a dangerous infection, will the health worker attending to that patient have the protective equipment needed to stay safe?

These questions may sound routine. But as Nigeria confronts a confirmed case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease, they go to the heart of a more difficult question: how prepared are the country’s hospitals to prevent another outbreak?

Nigeria has been here before. The 2014 Ebola outbreak tested the country’s ability to detect an imported infection, trace contacts and prevent wider transmission. The COVID-19 pandemic later exposed the importance of hand hygiene, personal protective equipment and infection prevention and control in health facilities.

Emergency measures were introduced. Isolation facilities were established, surveillance was strengthened and health workers were trained to respond to infectious threats.

But what happens when the emergency passes? Do the taps still run? Are protective supplies replenished? Can hospitals still isolate suspected cases safely? And do health workers have the equipment and practical support to implement the precautions they have been trained to observe?

For infectious disease experts, Nigeria’s latest Ebola alert is a reminder that preparedness cannot be measured by emergency announcements alone. It must be evident in the wards, consultation rooms and emergency units where patients first seek care.

One confirmed case, a nationwide test

Nigeria’s latest Ebola alert followed the confirmation of an imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory on October 20, 2026.

According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), the patient, a woman with a recent travel history involving Uganda, developed symptoms on October 7 and sought treatment at a private hospital in Abuja on October 11. Laboratory tests confirmed the infection on October 20.

Authorities identified 44 contacts for monitoring, including people who might have been exposed during the patient’s healthcare visits and travel. The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) activated its incident management system, while surveillance and infection-prevention measures were strengthened.

By October 23, the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Professor Muhammad Ali Pate, said the patient was showing signs of recovery. There was no evidence of community transmission in the information released at that point, although investigations and contact monitoring were continuing.

Genomic analysis also found that the virus detected in Nigeria was genetically related to the strain identified in Kenya’s index case. Pate cautioned that this similarity did not, by itself, establish a direct epidemiological link between the two patients or explain precisely how the infection reached Nigeria.

The response is therefore unfolding on two fronts. Authorities must establish whether anyone else has been infected, while ensuring that hospitals can recognise and safely manage any suspected cases that emerge.

Second responsibility

That second responsibility is particularly important. A patient with fever, headache, vomiting or diarrhoea may have any of several illnesses. But when the symptoms are accompanied by a relevant exposure history, health workers must know what questions to ask, whom to notify and how to protect themselves and others while the patient is assessed.

An outbreak may be detected by a laboratory, but preventing further transmission also depends on what happens at the patient’s first point of contact with the health system.

When the basics cannot be taken for granted

Running water, soap, hand sanitisers, cleaning materials, protective equipment and safe waste disposal rarely command the attention given to emergency operations centres or laboratory testing. Yet these ordinary provisions underpin the safe delivery of healthcare.

A tap without water cannot support handwashing. An empty sanitiser dispenser offers little protection. Personal protective equipment that is missing when needed can leave a health worker unable to follow the precautions required when caring for a suspected infectious case.

The problem is not necessarily that every Nigerian hospital lacks these facilities. It is that their availability, functionality and reliability cannot be assumed.

A UNICEF Nigeria WASH Gender Landscape Analysis published in January 2025 reported that only six per cent of healthcare facilities assessed had basic water, sanitation and hygiene services. The figure relates to the facilities covered by the assessment, rather than every hospital in the country, but it highlights a significant infrastructure challenge.

For Ebola preparedness, the implications are immediate. Infection prevention is not simply a matter of displaying instructions on a hospital wall. It requires dependable water supplies, adequate consumables, appropriate protective equipment, trained staff and systems that ensure these resources are available where and when they are needed.

Items to stop virus

The Medical and Dental Consultants’ Association of Nigeria (MDCAN), through its leadership, has called on hospital managements to provide running water, hand sanitisers, infrared thermometers, adequate personal protective equipment, other essential consumables and suitable isolation facilities.

The association has also advocated the reactivation of infection prevention and control committees and emergency drills to test the readiness of healthcare workers.

Its warning is straightforward, doctors and other health workers should not attend to suspected Ebola patients without appropriate protective equipment or manage them in open wards where other patients and staff could be exposed.

These are not special provisions to be considered only when Ebola appears. They are basic requirements for a health system expected to manage infectious diseases safely.

Training is not enough

The Federal Government had announced that it is strengthening detection, laboratory capacity, case management and public communication as part of the response.

“All hospitals should be sensitised and health workers be aware and, when there are suspected cases, to notify public health authorities,” Pate said.

The government has also announced plans to reinforce infection prevention and control protocols and train health workers to identify suspected cases, protect themselves and notify the relevant authorities promptly.

But experts say training alone cannot make a hospital ready. A health worker may understand the correct procedure and still be unable to follow it if protective equipment is unavailable, water is unreliable or there is no appropriate space to isolate a suspected patient.

In an interview with Sunday Vanguard, Professor Dimie Ogoina, a professor of medicine and infectious diseases at Bayelsa Medical University, stressed the need to equip health workers with both the knowledge and resources required to prevent transmission.

He warned that an imported case could lead to further spread if contacts became infected and passed the virus to others before preventive measures were put in place. Transmission could also occur during hospital visits or care if appropriate infection prevention and control measures were not observed.

“Supporting healthcare workers in adhering to IPC through training and the provision of IPC resources will help promote the adoption of these measures,” he said.

For Ogoina, the priority is to ensure that the country’s emergency response translates into practical readiness at federal and state levels.

He called for active case searches, effective contact tracing, prompt laboratory diagnosis, clear referral arrangements and suitable isolation facilities for suspected and confirmed cases. He also advocated the advance provision of infection-control supplies and the training and deployment of designated healthcare workers to manage such cases.

The point is not merely to have a protocol. It is to make sure that staff can carry it out when the need arises.

Finding the next case before it spreads

Contact tracing is one of the most important parts of an outbreak response, but identifying contacts is only the beginning.

Those identified must be followed up, symptoms monitored and any suspected infection investigated promptly. Laboratories must be able to process samples and return results in time to inform clinical decisions. Hospitals, in turn, need clear procedures for referral, isolation and communication with public health authorities.

Ogoina said Nigeria had taken proactive steps following the imported case, including identifying contacts for follow-up and sequencing the virus. He stressed that stronger surveillance and contact tracing would help authorities detect additional infections early and take steps to prevent onward transmission.

He also called for stronger risk communication and community engagement to address anxiety, correct misinformation and encourage cooperation with public health teams.

The response depends on a chain of connected actions: surveillance identifies a possible case; laboratory testing helps establish the diagnosis; hospitals provide safe assessment and isolation; and public health teams trace contacts and communicate appropriate advice.

If one part of that chain fails, the entire effort becomes more difficult.

Ebola is not an airborne infection. It spreads through direct contact with the blood or other body fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated materials. This distinction matters because accurate information can help people understand the risks and follow appropriate precautions without unnecessary panic.

For the public, cooperating with contact tracing, providing accurate exposure histories and seeking medical advice when directed are important parts of the response. Fear, stigma and misinformation can undermine these efforts by discouraging people from reporting symptoms or engaging with health authorities.

Fears

What if more cases emerge?

Renowned virologist and chairman of the West African National Academy of Scientists, Professor Oyewale Tomori, has urged authorities to prepare for the possibility that contacts could test positive.

That is not a prediction that further cases will occur. It is a reminder that emergency planning should not depend on the assumption that the response will remain limited to one patient.

If more infections are identified, hospitals could face simultaneous demands for assessment, testing, isolation and treatment. That would place additional pressure on trained personnel, protective supplies, isolation space and laboratory services, even as contact tracing and surveillance continue.

Tomori has also emphasised the importance of taking travel and exposure histories seriously when patients present with symptoms that could be consistent with Ebola.

The objective is not to treat every fever as Ebola. It is to ensure that health workers consider relevant exposure risks, recognise warning signs and follow established procedures when a suspected case is identified.

Preparedness means anticipating what the health system might need to do next, rather than waiting for additional cases to expose its limitations.

The lessons of 2014 and COVID-19

Nigeria’s experience during the 2014 Ebola outbreak demonstrated the value of rapid detection, coordinated contact tracing and decisive infection-control measures. COVID-19 reinforced the need for reliable hygiene facilities, protective equipment and sustained investment in healthcare preparedness.

But the challenge is preserving those gains after public attention moves elsewhere.

Handwashing stations and sanitiser dispensers are useful only when they work and are replenished. Isolation rooms matter only when they are suitable and available. Guidelines are effective only when staff understand them, practise them and have the resources to follow them.

NCDC Director-General, Dr Jide Idris, has called for renewed attention to environmental control, personal hygiene and handwashing, drawing lessons from Nigeria’s previous experience.

“It’s a contact issue. So, we need to address the issue of environmental control, personal hygiene, hand washing,” Idris said.

MDCAN has also called for stronger surveillance at airports, seaports and land borders, alongside the activation of emergency response arrangements and isolation facilities. It has urged authorities to strengthen laboratory capacity, contact tracing and collaboration across borders.

The association’s emphasis on staff welfare is equally significant. Health workers need appropriate equipment, training and practical support, as well as adequate welfare provisions, to carry out their duties safely.

Protecting them is inseparable from protecting patients. A health worker who lacks the means to follow infection-control procedures may face avoidable risks, while a facility unable to isolate a suspected case safely could expose others and complicate the wider response.

The consequences extend beyond Ebola. The same infrastructure and workplace practices are relevant to the safe management of other infectious diseases.

Public assurance

How will Nigerians know containment is working?

Public reassurance is important during an outbreak, but it must be accompanied by credible information about the progress of the response.

Ogoina identified several encouraging indicators: recovery of the index patient, effective identification and follow-up of contacts, prompt investigation and isolation of suspected cases, and adherence to preventive measures by healthcare workers and the public.

These indicators must be considered together. A patient’s recovery is encouraging, but it does not by itself establish that transmission has been interrupted. Authorities must also continue monitoring contacts, investigating symptoms promptly and communicating verified developments.

Regular public updates can help Nigerians understand what is known, what remains under investigation and what steps are being taken. They can also counter rumours before misinformation spreads.

The public, meanwhile, has a role to play by cooperating with health authorities, following official guidance and avoiding the stigmatisation of people who may have been exposed.

The real measure of preparedness

Nigeria has activated its public health response, identified contacts and strengthened surveillance following the confirmed case. The government has also announced measures to improve infection prevention and control and prepare health workers.

But the larger test lies in whether these actions are backed by the everyday capacity of hospitals to recognise suspected cases, isolate patients safely and protect those providing care.

That requires reliable water supplies, hygiene materials, adequate protective equipment, suitable isolation facilities, trained personnel, effective laboratory links and clear reporting procedures. It also requires sustained funding, supervision and accountability long after the immediate emergency has passed.

The experience of 2014 and COVID-19 should have made the importance of these measures unmistakable. The challenge now is to ensure that the lessons have not faded with the crises that brought them into sharp focus.

When a patient with symptoms and a relevant exposure history walks into a hospital, preparedness should not begin with a frantic search for gloves, a check for water or the discovery that an isolation room is unavailable.

It should begin with a system that is ready. For the health worker facing that patient, the difference between knowing what to do and being able to do it may depend on the most basic things in the hospital: clean water, protective equipment, practical training and a safe place to provide care.

For Nigeria, those basics could help determine whether the current Ebola alert remains a contained public health event or becomes a more difficult test of the health system.
