World.title: Man's murder, wife's death feed into local legend of "cursed" mansion
World.content:
The lake country straddling the Kentucky-Tennessee border has a quiet, majestic beauty. But in September 2022, that vast landscape seemed to have swallowed up Mike Harding, a California transplant who disappeared without a trace.

JULIE HARDING (phone call): Hi Captain, this is Julie Harding with the California Highway Patrol …

Mike's wife Julie Harding, a captain with the California Highway Patrol, began to place urgent phone calls to the Kentucky State Police from her home in Sacramento.

JULIE HARDING (phone call): I can't get any information. And I just, I need your help with this … My concern right now … is where he is. Is he OK? … and what's the status of this investigation?

The calls led her to a sheriff she knew — Brandon Boone of Clay County, Tennessee, whose office was spearheading the missing person's case. But the answers were few and far between and Boone says Julie Harding grew frustrated.

Sheriff Brandon Boone: She got very angry with a couple of — of my people, uh, because we wouldn't disclose certain information to her …

Within days, Julie was there in person on Sheriff Boone's doorstep.

JULIE HARDING (bodycam): Hi.

SHERIFF BRANDON BOONE: How are ya?

JULIE HARDING: I'm good, how are you? Well …

Bodycam video of Julie Harding with Clay County, Tennessee, Sheriff Brandon Boone. Clay County Sheriff's Office

In a moment recorded on a body camera, she immediately apologized for being rude.

JULIE HARDING (bodycam): Let me first apologize. My tone was inappropriate I was very irritated, umm, and I should have been more calm. My assumptions, umm, and my emotions in this, umm, killed my reasonableness so I apologize for how we spoke the other day.

OFFICER: Yes ma'am.

JULIE HARDING: OK. So, from now on, I, I hope it's calm. I hope it's cooperative. Umm, because all I want is Mike to come back in and go … I was in wherever fishing.

Boone sent her to a sheriff in Kentucky who had taken over the investigation.

SHERIFF BRANDON BOONE (bodycam): Cumberland County Sheriff's Office has called us. They need you there.

JULIE HARDING: OK.

SHERIFF BRANDON BOONE: That's all I can tell you.

JULIE HARDING: OK.

A grisly discovery

Just hours earlier, David Hammersley and his family were house hunting in nearby Burkesville, Kentucky. They went room to room at a vacant, three-building property — unaware of what lay ahead.

David Hammersley: … the rest of the party had gone to this building here …

Hammersley wandered into the garage and was surprised that there was a large pickup truck parked inside.

Peter Van Sant: The rest of the family has moved on to this cottage. What do you hear from the garage?

David Hammersley: Well, as they're attempting to open the door, I hear this awful screech and, "Oh, it's — it's terrible. There's something dead over here!"

Hammersley says his family figured some sort of animal must have wandered in and never got out. David walked over and stopped just inside the cottage's front door.

David Hammersley: It was over 100 degrees at the time, I believe … and I was just attacked, if you will, by flies. … And the odor was just so overpowering.

The Kentucky property that became a crime scene. CBS News

What he then saw was far worse.

David Hammersley: I saw a man on the floor, his arm outstretched … obviously, dead from gunshot wounds … (sighs) Ah, sorry. … his life is gone under violent circumstances and just left there. It — it — it was devastating.

The dead body was Mike Harding, says prosecutor Ann Marie Gordon Anderson.

Ann Marie Gordon Anderson: It seemed like he had probably been there for a week, from September 19th [to] the 26th.

The Cumberland County Sheriff immediately called in the Kentucky State Police. Detective BJ Burton was assigned to lead the investigation. He learned that Mike Harding had been shot four times, twice in the torso and twice in the head.

Detective BJ Burton: It kind of looks like somebody that wants to be a professional hit man — but is not quite there.

Burton said the killer removed evidence from the scene, including the murder weapon and three shell casings. But the assassin left behind one distinctive shell casing; investigators determined it was from a Hornady Critical Defense bullet.

Back in Sacramento, Mike's son Steven Harding, from Mike's first marriage, was told his father had been murdered.

Peter Van Sant: And can you put into words the horror of this news for you?

Steven Harding: There's really no words for it other than your best friend is gone (crying).

Mike Harding Cleary Family

For Steven's older sister Heather Cavalieri, also from Mike Harding's first marriage, news of their father's murder came from a friend.

Heather Cavalieri: I didn't want to believe it, you know. I loved my dad … So, all of it's just hard … it's been hard. It's been really hard.

At the crime scene, investigators were trying to figure out why Mike was at this seemingly random location. His cellphone was about to shed some light.

Detective BJ Burton: Once you start looking through the text messages and phone calls … it becomes very obvious early on that he was lured to the house.

The phone revealed texts from a realtor named James Fraser. He asked Mike — who owned an HVAC business — to check out the house.

Detective BJ Burton: He thought he was going there for … what he thought was a heating and air service call. … You see the text messages when Michael Harding is on his way there …

Around 4 p.m., Mike Harding texts James Fraser that he is "35 minutes out." Fraser texts, "No worries." Mike asks, "Is that good for you?" and Fraser tells him "Yes." The final exchange Mike texts, "See ya soon." Fraser replies "Perfect."

While those texts gave investigators a solid timeline, the investigation hit a roadblock early on: they could not find a realtor named James Fraser.

Detective BJ Burton: So, it was probably just a made up name.

But they did have some potential leads. When investigators later contacted the phone company of the number used to text Mike Harding, they discovered that number came from a prepaid cellphone used only to arrange Mike's murder.

Detective BJ Burton: It was pretty evident early on that this is a burner phone. …

Peter Van Sant: And for those who don't know, what is a burner phone?

Detective BJ Burton: Somebody … goes and buys a burner phone, they'll put in like John Doe, any town USA just they … think it's untraceable at which to some degree it is.

And remember that pickup Hammersley saw in the garage? Burton said it was Mike Harding's.

Detective BJ Burton: My thought is … whoever murdered him and then pulled the truck in the garage, there's a very good chance that their DNA may also be in the truck.

Burton tried to call Mike's wife, Julie, but she didn't pick up. Burton had been told she was heading his way — to the Cumberland County Sheriff's Office, so he waited there to give her the bad news face to face.

The local legend of the "cursed" mansion

Steven Harding: When you see your hero get taken from you … you know you're not untouchable …

After delivering the devastating news about Mike Harding's death to his children, Detective Burton was desperate to reach Mike's wife Julie, who indicated she was on her way to a local sheriff's office.

Det. BJ Burton: Myself and another detective waited there for some period of time. … She never showed up.

A few days later, Burton located her at a neighbor's house in Celina.

Detective BJ Burton: I introduced myself to her, uh, you know, try to talk to her. …

She referred all questions to her lawyer, which Burton thought was unusual for someone in law enforcement and the spouse of a murder victim.

Detective BJ Burton: She didn't want to talk to me …

Burton and his team began investigating the Harding's personal lives. They learned the two met online in 2018. Julie, 44, and Mike, 48, had both been through divorces. They married in 2019 and within months, Burton says they bought that spectacular house in Celina where they planned to live after retirement.

Mike and Julie Harding Kathleen Rourke/Facebook

Julie's close friend, Kathy Rourke says Julie was over the moon in love with Mike.

Kathy Rourke: She thought she had something that she — she wanted more than anything else … A man to come home to, a man to hug her, to comfort her, to make her feel like a woman.

Kathy Rourke: … she was so proud to be married, she was so proud …

When she turned 50, Julie would be eligible to retire from the California Highway Patrol — an iconic agency known around the world.

Kathy Rourke: Wearing her uniform was the greatest joy in her life.

Detective BJ Burton: I think early on in their marriage … the decision was made … Mike would go ahead and move to the lake house in Celina, Tennessee, so he could get his HVAC service repair business started there.

Julie planned to join Mike full time when she retired. But she was a frequent visitor, and the couple made the house a home, complete with Julie's dog Chippy the Chihuahua and Mike's boxer Charlie.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: The one thing that would always put a smile on Captain Julie Harding's face were her dogs.

Julie and Mike Harding became friendly with the locals — including Sheriff Brandon Boone.

Sheriff Brandon Boone: … uh, very nice couple, talked about couldn't wait to retire to get here full time.

Peter Van Sant: She seemed like a pleasant woman when you met her?

Sheriff Brandon Boone: Yes, she did. Very pleasant … They seemed like a, a wonderful couple together

Mike Harding's children understood how their father felt about Julie but thought he was making a mistake.

Heather Cavalieri: I feel like he was blinded by love. He truly loved her … So, I thought he found his dream girl. But to me personally, I just, I didn't like her.

Cavalieri says Julie Harding was arrogant and made her feel uncomfortable.

Peter Van Sant: Did the two of you ever go out and visit, uh, at the house in Tennessee?

Heather Cavalieri: No, I didn't think that I would be welcome there.

Locals say the Harding's dream home overlooking Dale Hollow Lake was cursed. CBS News

Steven and Heather said they stayed away from the mansion, as did many locals. The house, Boone says, had a reputation for being cursed.

Sheriff Brandon Boone: There was a divorce that happened here that, that got pretty nasty. … We've had calls in the past of uh, gunshots that happened here that later ended up being a murder right in Burkesville. Uh, the gentleman who lived here shot the person up there.

Peter Van Sant: Now, is it true that a realtor actually brought some sort of spiritual person out here to try to purge the evil spirits from the house?

Sheriff Brandon Boone: Yes, that's what the realtor advised me and told me — that he had, he had brought a guy here to uh, get the spirits to go away.

Peter Van Sant: And you're serious?

Sheriff Brandon Boone: I'm serious.

And then there's the legend of Dale Hollow Lake, which was created when the Army Corps of Engineers flooded a small town that became known as "the town that drowned." Even today, the eerie foundations of the long-ago town are visible when the lake is low.

But Mike and Julie Harding ignored all the country rumors. And their long-distance marriage seemed to work.

Preston Cleary: Mike seemed pretty happy. He always bragged on her, how smart she was … he really cared about her. He'd do anything for her.

Sergeant Brian Wittmer worked side by side with Captain Julie Harding for several years.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: They looked like a very cute couple.

But Wittmer said sometime in 2022 he noticed a change in Julie.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: So for the first several years … I had never seen her consume any alcohol.

But then she began drinking.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: … she was going to Napa Valley and having drinks, having wine, going to — to vineyards on weekend trips.

Wittmer said it was almost like someone flipped a switch.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: … she was … hyper. Uh, she would talk a lot. She, um, was anxious.

Mike Harding's friend Preston says that Mike also noticed the stark change in Julie's behavior.

Preston Cleary: Mike was mad because she didn't want to spend time with him …

Mike Harding revealed to Preston that he believed Julie Harding was cheating on him.

Peter Van Sant: Did Mike suspect there was another man in Julie's life?

Preston Cleary: He, he did.

Mike Harding had noticed lingerie purchases in their Amazon account.

Preston Cleary: And she … had no plan to be here to see him.

Those Amazon purchases, coupled with Julie Harding's drinking and the way she avoided spending time with Mike Harding, bruised his ego, Cleary says. But the biggest blow came when Julie told Mike she wanted to postpone her retirement for five years.

Preston Cleary: It was at that moment I seen a shift in their relationship and Mike … he had a different outlook toward her. … He was just crushed that she would choose to work five more years … he's just like, this is, this isn't going to work out.

Preston says Julie Harding filed for divorce in May 2022.

Preston Cleary: He was blinded. …he really, really loved her.

Sheriff Boone says the emotional turmoil took its toll on Mike Harding, who sensed Julie saw him as her enemy.

Peter Van Sant: Did you notice a change in Mike's attitude? Did you notice kind of a paranoia?

Sheriff Brandon Boone: Oh, absolutely.

After a break-in at his home, and fearing for his safety, Mike Harding wrapped chains with a padlock around his patio doors. Clay County Sheriff's Office

Mike Harding told Boone that someone had broken into his house one night while he was sleeping and he reported one of his guns had been stolen. After that, he made it a habit of wrapping chains with a padlock around his patio doors.

Sheriff Brandon Boone: And after seeing the locks and the chains around the door, you really think, whoa, you know, he was, he was afraid of something.

At the same time, Julie told friends and colleagues that she was afraid of Mike and feared he was engaged in some dangerous activities.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: She said that Mike … was potentially dealing ghost guns, drugs … was taking money from her bank accounts.

Mike Harding feared his wife, say family and friends

In May 2022, soon after Julie Harding filed for a divorce, Mike Harding told friends and family that he feared for his safety.

Steven Harding: There was solid steel chains wrapped around my dad's front door and as well as his back doors … he would do that so that no one would come in while he was sleeping. Or if it was Julie, the dogs aren't going to bark if you know the person.

Peter Van Sant: And so you're telling me that your father feared Julie?

Steven Harding: Yes.

Prosecutor Jesse Stockton.

Jesse Stockton: …he told his friends that … If he ever was murdered or disappeared or something nefarious happened to him, that they needed to make sure somebody looked at Julie Harding.

Mike Harding's friend, Preston Cleary, knew Mike also was worried about his savings, and he gave Mike some advice about the pending divorce.

Preston Cleary: … whoever gets to the bank first, you know, that's their money. So, Mike, if you want to be fair, you go take half the money out of the bank. He goes, "no." … He goes, "I'm going to do this in court."

Around the same time, Sgt. Brian Wittmer says Julie Harding called him to announce that she was going to raid the family funds.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: She said that she was driving from Sacramento to Tennessee and she was going to withdraw money from her bank accounts before Mike Harding did.

Mike and Capt. Julie Harding Preston and Crystal Cleary/Cumberland County Justice Center/CHP

At that point, Julie Harding was telling friends that Mike was involved with illegal weapons and narcotics.

Peter Van Sant: Did she think about turning in her own husband if he's selling ghost guns and dealing drugs, for goodness sakes?

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: Well, that's what you would expect from somebody … with her rank and her knowledge. And she would tell me that she had a friend working out in Tennessee law enforcement … that was potentially looking into things.

Peter Van Sant: Were you ever able to confirm that?

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: I was not.

Authorities say there is no evidence Mike Harding sold drugs or ghost guns or was involved in any other type of criminal activity.

Heather Cavalieri: I want people to know that he was a good man, he loved his family and he loved life. Any other narrative you hear is not the real narrative … We want the truth to be told, and that's why we're here.

Not long after telling Cleary he was not going to transfer any money out of the couple's bank accounts, Mike Harding got a call from the bank.

Preston Cleary: The bank … had told him, "Julie Harding was just here, and she cleared out almost all your savings in your accounts" …

Julie Harding reportedly withdrew around $360,000 from various bank accounts, according to what Mike Harding told his divorce attorney. Julie's friend Kathy Rourke says at least part of that money belonged to Julie.

Kathy Rourke: She didn't need his permission.

Peter Van Sant: So she's taking that money to do what with it?

Kathy Rourke: Bring it back here to California … She gave most of the money to her mom 'til she figured out what she was gonna do.

But Mike Harding's son Steven says a lot of that money belonged to his father.

Steven Harding: My dad was a very smart, well-educated man. He was very good with stocks. … He was very good with his finances.

Peter Van Sant: In the days prior to his disappearing, he'd heard all this bad news. Money had been taken … There's no reconciliation coming his way … How did that change him? …

Preston Cleary: It destroyed uh, the friend that I had … there was no more fishing for Mike … Mike was strictly business, trying to rebuild his life and get back to where he was.

Mike Harding Kathy Rourke

And Mike Harding would rely on his HVAC business to rebuild his life — which is why friends say he responded so quickly to the call from the mysterious "James Fraser" asking him for a repair estimate at that empty house in Burkesville, Kentucky. Investigators strongly suspected there was a connection between Fraser and Julie Harding.

Det. BJ Burton: It was obvious that really the only main conflict he had going on in his life was this contentious divorce involving property and money with — with Julie Harding.

Peter Van Sant: In other words, if somebody had a motive, it was her.

Det. BJ Burton: Correct. Yes.

Burton says investigators soon learned that Julie Harding was in California at the time of Mike's murder, but they suspected her just the same.

Det. BJ Burton: She contacted three different people involved in law enforcement during this time frame. And every one of them that she talked to … walked away with a feeling of suspicion that she was involved.

Lacking any cooperation from Julie Harding, Sheriff Boone, warrant in hand, led his armed deputies into the Harding mansion where Julie was staying after Mike's death.

The deputies went room to room looking for clues.

Investigators say taunting notes written by Julie Harding on Post-its were found around the home during their search. Cumberland County Justice Center

No one was home, but the deputies found yellow Post-it notes that investigators say were handwritten by Julie Harding when Mike Harding was still alive. They read: "0 $ Here," "0 $ here either," and "Whatcha lookin 4?"

Detective BJ Burton: So there's these little sticky notes when we did the search warrant down there that would say something like "no money here." "Nope, no money here."

Peter Van Sant: Taunting him.

Det. BJ Burton: Yeah, taunting.

Investigators began executing additional warrants — specifically for the call log of Julie Harding's cellphone in the months before Mike's murder. That's when something caught Burton's eye.

Det. BJ Burton: It jumps out that she's calling this one number, that they're talking almost every single day.

Peter Van Sant: … there were 194 calls made between her number and this other number, correct?

Det. BJ Burton: Yes, yes.

Peter Van Sant: That's a lot of calls.

Det. BJ Burton: Yes.

Investigators traced that number to a man named Thomas O'Donnell, a former car salesman from Houston, Texas. He had recently relocated to the wine country of Napa, California — a place Julie Harding was known to visit.

Did Julie Harding hire a hit man to kill her husband?

After investigators discovered Julie Harding was talking incessantly to a man named Thomas O'Donnell, they explored that connection and learned the two likely met on a dating website that catered to self-described millionaires.

Prosecutor Jesse Stockton: … they had, uh, an extensive and significant relationship. Whether it was romantic or not, I cannot say, but they communicated with each other by phone for months …

For prosecutors Jesse Stockton and Ann Marie Gordon Anderson, the math did not add up. Two months of constant calls — 194 of them — stopped cold only days before Mike Harding was murdered.

Ann Marie Gordon Anderson: I think based on that … can probably speculate that there — there may have been some type of conversation … about what was going to happen.

Peter Van Sant: A conspiracy in other words.

Ann Marie Gordon Anderson: Conspiracy.

Investigators already knew the texts used to lure Mike Harding to his death came from a burner phone. They pulled the phone's locational data from its service provider.

Detective BJ Burton: And the first thing you notice is … the phone is first turned on when it's … in the Houston, Texas … area.

Houston, Texas—Thomas O'Donnell's hometown. To investigators, that was too coincidental to be a coincidence.

Jesse Stockton: I don't think Mister O'Donnell got out here by accident. … The only connection that he had to Michael Harding was through Julie Harding.

Investigators developed a theory that Julie Harding had paid Thomas O'Donnell to kill Mike Harding. And they thought it likely that O'Donnell was the fictional "James Fraser" who had lured Mike to that empty house. The next step in their investigation was securing the call log from O'Donnell's personal cellphone.

Det. BJ Burton: When you start looking at the locational data from his personal phone and comparing it to the locational data with the burner phone, it — it matches up perfectly.

The FBI created maps that showed O'Donnell's phone and the burner phone.

The FBI map shows the prepaid burner phone (red) and Thomas O'Donnell's cellphone (black) were traveling together in the weeks before Mike Harding's murder. Cumberland County Justice Center

Ann Marie Gordon Anderson: … the red on the screen, it is the burner phone, that's what it's showing. Anything that you see that's black, that is Thomas O'Donnell's personal cellphone.

Investigators noted that the two phones were traveling in lockstep through the south in the weeks before Mike Harding's murder.

Peter Van Sant: We know the burner phone is involved in the murder.

Ann Marie Gordon Anderson: That's … it's only purpose.

Background checks showed that, years earlier, O'Donnell had been arrested for stalking a girlfriend. He eventually received probation. But what really struck Detective Burton was how "irresponsible" O'Donnell was with money. He was no millionaire; O'Donnell appeared to be a man desperate for cash, Burton said.

Det. BJ Burton: It seems like his whole life, like he's always just looking for the … next big thing that's going to make him be able to afford the lifestyle that he wants to — to lead …

And Julie Harding, who admitted raiding the couple's bank accounts, was loaded with cash after withdrawing hundreds of thousands of dollars from the couple's bank accounts.

Peter Van Sant: Authorities think she took out that cash so she could pay Thomas O'Donnell to murder Michael.

Kathy Rourke: Absolutely not. That's the most ludicrous thing. That's what kills me about this whole story …

Peter Van Sant: Were you ever able to make a connection from all this cash that she took out and any sort of payment for Thomas O'Donnell?

Det. BJ Burton: No … it's impossible to track. I mean if someone walks up and hands you a stack of cash … it's untraceable …

But it wasn't only money that Julie was after. Investigators say she wasn't leaving Tennessee without Mike's beloved dog Charlie.

Heather Cavalieri: I think she deemed Charlie hers. But that wasn't her dog, that was my dad's dog …

Police say Julie Harding was determined to get the dog back from a friend of Mike's who'd been caring for Charlie since Mike went missing.

Steven Harding: … she knew I wanted the dog after we knew that my dad was dead.

Doorbell camera video shows Julie Harding taking Charlie the boxer from the home of a friend who was caring for the dog after Mike Harding's murder. CBS News

But Julie Harding wasn't in the giving mood, Mike Harding's children say. Some two weeks after Mike's body was found, Julie simply took Charlie for herself. She is captured on a Ring doorbell camera, boldly opening the front door and stealing Charlie from the friend who was taking care of him. Steven says he never saw Charlie again.

Steven Harding: I would have taken that dog in a heartbeat. I just, I feel like it would be better under my hands because I — I am my father. … I — I would have loved it like my dad did. I would protect it.

The friend who cared for the dog wanted to press charges against Julie Harding, but at that point, Burton says the focus was on processing evidence from the murder scene.

Prosecutor Jesse Stockton: … people from the Kentucky State Police lab come to the scene … and then they take a lot of swabs from Michael Harding's truck because they also believe that whoever killed him moved his truck.

Peter Van Sant: Are they able to get a – a usable DNA sample?

Jesse Stockton: Yes …

That sample was found to be consistent with Thomas O'Donnell's DNA.

Det. BJ Burton: So, we got to a point where there was just so much overwhelming locational data coupled with other evidence … where we felt like we had enough to make an arrest …

In early December 2022, two months after Mike Harding's murder, investigators learned that O'Donnell was going to be at the Sacramento airport.

Det. BJ Burton: … most people aren't going to fly or travel without having their phone on them. So, the thought was … we can catch him in the airport … we can also seize his phones at the same time.

A still from video of Thomas O'Donnell's arrest at Sacramento International Airport. Kentucky State Police

Police searched O'Donnell's truck and say they found one of Mike Harding's guns. It was the same gun that had been stolen from Mike's house. Also in the truck was a box of Hornady Critical Defense bullets, the same type of ammunition used in the murder.

Burton says there was not enough evidence to charge Julie Harding with murder but on the same day of O'Donnell's arrest, Julie's dognapping of Charlie came back to bite her. She was arrested and charged with criminal trespass.

Burton was hoping either Julie Harding or O'Donnell would flip on the other, but neither did. O'Donnell was held on the murder charges, while Julie was released on her own recognizance. The next day, Dec. 9, 2022, Julie's superiors at the California Highway Patrol called her in Tennessee to inform her that her status as a peace officer was revoked.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: She's a normal citizen at that point.

Peter Van Sant: Does she have to turn in her badge and her gun?

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: Yes, she would have –

Peter Van Sant: She's disarmed.

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: Correct.

Peter Van Sant: Once she got released, did she give you a call?

Sgt. Brian Wittmer: I did not hear from Captain Julie Harding that evening.

Kathy Rourke: I think she was losing control … I think that anybody that wants to stand in her shoes needs to go and let themselves be booked into jail as a woman and go through what she went through. That broke her in two.

Julie Harding, the once proud captain of her own fate, was alone with her own thoughts in her supposedly cursed home overlooking Dale Hollow Lake.

An eerie fog descends on the supposed "cursed" mansion

It's the morning of Dec. 10, 2022. An armed deputy, wearing a body camera, makes his way toward the Harding house—shrouded in an eerie fog—searching for a potential killer.

DEPUTY (bodycam): Are you the mailman?

DAVID OGLETREE: I am.

Just minutes before, mail carrier David Ogletree and another man had made a tragic discovery — what looked like a body at the base of that distant tree. They called 911.

911 OPERATOR: What's going on honey? DAVID OGLETREE: OK, this, this is David Ogletree, I'm the mailman up here and we may have a body laying up here. 911 OPERATOR: OK … We'll get you someone up there in just a second OK.

Peter Van Sant: Hey David.

David Ogletree: Hello, how are you?

Peter Van Sant: Peter Van Sant, "48 Hours" CBS News. Nice to meet you.

David Ogletree: Nice to meet you.

What Ogletree saw that day is burned into his memory.

David Ogletree: She was, she was laying right up here beside this tree here face down.

Blood can be seen around the woman's body.

DEPUTY (bodycam): Until uh, we get her turned over and see if there's a gun, this could be a murder.

Sheriff Boone arrived at the scene. When investigators rolled the body over, they saw that it was Julie Harding. Her right hand was gripping a gun. An investigator concluded she took her own life.

The blood-stained note found in a bag next to Julie Harding's body. Clay County Sheriff's Office

Investigators also saw a bag next to Julie. Inside, note to Mike, stained in blood, which read:

"I lived a good life until a year ago. Mike, you win! You got what you wanted, me in a coffin…"

Det. BJ Burton: It was just bizarre … almost like she was obsessed with somehow trying to get back at Michael Harding or —I don't know, didn't really understand it.

But Burton had a theory, and it involved Thomas O'Donnell.

Det. BJ Burton: She knows her co-conspirator has been arrested. … She's been suspended in California Highway Patrol … she saw the writing on the wall, what the future looked like, and wasn't going to stick around for it.

But what role did Julie Harding play in her husband's death? Investigators hoped they'd learn something when Thomas O'Donnell agreed to talk.

DETECTIVE BJ BURTON (police interview): So let — let me ask you this. When or how — when did you first meet Julie or how do you know Julie?

THOMAS O'DONNELL: I don't know, Julie.

DETECTIVE BJ BURTON: Julie Harding?

THOMAS O'DONNELL: Doesn't ring a bell.

After 20 uneventful minutes, O'Donnell requested an attorney, immediately terminating the interview. Seven days later, he was indicted by a grand jury.

O'Donnell pleaded not guilty to the murder charge. Three years later, on April 27, 2026, he went on trial at the Cumberland County Justice Center in Burkesville, Kentucky for killing Mike Harding.

PROSECUTOR ANN MARIE GORDON ANDERSON (in court): This case is about the murder of Michael Harding.

PROSECUTOR ANN MARIE GORDON ANDERSON (in court): According to Julie Harding's phone records, between July 1st and September the 8th, of '22, there were over 100 phone calls between her and the defendant, Thomas O'Donnell.

Gordon Anderson said Julie and O'Donnell used those calls to meticulously plan Mike's murder. Why? Julie realized she'd likely lose hundreds of thousands of dollars in a divorce, said Detective Burton.

Peter Van Sant: One possible solution for Julie in this financial war is to do what?

Det. BJ Burton: Get rid of him.

Prosecutors believe O'Donnell posed as a realtor to get a key to gain access to the property in Kentucky. They told jurors the data from the burner phone puts him at the scene of the crime. And believe it or not, O'Donnell's attorneys agreed O'Donnell, they said, was at the scene of the crime. It was a new admission that caught the prosecutors off guard.

Thomas O'Donnell Kentucky Department of Corrections

Remember, after his arrest, O'Donnell told investigators he did not know Julie. Now, his lawyers said he not only knew Julie, O'Donnell worked with her to lure Mike to that house in Kentucky, but he never pulled the trigger.

Prosecutor Ann Marie Gordon Anderson: I was really shocked … they point-blank just said he was at the scene, he opened the door, but he let someone else in.

That "someone else," says defense attorney Sara Zeurcher was the real killer. The defense claimed a neighbor saw two men at the property the day Mike was murdered.

DEFENSE ATTORNEY SARA ZEURCHER (in court): A neighbor told police exactly what he saw on September the 19th. Two men at the scene.

Investigators could find no evidence to back up the neighbor's account. The defense also criticized the investigation itself and pointed out its shortcomings. The burner phone prosecutors talked about was never recovered. Neither was the murder weapon. And there was no evidence that Julie paid O'Donnell to kill her husband.

DEFENSE ATTORNEY SARA ZEURCHER (in court): If this case were a mystery novel … you'll never hear the final chapter that explains what actually happened because the Commonwealth doesn't know.

After five days of testimony, O'Donnell decided not to testify. The jury needed just two hours to reach a verdict.

JUDGE DAVID WILLIAMS (in court): We, the jury, agree by a unanimous vote that defendant Thomas O'Donnell is guilty of the offense of murder.

Jesse Stockton: … for the family, they finally got justice for their father … all I can do is take satisfaction that the proper thing was done.

Julie Harding's close friend, Kathy Rourke, says Julie played no role in the murder of Mike Harding.

Kathy Rourke: If you knew her, you would know that she would never do anything cowardly or anything illegal, let alone try to kill this guy.

Steven Harding: She was the true monster of all of this … she was the one that executed every move, other than physically pulling the trigger on my father.

Heather Cavalieri: My dad was the victim in this case, not Julie.

Mike Harding Kathy Rourke

Steven Harding and Heather Cavalieri said the victory at trial, while satisfying, will never temper their sense of eternal loss.

Steven Harding: He died before my 30th birthday and 29 years isn't enough. I mean, people think 29 years is a lot, but it's not …

Heather Cavalieri: I was close with my dad for a long time. … Just not having a dad, you know, someone to call, like he was a jokester, you know. He was fun with my kids. (crying) … It's hard not having him here.

Thomas O'Donnell was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 20 years.



Produced by Paul LaRosa. Jordan Kinsey and Cindy Cesare are the development producers. Nancy Bautista is the associate producer. Wini Dini, Eric Modena and Greg Kaplan are the editors. Anthony Batson is the senior producer. Nancy Kramer is the executive story editor. Judy Tygard is the executive producer.

World.title: In the Venezuelan stronghold of Doral, some voters discouraged by Trump's policies
World.content:
Latinos voted in record numbers for President Trump in 2024, but polling shows that voting bloc is up for grabs in the midterms.

And one region that reflects that shift is Florida's Miami-Dade County, where Latinos and Hispanics make up more than 70% of the population.

In January, CBS News met Andrea Ramos and her husband in Doral, Florida, as they were celebrating and closely following the capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.

Ramos, a naturalized U.S. citizen from Venezuela, told CBS News that she credited President Trump with Maduro's capture. Doral has the largest Venezuelan population of any city in the country.

"I had such big admiration for him," Ramos told CBS News about her sentiments for the president following Maduro's arrest and extradition to the U.S.

But about nine months later, her feelings have changed.

"I feel disappointed," Ramos said. "I feel, in a way, betrayed."

While disappointed with the economy, it is the Trump administration's immigration crackdown that has led Ramos to sour on Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.

"Overall, I'm not feeling like the law is being respected," Ramos said.

According to a CBS News Battleground Tracker poll released earlier this month, 60% of Hispanic likely voters said they were likely backing congressional Democrats in the upcoming midterms, compared to 39% who said they were likely backing Republicans.

That marked a considerable shift from 2024 CBS News exit polls, which found that 51% of Hispanics voted for Democrats, compared to 46% who voted for Republicans.

In the same new poll, 59% of Hispanic likely voters found that the Trump administration was trying to deport more people than they had expected, compared to 51% of all likely voters.

Asked in the poll about the Trump administration's focus on deportation, 59% of Hispanic likely voters responded that it was too much, compared to 49% of all likely voters.

Stephanie Caro's family-owned coffee shop in Doral is among many local businesses that have seen a decrease in foot traffic and sales as masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have been photographed on the city's streets.

"I'd say there is a heightened sense of fear," Caro said.

Some local business owners have said they're concerned they'll have to close their doors.

"It really impacts the entire community," Caro said. "People are scared to leave their houses. They're changing their daily routines."

Doral voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, driven by Venezuelan Americans who fled Maduro's socialist regime.

But ICE has increasingly targeted asylum seekers who have pending cases and active work permits, and Mr. Trump's close relationship to Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez has impacted his support in Doral.

When CBS News asked Doral's Republican Mayor Christi Fraga three times if she still supported Mr. Trump, Fraga refused to give a direct answer.

"There is a lot of things that I support, and there's also questions that I've raised," Fraga told CBS News.

Ramos remains undecided on who she will vote for in the upcoming midterms. On that question, Fraga also declined to advise her constituents to vote for Republicans.

Said Fraga, "Vote your conscience."

World.title: More than 1,000 arrested in France as protesters and police clash
World.content:
Nearly 1,000 people were arrested in nationwide protests in France, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Saturday, after demonstrations over the high cost of living and the country's education system earlier in the day remained largely peaceful.

Nuñez said the number of arrests is expected to rise significantly. He said marches "passed off well" in cities, but police officers found themselves confronted with "an extremely elevated level of violence" from "ultra-left" groups later in the day. Nuñez said some shops and businesses had been looted, but "the scale was far smaller" than a week earlier, when some 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted.

He said police acted more rapidly and conducted more pre-demonstration checks. Businesses and shopping centers had also been better protected. Earlier Saturday, the interior minister said police had confiscated weapons including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said.

The French Interior Ministry said about 410,000 people participated in about 298 protests around the country. Union organizers from the General Confederation of Labor put the number at around 800,000. An explanation for the discrepancy was not immediately available.

A protester waves the French flag near Porte de Vincennes during a demonstration in Paris on October 24, 2026. Aris MESSINIS /AFP via Getty Images

Some confrontations were reported between authorities and demonstrators in several cities, but as of Saturday evening there had been no repeat of the major street violence and rioting that erupted amid similar protests last week.

Nuñez previously said that French authorities were preparing to maintain order this weekend by maintaining up to 70,000 officers nationwide along with assets including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.

Nuñez said authorities will remain "on high alert" overnight and into Saturday.

Clashes break out in Paris after largely peaceful march

Paris had prepared for unrest, with shops boarded up and events including those related to the NFL's first French football game canceled, but authorities described the atmosphere in the city as "calm."

Thousands gathered at the Porte d'Italie on the city's southeastern rim for an authorized demonstration. The march had originally been set for the Bastille, near the city's center, and was changed to the more remote Porte d'Italie at the last minute. Union representative Murielle Guilbert told reporters that it was "scandalous" that Macron had forbidden protesters from demonstrating "where we wish to demonstrate," but participants complied with the change.

Protesters march during a demonstration in Paris, Saturday, on Oct. 24, 2026. Thibault Camus/AP

The front of the march ended without incident. Some chanted "We are not happy" as they peeled away from the Porte de Vincennes. Police said 110,000 people participated in the event, while union members put the number at 250,000.

As the evening went on, clashes were reported between police and demonstrators, the Agence France-Presse reported. Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists" had "gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters."

Clashes between protesters and police lasted about two hours, he said.

The Paris prosecutor's office said 64 people, including six minors, were arrested and 40 were placed in police custody. Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said. More than 3,000 were stopped and checked by officers, police said.

A protester clashes with police near Porte de Vincennes during a demonstration in Paris on October 24, 2026. Aris Messinis /AFP via Getty Images

Protesters march against far-right gathering

In Orleans, thousands of people marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party. Le Pen is launching her campaign to succeed Emmanuel Macron as France's president. Elections will be held in six months, and surveys show Le Pen is best-placed to win. Demonstrators in Orleans protested both Macron and Le Pen.

"Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled, according to the AFP. Police put their numbers at 11,000, while organizers said 26,000 took part. About 50 organizations, including labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups, had called for a protest against Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party.

A crowd marches along a sunken roadway during the cross-party protest against the National Rally in Orleans, France, on Oct. 24, 2026. Romain Gautier / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images

Some placards seen at the march referenced a shooting in Trappes, a Paris suburb, that left one person dead and several others injured across several locations. Macron called the rampage a "racist terror attack." Prosecutors are investigating the shooting as a terrorist incident.

French media reported that the protest against the congress ended peacefully early Saturday afternoon. The gathering is expected to continue through Sunday.

Protesters and police clash in smaller cities

Demonstrations had been banned in the southeast city of Lyon, but about 150 protesters near the city's center briefly tried to block a road. Police fired tear gas to disperse the group. Tear gas was also used to break up a group of around 1,000 people gathered in the south of the city. Street fires were also reported.

A police helicopter was seen flying over the city, and security forces, armored vehicles and riot police vans were patrolling. A 21-year-old student, who spoke to the Agence France-Presse on the condition of anonymity, described authorities as "really mobile."

In the western city of Nantes, thousands of protesters broke through police lines to enter the city center, the AFP reported. Officers used tear gas and a water cannon to try and disperse them. Some on the fringes of the demonstration threw projectiles and aimed fireworks at officers.

French policemen during a demonstration in Lyon, France on October 24, 2026. Mathieu Prudhomme/Anadolu via Getty Images

Police said about 17,000 attended an event in Marseille. Officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march's endpoint. Street fires were seen in the city.

Tear gas was also deployed in Clermont-Ferrand, Bordeaux and Strasbourg, police said. Nuñez said one person was seriously injured in Clermont-Ferrand, but did not provide any details.

In the city of Toulouse, a 20-year-old man reportedly had fingers blown off, Nuñez said. He did not provide more details about the person, their condition, or how they came to be injured.

Nuñez said that in the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier, authorities saw far-right activists who claimed they were there to protect businesses or sought confrontations with "ultra-left militants." He said it was the first time authorities witnessed this phenomenon.

A protester faces police officers in Toulouse, southwestern France on October 24, 2026. Matthieu Rondel /AFP via Getty Images

In Nice, where demonstrations had also been banned, 11 people were arrested after far-right extremists fought with demonstrators downtown, regional authorities said. Water cannons were also used in the city.

Organizers call for Halloween demonstrations

One group of protesters, the Yellow Vests, said they would hold another round of protests on Oct. 31. The Yellow Vests emerged about eight years ago as a loosely organized group that staged disruptive protests against Macron.

Organizers called for rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the "authoritarian drift" of Macron's government and urging citizens to stand up for "public freedoms."

The demonstrations have been ongoing since September, when high school students in the southeast of Paris protested for better conditions. The unrest quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs.

A protester holds a French flag during a demonstration against rising living costs in Strasbourg, France, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. Jean-Francois Badias/AP

More protests spread across Europe

Other protests took place across Europe on Saturday, encompassing a broad range of issues including pensions, housing costs, anti-war movements, education and corruption.

Italian police said in a statement that they carried out nine arrests and briefly detained 371 people during protests in eight cities on Saturday. Of the people who were detained and taken to police stations, 110 were minors, the statement said. Police on Saturday also said they had arrested a 30-year-old man suspected of being the figure behind the "October 17 Movement," a group which had called for the protests.

Soldiers were deployed to Milan, the nation's fashion and finance capital, ahead of fresh demonstrations one week after looting and police clashes. Many stores were boarded up with wooden planks on Saturday. Others remained defiantly open after a call by the city's mayor Giuseppe Sala not to "panic."

"We want to give the message that we are not scared by these kids," said Alessandro Buhne, 30, who works at the Philipp Plein menswear shop. "Tourists are scared of this situation so we want to give the signal that you are safe if you enter our store."

Italy Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters.

In Rome, authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up patrols around key sites.

Some protesters briefly broke into the Colosseum, officials said.

Police "managed to isolate and contain the violent fringes, with balance and professionalism," Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi said, according to Italian news agency ANSA.

"In Italy there can be no room for those who delude themselves that they can act with impunity," he said.

Several hundred students demonstrated peacefully in the historic city. Organizers of peaceful events sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and their hands visible.

Five hundred soldiers have been deployed to patrol Milan, Italy, on Oct. 23, 2026. Andrea Carrubba/Anadolu via Getty Images

In Albania's capital of Tirana, riot police used water cannons to subdue large groups of protesters. Some of the demonstrators threw projectiles at police, the AP reported. A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama turned violent earlier Saturday, with some activists lighting fires on the street. The demonstrators are mainly high school and university students, demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. A broader anti-government movement is calling for Rama's resignation.

In Spain, thousands of retirees and others marched through central Madrid to demand that public pensions aren't meddled with.

Protesters in Lisbon, Portugal, are expected to march across the city Saturday to demand affordable housing.

World.title: 1 arrested after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest mountain retreat
World.content:
A suspect has been arrested in Germany following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as Eagle's Nest, German police said.

Authorities were alerted to a fire at the Nazi leader's mountain residence on the peak of Obersalzberg at approximately 9:15 p.m. local time on Friday, Upper Bavaria South police said in a statement.

The building, also known as Kehlsteinhaus, was "completely engulfed in flames" when firefighters arrived, police said, but no one was found inside and no injuries were reported.

Fire trucks had some difficulty accessing the site "due to the local conditions," authorities added.

Still from a webcam of the Kehlsteinhaus early on Oct. 24, 2026, after a large fire broke out in the southern German state of Bavaria. Berchtesgaden /AFP via Getty Images

"Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came into the focus of investigators," the statement said, adding that the cause of the fire is now under criminal investigation and one person was taken into custody.

The 33-year-old suspect, a German citizen who has ties to the Berchtesgaden area but doesn't currently live there, prosecutors said, has been questioned, The Associated Press reported. They said he showed signs of mental illness and he was being sent to a psychiatric facility, but they also would look into the possibility of a political motive in view of the building's history.

There were no current indications that anyone else was involved, police said.

At an elevation of 6,017 feet, Hitler's Eagle's Nest was completed in 1938 and occasionally used by the Nazi leader as a temporary seat of government. The site was spared from Allied bombing during World War II, largely preserving its original state.

Since then, it has become a popular tourist attraction, which also operates as a restaurant and beer garden. According to its website, the Eagle's Nest is "one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era" and it "stands for the insanity of the regime."

Smoke is seen at the mountain guesthouse Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle's Nest, which once was Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, after a large fire had broken out. KERSTIN JOENSSON/AFP via Getty Images

Bavaria's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, indicated to reporters in Berchtesgaden that the Eagle's Nest would be restored. But what the site will look like in the future will be a matter for discussions with local officials, historians, preservationists and others.

"We're not going to leave a ruin there," Herrmann said, according to the AP, adding, "I think we will be able to find a sensible solution."

The minister stressed "it is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance."

World.title: German police arrest suspect following fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest
World.content: Suspect arrested in fire at Eagle's Nest German police said they have arrested a 33-year-old suspect following a fire at an alpine retreat known as Eagle's Nest that was once used by the Nazis and Adolf Hitler. More

World.title: Drought, fire and high diesel prices 'addin' up tough' for Oregon ranchers
World.content:
Drought, fire and high diesel prices 'addin' up tough' for Oregon ranchers

toggle caption i Anna King/NWPB

HARNEY COUNTY, ORE. - Late bloomin' rabbitbrush – wads of swaying ochre – stud the roadsides and steep eroded-basalt buttes rising up from the basin floor outside of Hines, Oregon.

In a broad open field, horses munch standing hay as Katie Baltzor watches her black angus cattle on this fall day.

We've ridden out here in a side-by-side vehicle – it's like an overgrown golf cart with a pickup bed in the back made for rough ranch work.

All the animals are quiet. Happy. With their heads down grazing.

"You see that horse, how he's got speckled colors?" said Baltzor with a smile in her voice. "Looks like country gravy, I guess that's why they called him Gravy."

Sponsor Message

Diesel prices remain near record highs , despite recent actions by President Trump as the mid-term elections get closer.

The high prices are adding to pain for cattle ranchers in western states, who were already struggling with persistent drought . And in Harney County, where bovines outnumber the people – by a lot - there's many mouths to feed.

toggle caption i Anna King/NWPB

'Everything has gone up'

"Fuel costs, parts costs, everything has gone up," Baltzor said. "People say that prices have gone up, but calf prices (paid to ranchers) have (too).

"But calf prices still have not kept up with inflation – and so that's what makes it tough for ranchers to keep in business. If everything else goes up and cattle prices don't, you're just spinning your wheels a bit – you better like what you do."

Baltzor's face shows a life spent working in the desert sun. Her long ponytail glints a bit reddish in the afternoon light.

Baltzor and her husband Keith, had just finished riding a bunch of about 150 hundred head of their cattle down Highway 205 on horseback from another pasture.

"Sometimes it is dicey," she said. "There were cars starting to come through our bunch of cows … unfortunately a woman opened up her door and jumped out. And those cows would not go near her. It scared them, they wanted to come back anyway. Then she got out again and still was stopped. People just don't understand, they don't know. When you see a herd of cows and they're coming towards you, don't stop, just keep coming through them."

Sponsor Message

Baltzor was moving the cattle so they could work them closer to home. They are going preg-check the mother cows to make sure they're carrying new babies, and give all the cattle and calves vaccinations and dewormer.

toggle caption i Anna King/NWPB

Wildfires brought them home

But for Baltzor, this year is already addin' up tough. The places where Baltzor typically ranges her cattle in the mountains were ravaged by record-size wildfires this summer, robbing them of the grass the herds usually eat. Baltzor, and hired riders, had to hoof it through heavy smoke into the mountains to extract their cattle from the path of the fires.

"So all our cows, instead of coming home the second week of September, we had to bring them home the third week in July," Baltzor said. "Other folks had to do the same. And some people had to start feeding – we didn't, we had the rakebrunch."

Rakebunching means just raking pasture hay into piles, and leaving it in the field for animals.

Now, it's gonna take time 'til the mountain grass comes back. In some areas where her neighbors' ground has been burned over, it's taken years for them to be able to return their animals to graze, Baltzor said.

"Where are we gonna run cows?" she said. "Some of those fields that burned, the allotments you can't go back on them for a couple of years. And because so many acres burned in Harney County, it's not just my husband and myself that have this issue."

With no grass, ranchers need hay to feed their cattle. But the drought that set the stage for the fires has dried up Baltzor's hay meadows, too.

"So, the meadows were very short," Baltzor said. "Some of them got some water and you were able to cut a little bit. Some of them didn't even get water and you couldn't even cut some of the fields."

toggle caption i Anna King/NWPB

Rakebunch

Here's where the high diesel prices add up tough – what little hay there is, is a lot more expensive to harvest.

Sponsor Message

"The tractors, you know everything is diesel, and it's expensive and it costs a lot to keep them running," she said.

Haying typically takes several passes with a tractor – you have to cut it, turn the windrows to sun dry, and then bale them and stack them. Each time they fill the tractor with diesel now, it's about $300.

"And so just like this year when we were trying to decide, 'Should we try to run and bale some of this hay? Or it's not very good, it's very light, should we just rakebunch it?" she said. "Part of that was looking at the cost of diesel."

Rakebunching means going over it fewer times with the tractor. They also rakebunched because they feared more wildfire would force them back to their homeplace with the drought. Rakebunching is a good solution for the late summer and fall, but it will leave them short of hay later.

"But the bigger problem becomes next year," Baltzor said. "If we don't get the precipitation, then we don't have the irrigation water and then we'd be looking at purchasing hay."

Purchasing hay can mean driving long distances to get it, or having it delivered, in big trucks that burn a lot of diesel.

Baltzor drives her side-by-side through grass the color of a flaxen palomino.

toggle caption i Anna King/NWPB

'You keep a heifer'

This year's high diesel prices come at a time when the price of beef in the supermarket is also way up. Ranchers can sell their calves now for pretty good money. But, "It's not something you just do," Baltzor said. "You keep a heifer."

Heifers are young females, ranchers like to keep some or all of the ones born every year, so they can produce more calves, and replace cows that are too old for that. It's a longer term investment.

Sponsor Message

"It's two years [for a heifer to be bred and] before you have a calf," she said. "You know, a product. It's not that they're going to have a calf right away. And sometimes people don't understand that."

toggle caption i Anna King/NWPB

Break point and winter

Baltzor said she and her husband and ranch partner have switched to gas pickups to try to save a little on diesel. But she said every ranch here has a different break point

"Do you have vehicle loans?" Baltzor said. "Do you have cow loans? Do you have land loans?"

Baltzor said she and her husband worked outside jobs for years to be able to build their herd and accumulate land.

"It will pencil for us," Baltzor said. "Because we're lucky we worked really hard not to have debt. But not everyone's that lucky. And when we first started out we had a lot of debt …. Nobody gave it to us. We had to find places to rent, and we had to buy cattle. And we had to take out loans to do all of that."

On the way out of the pasture, a metal gate squawks a lot as it's closed and then clanks shut, held fast by a rope.

"There's different ways to get into the cattle business, and ours wasn't the easiest way," Baltzor said. "But I think it's very worthwhile. Because you appreciate what you have."

But times are lean for many in southeast Oregon, and now – here comes winter.

World.title: Archdiocese of New York agrees to $800 million settlement over sexual abuse claims
World.content:
Archdiocese of New York agrees to $800 million settlement over sexual abuse claims

toggle caption i Yuki Iwamura/AP

The Archdiocese of New York has agreed to pay $800 million to settle the claims brought against the church by some 1,300 people who say they faced sexual abuse from clergy members and lay workers.

Jeff Anderson, a lawyer whose firm represents more than 250 of the plaintiffs, said the settlement was finalized, pending signed paperwork, and that all plaintiffs had agreed to the settlement.

In an email sent to priests of the archdiocese on Saturday afternoon and shared with NPR, Archbishop Ronald Hicks also said the deal had not yet been signed but that an agreement had been reached with plaintiffs and their attorneys.

Sponsor Message

"We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors," Hicks wrote in the email. "This agreement will also allow the archdiocese to turn its full attention once again to its mission of preaching the Gospel, healing the sick, caring for the poor and needy, welcoming the stranger, and educating our children."

Anderson says that following the agreement, his clients have expressed mixed feelings of both sorrow about the abuse they experienced as well as relief that the legal fight is over.

"The first is a real sense of relief and achievement," Anderson said, and "the belief that having stood up at least they have now a chance to move forward and have done something to protect others in the future and clean up the archdiocese of New York."

The agreement was first reported by The New York Times.

This is one of the largest settlements in the Catholic church related to sexual abuse claims. In 2024, the Archdiocese of Los Angeles agreed to a $880 million settlement to victims of sexual abuse by its clergy.

In December 2025, the Archdiocese of New York agreed to mediation to settle the 1,300 sexual abuse claims and said it had laid off staff and planned to sell some of its Manhattan properties in effort to raise $300 million to pay survivors.

Sponsor Message

NPR's Daniel Burke contributed reporting.

World.title: Trade tariffs cause whiplash at Port Milwaukee
World.content:
Trade tariffs cause whiplash at Port Milwaukee

Sacha Pfeiffer visits Port Milwaukee to see how President Trump's tariffs have affected the flow of goods and impacted the regional economy.

Transcript

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

As we heard from those early voters in Texas and from coverage of the protests in France, the economy and affordability are surging concerns globally. It's also a concern locally in Milwaukee, where I'm hosting this program tonight. If you look at a map, you realize the city is located on a massive superhighway of water. Milwaukee is on Lake Michigan, part of the Great Lakes region, and that region is its own economy. Cargo from around the world is shipped across the Great Lakes, and all that maritime trade contributes to a regional economy worth about $9 trillion.

Now look at that map again. Four of the five great lakes are shared between the United States and Canada. Those two countries are now in an economic battle due to President Trump's tariffs, and that fight is harming port cities like Milwaukee. That is why I found myself this week on a long concrete pier on the port of Milwaukee, overlooking the vast expanse of Lake Michigan and talking with port director Benji Timm.

BENJI TIMM: So the boat is coming from the East. You can see the breakwater. There's a break in the breakwater out there. And there's...

PFEIFFER: A little passage for boats to get through. Yeah.

TIMM: Yes, between the light - the two lighthouses. That's where the vessels would come in. And if they're going into our inner mooring basin, they'd pass underneath the Hoan Bridge in the highway. If they're coming into one of our terminals here, they'd come straight in into one of these slips.

PFEIFFER: So whether they're coming from Canada or Europe, that is the way they get in.

TIMM: That's our gateway.

PFEIFFER: Port Milwaukee does business with more than 300 ships a year that import goods from all over.

TIMM: So there are steel beams on the terminal, and this steel came in from Luxembourg. It came in for a hospital project from Minnesota. It's unloaded from a vessel here, and then it's loaded up onto trucks and then trucked over to Minnesota.

(SOUNDBITE OF STEEL BANGING)

PFEIFFER: Can we not make this in the United States?

TIMM: That was a special gauge of steel, I know.

PFEIFFER: I mean, and is that partly what the Trump administration hopes for eventually, is that we can make this steel at home? And by these tariffs, we won't have to bring it in from Europe?

TIMM: That's the idea, yeah, is that we increase our production here. And again, I don't think anybody would argue with that, but we have to put the components into place to get us to that point.

PFEIFFER: Over the past year, Timm watched anxiously as the Trump administration added or threatened tariffs on all sorts of items - steel, auto parts, salt, agricultural commodities, timber. The tariffs could come at any time, and that affects the budgets and supply chains of countless companies that rely on this port.

What is your distress level about the impact that tariffs are having on the Milwaukee economy?

TIMM: It's kind of whiplash. You know, it's - it has not been consistent. When the administration makes an announcement, we listen very closely, and then we try and figure out how it'll affect us. We try not to freak out because oftentimes it'll change.

PFEIFFER: Sometimes you're inclined to freak out?

TIMM: Sometimes. You know, we try and reserve the freak out. But...

PFEIFFER: Imported products were all around us in warehouses and silos and massive domed containers. So we got in a van with Benji Timm and the mayor of Milwaukee, Cavalier Johnson, to get an up close look.

(SOUNDBITE OF CAR DOOR CLOSING)

CAVALIER JOHNSON: This peanut butter spread of tariffs just, you know, across the board, it's kind of - it's harmful.

PFEIFFER: Remember that steel? There is now a 50% tariff on foreign steel imports to the U.S.

We are passing by a shipping bay where it looks like, I don't know, steel cord - what are we seeing stacked up there?

TIMM: So those are coils of steel. That's the tin plate steel that's primarily imported from the Netherlands, and it comes here and is used in canning, like food cans. There are a number of canning...

PFEIFFER: Things we see on grocery store shelves - that's how it starts, right there.

TIMM: Exactly. Yep.

PFEIFFER: One of the things that's been tariffed is steel, and a lot of steel comes into Milwaukee. How has that affected the steel coming and going?

TIMM: So the steel that comes into Port Milwaukee is not produced by U.S. steelmakers, so it has to be imported. And the steel is down approximately 30%, and that's kind of systemwide. So it's expensive, and production is down. You know, costs are going up, so there are less sales overall.

PFEIFFER: The goal of these tariffs by the Trump administration is to try to have more manufacturing done in the United States, and that will take time. When you talk to the businesses in your state and your city that are affected by the tariffs, how patient are they feeling about waiting to see if the tariffs have the payoff that the Trump administration hopes for?

TIMM: Well, that's the thing, is that our businesses and our consumers - they shouldn't be subject to the whims, the ups and downs, the back and forth, the unpredictability, the instability that's happening out of Washington.

PFEIFFER: And that instability can have international ripple effects.

All right, so we are seeing a very large ship. It is not a container ship. What are we seeing?

TIMM: So that's a bulk carrier vessel. It's from...

PFEIFFER: Bulk carrier?

TIMM: Bulk carrier, yeah. So they have bays within cargo holds within the vessel, where they store bulk materials.

PFEIFFER: And did you start to say it's from Bulgaria?

TIMM: So the vessel itself is from Bulgaria, and it's going to take the DDGs to Spain.

PFEIFFER: Do you think people would be surprised to know that a ship from Bulgaria is stopping in Milwaukee to then deliver things to Spain?

TIMM: I do.

PFEIFFER: Near the Bulgarian boat are huge mounds of something covered with tarps.

TIMM: So on the left, those are salt piles. So one of the biggest commodities that Port Milwaukee brings in is salt, and that salt is used for road safety. It's used for component animal feed. It's also used for water softeners. Last year, we had a pretty harsh winter, and states as far away as Kentucky, Minnesota, Iowa, were coming here to get salt.

PFEIFFER: A lot of Milwaukee salt comes from Canada. The Trump administration wanted to put tariffs on that, too.

When you heard that salt Well, salt and many other products may be tariffed, what was your concern for Milwaukee?

TIMM: So because salt is the biggest commodity that we import here, that would have had a significant impact on not only the city of Milwaukee's budget, but also other municipalities' budgets.

PFEIFFER: The Trump administration removed salt from its tariff list after lobbying from Congress.

But back on the pier, Timm told me the uncertainty is destabilizing.

TIMM: Everyone wants predictability. They want to be able to plan for the future. They want to be able to plan, you know, acquisitions, improvements, investments in their businesses. And that's hard to do when prices change so frequently.

PFEIFFER: What is your worry level about whether this will take a change of administration to improve the situation, whether the Trump administration may eventually lower the tariffs and it will create some relief for Milwaukee?

TIMM: Yeah, my biggest worry is our relationship with Canada and making sure that we keep that strong. So they're Wisconsin's largest trading partner. They're a significant part of our economy here in Milwaukee.

PFEIFFER: What do they...

The U.S. and Canada are so interlinked by the Great Lakes that a ship going between the two countries can cross the international border 27 times. They're partners.

TIMM: It's really interesting. Because there's such a tight relationship between the United States and Canada, we have a lot of the same companies on both sides of the border, and essentially, we trade components, and we trade equipment back and forth. And when you have disruptions like tariffs, when you have other disruptions in the transportation network, it can be really harmful and really kind of just slow down business. So I'd...

PFEIFFER: President Trump is trying to use tariffs to reshape global trade and protect the U.S. economy. But that's leaving people like Port Milwaukee director Benji Timm to reassure his city's foreign trading partners. He has to keep goods flowing nationwide and worldwide. He has to brace for products suddenly becoming more scarce or more expensive, and he has no idea when that volatility will end.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

PFEIFFER: Stay with us for more coverage from Wisconsin, an important bellweather state, where we are this weekend just ahead of the midterm elections.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

World.title: How data centers became a bipartisan political issue in Wisconsin
World.content:
How data centers became a bipartisan political issue in Wisconsin

Data centers are a big issue across the country. As midterms approach, many look to the swing state of Wisconsin for lessons for how that issue could play out nationally.

Transcript

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

In the center of the world...

(CHEERING)

PFEIFFER: ...That's where all sorts of Wisconsinites told me we were yesterday as they watched the Brewers win game one of the World Series. One of those people was Kristi Draver (ph).

KRISTI DRAVER: Everybody knows it. Driving around Milwaukee, driving in from out of Milwaukee - everybody knows this is it, the center of the world, right here in Milwaukee.

PFEIFFER: And I'm in Milwaukee today, hosting this program from NPR member station WUWM. Wisconsin, along with its Brewers fame, is known for its pivotal role in U.S. politics because of its rust belt geography and its urban rural divides. The midterms are 10 days from now, and Wisconsin is front and center on a contentious national issue, data centers. Many voters on the left and right dislike them, and midterm candidates are having to adapt.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

TOM TIFFANY: I have been consistent over the last year that we are not going to pay those subsidies to these companies. He just came around in the last week when he figured out, that's where the public is. I will not put my finger to the wind when making decisions like...

PFEIFFER: That was the Republican contender for Wisconsin governor Tom Tiffany in this week's gubernatorial debate here. Just last week, the city of Milwaukee enacted a one-year moratorium on new data center construction. WUWM's Eddie Morales has been covering this, and he's with me in his station's studios right here in Milwaukee. Hi, Eddie.

EDDIE MORALES, BYLINE: Hi, Sacha.

PFEIFFER: What prompted this moratorium?

MORALES: So there was a proposal to turn a vacant Walmart into a data center, and local community organizers - they rallied to stop that developer. Then residents mobilized in favor of a moratorium, with dozens coming to speak at city meetings. It's just one of several cities in Wisconsin to actually pause new data center construction. There are more than 50 different kinds of data centers already in Wisconsin, and the businesses who want to develop more say their projects will help stimulate the economy.

PFEIFFER: This is definitely not the first time there's been backlash in Wisconsin to big tech companies coming in. Some of our listeners might remember the name Foxconn. Tell us about that history.

MORALES: Yeah, so part of the reason why the anti-tech sentiment has been so quick and so strong here is because of that Foxconn deal. It was during President Trump's first term when he championed a massive project by the tech manufacturer Foxconn. The deal was supposed to bring more than 10,000 jobs to Wisconsin, and the state offered this substantial incentives package. But the company then dramatically shifted their plans. There was this public outcry, and it became a political mess for the governor's office, and it created this legacy of mistrust for Big Tech in Wisconsin.

PFEIFFER: And, Eddie, as you know, the data center issue has even reached the governor's race. I've heard this week this ad with one candidate calling the other Data Center Dave - not a compliment. What's going on there?

MORALES: Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany have accused each other of being too supportive of the data center industry, as we heard in that clip in your intro. Now, both candidates are trying to position each other as flip-floppers.

PFEIFFER: There are different kinds of data centers. The new ones are the big hyper-scale ones people are concerned about, but I understand you've been on a tour of a different, more traditional one. What did you see?

MORALES: Right, it was Potawatomi's Data Holdings. So that's on land that's owned by the Potawatomi tribe. And the building is really interesting. It has this design of a brick facade and fake windows that match the neighborhood's aesthetic. It's a 46,000-square-foot data center. It's small compared to the much bigger sites that are being built around the country for AI processing and that have been a little bit more in the public eye. The manager, Ryan Brooks - he took me on a tour, and while we were there, he told me that he's actually for the moratorium.

PFEIFFER: The manager? - the management told you they're for the moratorium.

MORALES: Mm-hmm. Well, he strongly supports data center regulations because he doesn't want more of the huge - what they call - hyperscale AI data centers versus his smaller data center, which has been operating for years. He's kind of worried about his business.

RYAN BROOKS: The number of these large hyperscalers that are coming into town, the amount of power that they require - or coming into the state, even - the amount of power that they require is more than is planned by all the energy providers in your state. So someone's not going to make it.

MORALES: So he thinks some of the other companies building the huge new sites don't have the community in mind, and he says his company is built on tribal land, so it's there to stay. But of course, his company does have its own incentives to take a position in this moment.

PFEIFFER: Eddie, for communities who have been going through this, what have they learned? Any lessons here?

MORALES: Well, Milwaukee, like in many places - it doesn't have the regulatory structures and the zoning laws in place to really manage the goals of huge new - of these huge companies who really want things done fast. And data centers, they can provide a lot of jobs, mostly construction jobs needed to build them, but then often it's just a very small number of jobs to maintain them. So different communities can offer a range of incentives to keep generating revenue like property taxes.

But these centers can also create a lot of strain on a municipality's resources, and the public has been worried about issues like energy and water use. But now, I should say that in some places, like Potawatomi's Data Holdings, where I went with Ryan Brooks - they operate with zero water usage, and it has on-site solar, but it's not a hyperscale site.

PFEIFFER: The data center opponents in Wisconsin - have they had much success?

MORALES: Well, the public outcry here has quickly turned into action, and grassroots action has yielded petitions, social media work, organizing local referendums and pressure on local officials to be more transparent, which is a lesson. It's a lack of initial transparency and public input that contributed to the backlash and propelled the Big-Tech-versus-small-town narrative that took hold here so quickly. But it is important to note that a moratorium is on its - is really a way to slow it down but not stop it.

PFEIFFER: That is Eddie Morales with WUWM. Thanks, Eddie.

MORALES: Thank you.
