World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: Burnham tells Trump of the “economic consequences” of Argentina’s Falklands measures
World.content:
Burnham tells Trump of the “economic consequences” of Argentina’s Falklands measures

24th Saturday, October 2026 - 08:32 UTC Full article

Trump has said in recent weeks that the US position of neutrality on sovereignty over the archipelago is under review

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham set out to US President Donald Trump on Friday “the economic consequences that Argentina’s coercive measures have for the United Kingdom and the United States”, in a phone call focused on the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, according to a Downing Street statement quoted by the EFE news agency. Burnham reiterated the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources.

The call came a day after US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau acknowledged in Buenos Aires that Washington is closely watching the impact Argentina’s National Sovereignty Defence bill could have on its companies. The bill, still stalled in the Chamber of Deputies, extends sanctions to affiliates, shareholders, financiers and suppliers of companies operating in the islands. Trump has said in recent weeks that the US position of neutrality on sovereignty over the archipelago is under review.

The same day, Burnham spoke with Chilean President José Antonio Kast, to whom he raised “the UK’s interest in ensuring that Falkland Islanders retain the ability to exercise their right to self-determination”, according to Downing Street. The two agreed on the need to work together to modernise their defence capabilities and that there are “untapped trade opportunities” between their countries. Kast reiterated Chile’s support for Argentina’s sovereignty claim during a state visit to Buenos Aires in April, while his government described the new commercial route between Punta Arenas and Stanley in September as “a business between private parties”.

Argentina launched sanctions proceedings in September against dozens of people and companies linked to Sea Lion, operated by Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, and asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order a halt to the project. The tribunal will hold its hearing on November 10 and 11 in Hamburg. The United Kingdom has announced measures to protect its companies from Argentine sanctions and maintains that the islanders’ decision to remain British, expressed by 99.8% of voters in the 2013 referendum, must be respected.

World.title: Eight in ten Argentines barely make it or fall short by the end of the month, survey finds
World.content:
Eight in ten Argentines barely make it or fall short by the end of the month, survey finds

24th Saturday, October 2026 - 02:00 UTC Full article

Some 79% of respondents have a credit card

Some 45% of Argentines just about reach the end of the month and 34% fail to cover their expenses, according to a survey by consultancy Brain Network carried out in September, which describes a picture of financial stress, rising debt and little capacity to save. Among those who had trouble paying, 40% use their credit card to cover shortfalls.

The study classifies respondents into three groups. The “Jugglers”, 57%, keep up with payments through frequent adjustments and a fragile balance; the “Up to date”, 22%, are more stable; and the “Overwhelmed”, 21%, have insufficient income and recurring arrears. People over 50 predominate in the first group, and those aged 30 to 39 among those facing the most severe difficulties.

Some 79% of respondents have a credit card. Besides using it to cover shortfalls, those who had trouble paying resorted to cutting spending, 31%; borrowing from family or friends, 23%; delaying payments, 17%; and taking out loans, 16%. In the past six months, 60% of those with bank debts and 65% of those owing digital finance platforms had difficulty paying. Among the “Overwhelmed” with problems, 21% took out a new loan to cover another debt.

“The market is not in default, it is juggling,” said Lionel Holzman of Brain Network, who recommended that lenders offer refinancing before the situation worsens. Some 45% of those in arrears say they have not received any such offer.

President Javier Milei recently challenged the idea that people cannot make ends meet: “If they really run out of money on the 20th, how do they live ten days without eating or drinking?” he said in Neuquén. According to the survey, 44% believe their situation will improve next year, 36% that it will stay the same and 20% that it will worsen.

World.title: Bolsonaro apologises twice to Lula in a calmer final debate as polls show a dead heat
World.content:
Bolsonaro apologises twice to Lula in a calmer final debate as polls show a dead heat

24th Saturday, October 2026 - 01:39 UTC Full article

The first apology came when Lula asked why he had voted against extending maternity leave as a state deputy in Rio de Janeiro. “It was a mistake,” Bolsonaro replied

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro apologised twice to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva during the last televised debate before Sunday’s runoff in Brazil, held on Friday night on TV Globo, which was more measured in tone than the first. The candidates arrived level: the latest Datafolha poll, published on Thursday, gives each 50% of valid votes.

The first apology came when Lula asked why he had voted against extending maternity leave as a state deputy in Rio de Janeiro. “It was a mistake,” Bolsonaro replied. “Today, after having children, I would vote completely differently.” Lula retorted: “When you had the chance to vote in favour, you didn’t.” The second came after the senator called the president “nine fingers”, a nickname referring to the finger he lost in a workplace accident as a metalworker. “I will not allow a militiaman to call me nine fingers,” Lula replied, contrasting his working-class background with his rival’s. Lula also asked him about having once referred to Bolsa Família as “Bolsa Fodder”.

Argentine President Javier Milei featured again. Lula compared his rival’s proposals with those of the Argentine government, and Bolsonaro turned the argument around: “In Argentina, the left governed for 20 years and destroyed the country. Milei began his government with 200% inflation.”

Bolsonaro, who won the first round with 47.03% of the vote against Lula’s 45.16%, focused on the cost of living and public debt. He promised to cut taxes, raise the minimum wage and pensions above inflation and not to privatise oil company Petrobras or Banco do Brasil, and challenged Lula for the vote in the northeast, his main stronghold: “I will be the most northeastern carioca you have ever seen.” Lula defended his investment in infrastructure and in that region, accused his rival of not knowing the country and recalled the oxygen shortage in Manaus hospitals during the pandemic.

The debate was held under new rules barring candidates from entering each other’s space, requested by Lula’s campaign after the first encounter. On Saturday, candidates may take part in events but can no longer ask for votes.

World.title: Lula accuses Bolsonaro of “licking Trump’s boots” in the final debate
World.content:
Lula accuses Bolsonaro of “licking Trump’s boots” in the final debate

24th Saturday, October 2026 - 01:30 UTC Full article

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Friday accused his runoff rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, of “licking the boots” of US President Donald Trump during the last televised debate before Sunday’s election.

Lula said Bolsonaro was behind Trump’s decision to impose tariffs on Brazilian imports, a recurring accusation the senator has repeatedly denied. “But I wasn’t worried; if Trump doesn’t want to buy from Brazil, I’ll sell elsewhere,” he said in the TV Globo debate, referring to the opening of new markets during his term. Brazil “has never exported so much” as it does now, he added.

Bolsonaro, for his part, accused Lula of “massacring” the farm sector with high interest rates and reminded him that he had recently said farmers should “kneel” before him for his government’s investment. “Why do you humiliate people, why do you treat the farm sector so badly?” he asked. Lula replied that his rival “memorises but doesn’t learn” and that agriculture received more resources under his government than under former president Jair Bolsonaro, the candidate’s father.

Bolsonaro won the first round with 47.03% of the vote against Lula’s 45.16%, and the latest Datafolha poll puts them level at 50% of valid votes each.

World.title: The Pope cancels a visit to Assisi as a medical precaution, two weeks before his South American tour
World.content:
The Pope cancels a visit to Assisi as a medical precaution, two weeks before his South American tour

23rd Friday, October 2026 - 18:19 UTC Full article

According to a medical bulletin released by the Vatican on Friday, a follow-up chest X-ray “confirmed his optimal post-operative recovery”

Pope Leo XIV has cancelled a visit planned for Tuesday, October 27, to Assisi, in central Italy, after his doctors advised against helicopter travel so soon after the lung surgery he underwent on October 13. It is the first engagement on his schedule to be called off since the operation, two weeks before the start of his tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

According to a medical bulletin released by the Vatican on Friday, a follow-up chest X-ray “confirmed his optimal post-operative recovery”. “However, given the short time that has elapsed since surgery, the attending physicians considered it appropriate to advise against the helicopter flight planned for October 27 as a precautionary measure,” it added.

In Assisi, the Pope was due to take part in a peace gathering marking the 40th anniversary of the World Day of Prayer for Peace convened by John Paul II. He will send a message to the organisers and participants.

Leo XIV, 71, underwent surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, where he was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma. On Wednesday, the Vatican said the tumour was localised and that he will not need further treatment. On Sunday, in his first appearance before the faithful since the operation, the Pope said he would resume his activities “gradually”.

The Vatican has announced no changes to the South American tour, scheduled from November 6 to 17, which will begin in Uruguay, from the 6th to the 8th, and continue in Argentina, until the 11th, and in Peru.

World.title: US confirms concern over the impact of Argentina’s Falklands bill on its companies
World.content:
US confirms concern over the impact of Argentina’s Falklands bill on its companies

23rd Friday, October 2026 - 10:25 UTC Full article

Landau also defended the US proposal to end the UN Decolonisation Committee, before which Argentina presents its claim every year

US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau acknowledged in Buenos Aires on Thursday that Washington is closely watching the impact that Argentina’s National Sovereignty Defence bill, which toughens sanctions against those involved in hydrocarbon exploitation in the Falklands, could have on its companies. Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno defended the initiative.

“We are obviously looking at the interests of our companies. It is natural for any country to be concerned about that, but I want to stress that we respect the legislative process of the great Argentine nation,” Landau said at a joint press conference at the San Martín Palace, after meeting Quirno together with Assistant Secretary for Western Hemisphere Affairs Juan Pablo Segura. The US concern centres on the bill’s extension of sanctions to affiliates, shareholders, financiers and suppliers of the companies involved, as the newspaper Clarín reported on Sunday.

Quirno said current legislation needs changes to give the country better tools and denied that the bill targets anyone in particular: “This law is not against anyone in particular, it is not against any company in particular.” He explained that it seeks to make companies choose between investing on the mainland or in the islands. “We hope they will always choose the Argentine mainland over the illegitimate licences of the Malvinas Islands,” he said. The bill remains stalled in the Chamber of Deputies.

Landau also defended the US proposal to end the UN Decolonisation Committee, before which Argentina presents its claim every year, as part of a broader reform of multilateral bodies, and asked that it not be read in light of any specific dispute. Quirno replied that its possible disappearance would not weaken Argentina’s claim or UN resolutions: “Our claim is global, in every international forum and above all at the United Nations.” He reiterated that Argentina seeks a peaceful negotiation with the United Kingdom.

On bilateral matters, Quirno announced US funding against drug trafficking and child trafficking and for a cybersecurity centre, and a framework with the Export-Import Bank to explore up to US$7 billion in financing for the Andes-Atlantic Corridor. On the conditions of Washington’s support, he said: “The only condition is that we keep doing what we are doing.” US Vice President JD Vance is expected to visit Argentina in November.

World.title: Lula and Bolsonaro agree to open their bank and phone records days before the runoff
World.content:
Lula and Bolsonaro agree to open their bank and phone records days before the runoff

23rd Friday, October 2026 - 10:13 UTC Full article

The initiative arose from a challenge Lula issued to his rival during Sunday’s televised debate

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro signed an agreement at the Superior Electoral Court on Thursday to simultaneously lift the secrecy of their bank, tax and phone records, and those of relatives and linked companies, three days before Sunday’s presidential runoff. Release of the data now depends on a decision by Judge André Mendonça, the case rapporteur.

The document covers the past eight years and provides for the information, requested from the Central Bank, financial institutions, the tax authority and phone companies, to be published on a public portal of the electoral courts. Lula signed in person; Bolsonaro did so through his lawyer, Maria Claudia Bucchianeri, who had sought to extend the period covered. Allies of the president expressed doubts about whether the senator would comply.

The initiative arose from a challenge Lula issued to his rival during Sunday’s televised debate. On Tuesday, the president filed authorisation with the court to open his data if Bolsonaro did the same. The senator made his acceptance conditional on including presidential corporate card spending since 2023, the schedule of First Lady Janja Lula da Silva, visits by the president’s children to the official residence, the use of official helicopters and the government’s links with former banker Daniel Vorcaro. Lula’s campaign accepted the conditions, according to its coordinator, Senator Camilo Santana.

The agreement comes amid mutual accusations of corruption. Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering in connection with the Banco Master case, and one of the president’s sons, Fábio Luís Lula da Silva, for alleged influence peddling. Both deny the accusations.

Polls show a statistical tie between the two candidates, who hold their final debate on Friday on TV Globo.

World.title: Lula and Bolsonaro chase non-voters in the final stretch of Brazil’s campaign
World.content:
Lula and Bolsonaro chase non-voters in the final stretch of Brazil’s campaign

23rd Friday, October 2026 - 10:02 UTC Full article

The latest Datafolha poll gives Bolsonaro 51% of valid votes and Lula 49%, within the margin of error, while Quaest puts them at 46% and 44% of total voting intentions

Two days before Brazil’s presidential runoff, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro are focusing their final efforts on the same target: the roughly 33 million voters who stayed away in the first round. With polls showing a statistical tie and just 1% or 2% undecided, mobilising those who stayed at home on October 4 could decide the outcome.

The latest Datafolha poll gives Bolsonaro 51% of valid votes and Lula 49%, within the margin of error, while Quaest puts them at 46% and 44% of total voting intentions. In the first round, Bolsonaro won 47.03% and Lula 45.16%. Since direct elections returned in 1989, no candidate who came second in the first round has won the presidency.

Both campaigns are targeting two groups for whom voting is optional: people over 70, who have high abstention rates, and 16- and 17-year-olds. Lula’s campaign has mobilised activists and supporters on the streets and online, with large events such as the rally on São Paulo’s Avenida Paulista and the “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel, with millions of followers. This week the government began paying the 15% increase in Bolsa Família, and the Senate approved the 40-hour working week, one of the president’s flagship pledges.

Bolsonaro, for his part, has the backing of almost all right-wing and centre-right parties and of ten governors elected in the first round. He has centred his message on security and the economy, promises to create a Ministry of Prosperity and keep social programmes, and has also called his supporters to Avenida Paulista and mobilised them online through channels such as “Flávio’s Troop”.

The digital battle has reached the courts: both campaigns accuse Meta of unequal treatment on its platforms, and the Superior Electoral Court has ordered it to guarantee equality between the candidates. Lula and Bolsonaro face each other on Friday in their final debate, on TV Globo, before Sunday’s vote.

World.title: MND Tutor | Afro-Mexican celebration
World.content:
Welcome to MND Tutor! This interactive learning tool helps you improve your Spanish by exploring real news articles from Mexico News Daily. Instead of just memorizing vocabulary lists or grammar rules, you’ll dive into authentic stories about Mexican culture, current events and daily news.

Oaxaca held its first Afro Guelaguetza in the coastal community of Chacahua Isla, bringing together 12 delegations to celebrate Afro-Mexican heritage through music, masked dances and traditional performances. The festival, known as La Rejunjuneada, gave Afro-Mexican communities a dedicated platform to showcase their cultural traditions, which also feature in the state’s larger annual Guelaguetza celebration. Officials described the event as an opportunity to recognize communities whose histories have long been overlooked, emphasizing the importance of rights, justice and cultural pride.

Discover more about this unique Oaxacan festival and why it matters in our latest MND Tutor.

World.title: Full speed ahead: The 39th Carrera Panamericana lives up to its billing
World.content:
“Mexico is the only place in the world where you can pass the police while going 180 mph, and they’ll smile and wave at you,” said Jan Bednar, a professional race car driver who made his debut in Mexico. “I love it. I’m having the best time.”

A few days prior, Bednar had arrived in Mexico from Czechia to compete in the legendary La Carrera Panamericana, or the Pan-American Race.

The Czech driver brought a restored 1969 BMW 3.0 CS that once competed in the Pan-Am over a decade ago. He even gathered the original team that had once raced in Mexico with the same vehicle — a classic German speedster that he said he found collecting dust in a forlorn garage in Eastern Europe. He was inspired when, after asking around, he found out about its former days in the Pan-Am.

Bednar was one of many international motorists from 15 countries to have saved up enough resources — upwards of $75,000 — to race in the 39th edition of La Carrera Panamericana.

A deadly origin story on the open highway

The race has developed a notorious reputation as one of the most dangerous, even deadly, open-road endurance rallies in the world. It launched in 1950 as part of an initiative from the Mexican government to highlight its completion of the Pan-American Highway.

The highway itself, which spans 19,000 miles, was proposed by the United States as a railroad in 1889. In 1923, that idea evolved into an automobile thoroughfare and was revisited at the International Conference of American States in Santiago, Chile.

It took 13 years for the 21 involved nations to sign on to build their respective sections, a sprawling agreement finalized at the Convention on the Pan-American Highway in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

In 1936, the highway — heralded as an international diplomatic success — announced the completion of its first section from Laredo, Texas, to Mexico City. Eventually, Mexico became the first country to finish its border-to-border commitment, prompting the idea for the inaugural Pan-Am race.

The race has since had a controversial, albeit exhilarating, history that brings professional racers, amateurs and hobbyists to Mexico for the landmark event. Known for its high death toll, with more than 30 fatalities in the first five years of its existence, the race was canceled in 1955 and remained dormant until 1988, when it returned in a modernized and regulated format.

A modern course winding through mountain passes

Today, the course extends from Chiapas to Chihuahua, covering eight states and nearly 2,400 miles for a seven-day haul across Mexico’s public roads. It is sectioned into timed portions and various classifications.

While Mexican road conditions have significantly improved since the 1950s, the race is still seen as a perilous task and offers a highly coveted trophy.

After kicking off on Friday, Oct. 16, in Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the 50 registered crews and their vehicles — mostly vintage Porsches, Fords, Studebakers and Chevrolets — flock northward along the coast of Veracruz and up to the state’s port city before banking inland and ascending up the rainy highway into the Sierra Madre mountains toward Puebla.

The 100 drivers made a colorful pit stop in Xalapa, where hundreds of local fans gathered in the parking lot of a science museum to cheer on the competitors, who drove through the city’s avenues as a caravan. Many drivers got out to mingle with supporters and took a smoke break before blazing off in an impressive procession of throttling engines.

The loudest applause came when Xalapa’s first local team, Don Justo, made its anticipated debut. Its two Mexican drivers, Iván Martínez and Salvador Aburto, received a hero’s welcome on their home turf.

Local fandom and international drivers unite

Fans of all ages gathered to witness La Carrera Panamericana in person, which has only passed through Veracruz a handful of times because the route continuously shifts with each edition.

“Motorsports have had a major boom in Mexico since Checo Pérez (debuted in Formula One in 2013),” said Arturo Ibáñez Gómez, a fan from Xalapa. “But it’s not common to always see these racers up close, especially in smaller cities.”

Despite a busy work schedule, Ibáñez Gómez said he wouldn’t miss the rare chance to see the race cars up close, even braving the scattered rain and high winds that morning.

He certainly wasn’t alone in his dedicated fandom. Ramsés López and his father, Alejandro, were in attendance among hundreds of others as car enthusiasts and vintage collectors. For them, having the race in their hometown was a blessing.

For others, being in Xalapa — let alone Mexico — was an unlikely yet thrilling moment. Carter Fournier of Dallas, Texas, entered the race with his 1970 Porsche 911. Like many participants, it was his first time racing south of the U.S. border.

“This is the last road race like this of its kind in the world. It’s special,” Fournier said. “There’s nothing like it left. This is the best of the best. It doesn’t get any better.”

A timeless tradition in North American racing

Notable racers included former Production World Rally Championship champion Benito Guerra Jr., a Mexican legend who was swarmed by fans in his 1983 Porsche 911. His small but muscular car was tailored with RSR specs built specifically for tarmac rally racing.

Though the race has lost some of its universal fame over the decades, it still evokes a sense of romantic timelessness from a renegade era of Mexican motorsports.

For those in the know, it’s a holy grail event in North American racing lore — and worth standing around in inclement weather as part of a large crowd just to give a driver a thumbs-up (trust me, they’ll always give you one back).

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: From the archive: What’s inside that piñata? A guide to Mexican candy
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in June 2025 — is a humorous yet informative look at the candies waiting to be liberated inside Mexico’s iconic piñatas.

If you’ve been in Mexico for a while, chances are you’ve been invited to — and perhaps attended — a few children’s parties.

Whether or not you know the child being celebrated is truly irrelevant. A party is something their parents throw, and they get a big say in who attends. This is only right because parties are expensive.

Sure, at least some of the kid’s friends will be there too. But you’d be forgiven for peeking into a salón de fiesta and wondering why a bunch of beer-drinking grown-ups rented a bouncy house.

A central feature of the Mexican kid’s party — and Christmas party, and New Year’s party — is, of course, the piñata.

Piñatas, as you might guess, have been around for quite a while. Before the papier-mâché varieties of today, for example, piñatas were literally clay pots. (For an informative read on the history of piñatas, check out MND’s excellent article on the subject.)

As a parent, I have watched as my daughter and other guests take turns trying to smash many a piñata to smithereens. My voice has gone hoarse from singing the “dale dale” song; thankfully, I usually have a beer to soothe it. And of course, my heart has stopped many times as I watched particularly enthusiastic children swing with all their might, even as others rushed toward them, one or two pieces of candy on the ground already.

Piñata candy-collecting is not a sport for the weak. You either rush in there and scoop up candy as fast as you can — or you don’t get candy. My daughter, whom I’ve infected with some of my gringa sensibilities, tends to hang back and grab stragglers, often sharing with smaller kids. This is kind, yes, but it’s also safe: She knows she’ll get a gift bag at the end of the party too. Under no circumstances will she go without.

You might think that once your kids get candy, you’ll get candy. This is true. There’s usually plenty to go around, along with — thank goodness — a big supply of local dentists.

Some of the candy is what we’re already familiar with, like chocolate. There are paletas (suckers) too, of course, and the little pieces of hard candy called caramelos.

But, oh, the variety. Everyone seems to love these things around here, so let’s have a look at what some of the less-familiar ones are!

Miguelitos

I have not met a Mexican who does not love miguelitos. My daughter loves them too. I, myself, would rather eat paint chips.

What are miguelitos, you may ask? Well, they’re little paper or plastic packets of powder that, since they’re sold as candy, you would think would be sweet. Basically, it’s a chamoy-flavored powder.

And what is chamoy, you may ask? It’s the stuff on the rim of your glass if you have a michelada, for one. It’s sweet, sour, salty and spicy all at the same time, and Mexicans go nuts for it. In powder or sauce, it goes on fruit, candy, popcorn, the rims of glasses or straight into the mouth. For a fascinating history of chamoy in Mexico, check out this video.

Pelón Pelo Rico

This is another favorite of pretty much every kid I know, including my daughter, and is in the tamarind candy category. Its presentation is silly: it’s a push-up goo made to look like a little green fellow’s red hair. It’s tangy and spicy, and also a little … salty? Not my bag, but it doesn’t have to be: It’s got tons of fans.

Tamarind is the featured flavor in a few other popular Mexican candies as well, like Pulparindo, which my partner calls his personal favorite. This one is just a bit heavier on the spiciness and saltiness — and it’s chewy, like a fruit roll-up. Salty fruit roll-ups, anyone? There’s also a kind of tamarind pulp sold in an actual plastic spoon to lick off!

Mazapán

Now that we’ve talked about some of the many things they put salt and chile in, let’s move on to something, in my opinion, much tastier. Mazapán — De la Rosa is the brand — is a round disk of ground peanuts and sugar pressed together. It’s technically a solid, but it has a way of both breaking off and then melting in your mouth that’s just so satisfying.

Obleas

I was very confused the first time someone handed me one of these. “Are these two body-of-Christ wafers with caramel in the middle?” That’s exactly what they are.

The cream in the middle is cajeta, a gooey caramel made from goat’s milk (the similar dulce de leche is made from cow’s milk). There are also cajeta suckers, which are delicious, and rollos de guayaba filled with cajeta, which are also worth seeking out, though they can’t typically be found in a piñata. I just wanted to mention them because I love them.

Paleta payaso

If you’re lucky, there will be a few of these in the piñata. The paleta payaso is a chocolate-covered marshmallow on a stick with a candied smiley face.

Unwrapping one is always a comical event, because the face is always misshapen. I remember frowning for a good five seconds the first time someone handed me one. But it’s pretty good.

Which Mexican candies do you like?

This article isn’t a complete list — obviously. I tried to stick mostly to things that might seem foreign to … well, foreigners.

Even after 23 years, there are some of these candies that I just don’t like: chile and salt with sweet and sour, for example, will never be okay in my book. But most candies, I do like.

So come on, out with it: What are your Mexican faves?

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Trade optimism holds despite a CIA-linked treason case
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico and the United States were “very close” to a trade deal, both presidents said this week — but lower tariffs were still a negotiating goal, not an agreement. Meanwhile, the arrest of Chihuahua’s former attorney general over alleged unauthorized CIA involvement in a drug raid sharpened the dispute over foreign agents operating in Mexico.

At home, Sheinbaum acknowledged that fuel seized in a much-publicized bust was not stolen, while Guadalajara residents continued to march for clean water. Water is on the mind of many outside Jalisco as well, as recent rains have proven insufficient to ease drought across areas of the country. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Tariff talks and sovereignty

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Monday that Mexico hoped for U.S. tariff reductions before year-end. Steel and aluminum face 50% duties, while vehicle tariffs include exemptions for U.S. content. USMCA remains in effect despite Washington’s July decision not to extend it another 16 years.

On Tuesday, Sheinbaum outlined the remaining obstacles to a trade agreement: Washington was offering tariff reductions in exchange for concessions Mexico had not fully accepted. She said Mexico would not accept terms that run contrary to its laws or that damage the economy or jobs.

Meanwhile, former Chihuahua Attorney General César Jáuregui was arrested for treason over allegations he authorized CIA participation in an April drug-lab raid without federal approval. On Friday, Sheinbaum recounted how Chihuahua Gov. Maru Campos denied authorizing foreign agents, accusing Jáuregui during a tense private meeting in September.

Mexico also announced plans to file a complaint over Emiliano Andrade Covarrubias’ death in ICE custody. The Foreign Ministry counted 18 Mexican deaths in custody or during immigration operations since Trump’s second term began. At the same time, U.S. authorization to test a heat ray along the Mexico-U.S. border raised concerns about possible burn injuries to targets on both sides of the border.

Security claims under scrutiny

On Tuesday, the U.N. Committee on Enforced Disappearances’ chairman urged General Assembly consideration of Mexico’s disappearances crisis. Mexico rejects the committee’s crimes-against-humanity characterization.

Wednesday brought official figures of 2,539 fuel-related arrests since October 2024, but also a qualification: Sheinbaum said 59 million liters confiscated in Guanajuato were not stolen or illegally imported. The company from which the fuel was confiscated had produced documentation establishing the facility’s legal operation, while the federal prosecutor in Guanajuato was fired and placed under investigation over irregularities in the bust.

Friday’s urban security survey found 58.1% of adults in surveyed cities felt unsafe, the lowest proportion in the series begun in 2013.

Water protests and persistent drought

Guadalajara’s contaminated-water crisis drew another mass protest a week after a similar protest ended with arrests and accusations of police brutality. This past Sunday, some 10,000 people marched. Participants blamed masked infiltrators for violence along the route, but their affiliations remained unestablished. Residents’ demands for clean tap water remained unresolved.

Nationally, rainfall had not erased accumulated drought deficits. Moderate-to-severe drought covered 12.7% of Mexico on Oct. 15, compared with 7.5% a year earlier. Rain helped some northern areas but failed to reverse earlier shortfalls in the south and southeast.

Economy and labor

The peso closed Thursday at 18.71 per dollar, depreciating 9.7% since Sept. 4. A narrower Mexico-U.S. interest-rate gap and trade uncertainty contributed to the slide.

Also on Thursday, the government announced 20 additional industrial parks, bringing Plan México’s operating total to 40.

In labor news, healthcare workers’ protests appear to be winding down after the union representing IMSS workers negotiated a new pay agreement. The package combines 4% more base pay with 4% in housing assistance, below the requested 10% base-pay increase; demonstrators also demanded medicines and better conditions. While protesters have promised to keep pressing for a better deal, attendance at the most recent marches dwindled following the improved pay offer.

Healthcare was not the only public service under examination: MND’s education deep dive found that more young adults are completing upper secondary education, even as education spending as a share of GDP and student test scores declined over the periods reviewed.

Politics and legislation

The Morena party’s dominance in Mexican politics appears to be holding strong, with early polling showing Morena as the overwhelming favorite in next year’s 2027 midterm elections. The party is preferred by 46% of Mexicans, although 31% expressed no preference and party preferences for gubernatorial contests were more varied.

Senators approved legislation that would allow the Finance Ministry to require digital payments in designated sectors, with gas stations and highway tollbooths expected to be among the first affected. Supporters say the measure would combat tax evasion; opponents warn it could exclude people who rely on cash

Congress also approved the so-called “anti-meme law,” penalizing misuse of official government logos. Supporters say it targets fraud; opponents warn ambiguous wording could threaten satire and political criticism.

Culture

In San Cristóbal de las Casas, a new textile conservation laboratory will repair damaged garments and protect the Maya World Textile Center’s 3,400-piece collection from insects and fungi. Other traditions found an audience onstage: 12 delegations brought music and masked dances to Oaxaca’s first Afro Guelaguetza, a dedicated celebration of Afro-Mexican heritage in Chacahua Isla. Further afield, Ballet Folklórico will celebrate its 75th anniversary with a 24-city U.S. tour, featuring regional dances and live music.

Other news from across Mexico

Looking ahead

The week ends with tariff relief still unresolved and new payments legislation awaiting promulgation. The Federal Reserve’s Oct. 27–28 meeting, followed by Banxico’s Nov. 5 decision, will put interest rates back in focus after the peso’s recent slide. Businesses and consumers will also be watching for Hacienda’s designation of sectors facing cash-payment restrictions once the legislation takes effect. Meanwhile, across Mexico, families and communities are preparing to remember their dead on Nov. 1–2.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: 20 years of ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’: 5 facts about Del Toro’s masterpiece
World.content:
Two decades after its theatrical release, “El Laberinto del Fauno” (“Pan’s Labyrinth”) remains Guillermo del Toro’s magnum opus and a timeless classic of popular culture. What began as a modest, independent project between Mexico and Spain ended up breaking records and conventions on a global scale: It moved the Cannes Film Festival with a legendary 20-minute standing ovation, grossed over US $80 million worldwide at the box office, and cemented its critical success by winning three Oscars and numerous awards at national and international ceremonies.

Set in the postwar period of 1944, this R-rated film follows Ofelia (Ivana Baquero), a young girl sent to an oppressive military camp controlled by her violent stepfather, Captain Vidal (Sergi López), a Francoist officer obsessed with eradicating the guerrilla resistance. In this hostile environment, Ofelia discovers a labyrinth where an ancient faun (Doug Jones) reveals a delicate truth to her: She is Princess Moanna, ruler of the underground kingdom, and must complete supernatural tasks to reclaim her throne.

Weaving historical horrors with fantasy, “El Laberinto del Fauno” serves as a profound allegory about the loss of innocence and the importance of ethical disobedience in the face of injustice and oppression.

To mark its 20th anniversary and re-release in theaters, we’re delving into the depths of this legendary labyrinth to bring you the most amazing and unexpected behind-the-scenes facts: from its original conception and its connection to “El Espinazo del Diablo” (“The Devil’s Backbone”), to how the story managed to make Stephen King himself squirm in his seat.

1. The original script was darker and more sexual

Little Ofelia’s journey — forced to overcome dangerous, fantastical challenges after moving to a military setting — did not always have the tone or the ending that we have come to love and admire. Few people know that, in its early stages of development, “El Laberinto del Fauno” did not feature a young girl as the protagonist, nor was it set in postwar Spain.

In the original version, Guillermo del Toro wrote a much rawer, darker and more erotically charged draft set in the Victorian era. The protagonist was an adult, pregnant woman who discovered the labyrinth after moving with her husband into an old mansion. There she met the faun, but instead of undertaking fantastical tasks to reclaim her throne, she became entangled in a dark, passionate relationship with the creature.

In the official DVD commentary, the director shares details of this concept: “They made passionate love, she fell in love with him, and he asked for the blood of the firstborn in return for the labyrinth to open and for her to go to the magical kingdom with him.”

By shifting his focus to childhood, Del Toro transformed that idea of adult horror into the fascinating gem of innocence, resilience and rebellion that made it to the big screen. Fortunately for the history of cinema, the Mexican director changed his mind just in time.

2. Two films connected

“El Laberinto del Fauno” was conceived by Del Toro as a companion piece to his 2001 film “El Espinazo del Diablo” (“The Devil’s Backbone”). Although they lack a direct narrative connection or shared characters, the director has formally defined them as “mirror films” due to their profound parallels. Together, they function as a diptych that explores the horror of war through the vulnerable and unspoiled eyes of childhood.

Beyond the historical context — with “El Espinazo del Diablo” set in 1939 during the Spanish Civil War and “El Laberinto del Fauno” in 1944 during the postwar Franco era — the closest connection between the two films is that neither uses horror in a superficial way.

The supernatural appears in Del Toro’s films from a profound and metaphorical dimension to help us process social tragedies and shed light on the darkest corners of the human condition. As the filmmaker explained to Voices of Monterey Bay: “In fairy tales, monsters exist to be a manifestation of something we need to understand, not just a problem we need to overcome.”

Like its predecessor, “El Laberinto del Fauno” demonstrates that true monstrosity does not stem from the supernatural realm — symbolized by the faun and the creatures of the underworld — but rather from the cruelty of human beings.

In both stories, the authentic villains are bloodthirsty, heartless men — such as Jacinto and Captain Vidal — who are obsessed with money, weapons and absolute control. It is in the face of these oppressors’ brutality that the child protagonists use their imagination and sensitivity to come to terms with the world they find themselves living in, defy the tyrants and defend their very existence.

3. The origin of the faun

Long before becoming an iconic figure in modern fantasy, the faun was already haunting Guillermo del Toro’s mind. During his childhood, the director used to have intense lucid dreams in which this creature came to life, emerging from the back of an old family wardrobe.

“I used to sleep at my grandmother’s house … And every night, right at midnight, in my bedroom, a faun would come out of the armoire. It must have been lucid dreaming, but for a child, it was as if it were real,” he told The Guardian. “I would see the faun’s human hand emerge from the armoire, then the smiling face of a goat, and then the hairy leg of a goat. I could clearly see him pulling his body out of the armoire, and I would start screaming.”

For Del Toro, bringing the monster that made him scream at night to the big screen was his way of coming to terms with his childhood fears. Although the faun we see in the film underwent countless changes in appearance, the idea was born from that peculiar childhood experience. Who would have thought that those terrifying sleepless nights would be the origin of the fantastical universe that would ultimately establish him as an international star?

4. The bold rejection of Hollywood that preserved the film’s identity

When the major studios read the story of “El Laberinto del Fauno,” they tried to entice Guillermo del Toro by offering to double the budget, on the condition that he relocate the story to the U.S. market.

However, true to his artistic vision, the filmmaker flatly refused. He believed that if he accepted the change in language and setting, the story would lose all its political power, its historical context and its authentic identity.

During an interview with KPBS, he clarified the direction the film would have taken under the industry’s commercial demands: “I never would have attempted to make ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ in Hollywood because we would have audience-tested it, and we would have had a super-happy ending with dancing little creatures.”

5. The movie terrified the ‘master of horror’ himself

Sharing your work with an icon like Stephen King is a dream come true for any filmmaker, but to make the master of horror himself squirm with fear at your own movie is an achievement reserved for very few. That’s exactly what Del Toro experienced in New England during a special screening of “El Laberinto del Fauno.”

During the iconic scene where the unsettling Pale Man comes to life to chase Ofelia, the Mexican director noticed that the celebrated writer began shifting uncomfortably in his seat, completely overwhelmed by the tension.

As you can imagine, witnessing the obvious unease of one of his greatest artistic influences was one of the most significant moments of recognition in his entire career.

As Del Toro explains in the film’s official commentary: “I must say, it remains the single best screening experience of my life — sitting next to Stephen King and watching him squirm during the Pale Man sequence. That, for me, is an Oscar. That’s absolutely the best thing that ever happened to me in my life.”

Disobedience as a legacy

Two decades have passed since Ofelia first entered the labyrinth, and the good news is that this dark fairy tale retains its ability to delight and unsettle us. Beyond its global box office success and a historic awards season — in which it won three Oscars (art direction, cinematography and makeup), three BAFTAs, seven Goya Awards, and nine Ariel Awards, among others — the deepest impact of Guillermo del Toro’s masterpiece lies in its power to engage with the challenges of modern times.

Far from being a childish escapist fable, this film stands as a manifesto on individual sovereignty and civil disobedience in the face of the dangers of blind, mechanical and unconditional submission. The lesson the film continues to impart to us today is that, in the face of overwhelming and dehumanizing authority, dissent is not an act of immature rebellion, but rather a moral virtue and an indispensable tool for survival.

As Dr. Ferreiro so aptly put it before his execution: “To obey just like that, for the sake of obeying, without questioning … That’s something only people like you can do, Captain.”

Twenty years later, that call to think for oneself and to challenge tyrants — both on and off the screen — remains more alive and urgent than ever.

Carolina Alvarado is a Venezuelan journalist who has devoted much of her career to creative writing, university teaching and social work. She has been published in Lady Science, Latina Media, Global Comment, Psiquide, Cinetopic, Get Me Giddy and Reader’s Digest, among others.

World.title: Mexican Americans are Mexico’s untapped opportunity: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Being married to a woman born in India, I have watched in amazement over the years at the level of engagement and activity that the Indian American community has with India. I think a lot of that starts with a deep-rooted sense of pride. Despite the country’s economic and other challenges, India’s education system instills a sense of pride in its history, culture and contributions to the world — a pride that people carry with them when they move abroad. You often see a similar sense of pride among immigrants from other countries. Many Indian businesses in the United States, despite the geographical distance from India, stay closely connected with the country. They look customers to grow, for suppliers to source from, and for talent to staff their teams. They look to create businesses that can operate in both countries and take advantage of the strengths of each country.

Just as importantly, the Indian government has worked hard to keep Indian Americans informed and educated about modern India — motivating them to stay engaged with the country. India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, has taken 10 trips to the U.S. since he was first elected prime minister in 2014. On these visits, he often focuses on the business community. He has done rallies in Madison Square Garden in New York City, met with technology executives in San Francisco, and on his “Howdy Modi” tour in 2019, even gave a speech to over 50,000 people in a football stadium in Houston, Texas. His messages to the Indian American community — urging them to remember and invest in India — are crystal clear. He is aware that the Indian American community, estimated to be 5.6 million people, less than 0.4% of the Indian population in India, is vital to the success of his country. He has leveraged their cultural pride and inspired them to turn it into action. It’s about more than a community remembering its roots; instead, he has turned it into a recognition of the diaspora’s central role in India’s future.

By comparison, an estimated 38 million Mexican Americans live in the United States, equivalent to almost 30% of the Mexican population actually living in Mexico. A recent study by the Latino Donor Collaborative estimated the GDP of Hispanic Americans (of whom over 60% are Mexican) to be US $4.4 trillion, which would make it the fourth-largest economy in the world.

Despite the geographic proximity of Mexico to the U.S., the significant trade between the two countries, and the massive Mexican diaspora in the U.S., Mexican presidents have rarely spent much time in the U.S. President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, Sheinbaum’s predecessor, came to the U.S. just five times in his six years in office, each time to attend a large global conference like U.N. Security Council meetings or the APEC summit. Sheinbaum, in over two years, has gone just twice: once to attend the FIFA World Cup draw and the other time to attend the FIFA World Cup final. Neither president spent significant time engaging the Mexican American community or the business community in the U.S.

Think about that for a moment: India’s Prime Minister has come to the U.S. more frequently over the past decade than Mexico’s presidents have. For some further perspective, Canada’s Prime Minister, Mark Carney, has been to the U.S. seven times already in just his first 18 months in office. Other members of Sheinbaum’s cabinet do travel more often to the U.S. Her economy minister, Marcelo Ebrard, frequently travels to the U.S., usually to Washington, D.C., for trade negotiations. Her foreign minister, Roberto Velasco, has also gone several times in his first few months in office, but does not yet have the experience or gravitas of la presidenta.

So what is going on here? Does it matter that Mexico’s presidents for the past eight years have spent so little time in the U.S.? And if it does matter, why?

I think Mexico is missing out on a huge opportunity. It’s extremely important to understand that, despite the significant Mexican American population in the U.S., net migration of Mexicans to the U.S. has been essentially flat for nearly two decades. What that means is that many, if not most, Mexican Americans living in the U.S. today have an increasingly outdated perspective on modern-day Mexico. Many are second or third generation, and as a result have few direct ties to the country. Many others know little more about the country than what they hear from family members back in their hometowns. Still others have never been to Mexico, or perhaps haven’t been there for decades. Most can’t fathom doing business in Mexico, let alone moving back there someday.

I have seen this firsthand countless times. I have had hundreds of conversations with Mexican Americans throughout the U.S. who often know shockingly little about Mexico. They know where their family is originally from. They are, of course, connected culturally through language, religion, food and music. But they often recite the same generic, outdated and negative soundbites about the country that a typical non-Mexican American would have. When asked, they almost always focus on the violence, the cartels, the drug problems, etc. Both the U.S. and Mexican media are in part to blame for this, but it goes beyond that.

As our team was developing MND Kids and was speaking to dozens of Mexican American school administrators from majority Mexican American school districts, we were constantly amazed at how many of them had never been to Mexico. Sadly, when asked why, many of them cited violence and didn’t even express a desire to visit. I have been equally shocked at how many Mexican American businesspeople I’ve met who haven’t considered Mexico as a place to grow their businesses with new customers, to expand their supplier base, or to build a bi-national business that taps into the talent of Mexico. There are many tens of thousands of medium and small businesses that could benefit from doing business in Mexico. Let me be clear: I am not saying that Mexican Americans should engage with Mexico out of obligation, but rather see engagement as an opportunity for their own business or family.

It’s also important to point out that millions of Mexican Americans send remittances (over US $60 billion in 2025) back to family members in Mexico each year. As Sheinbaum has often said, these people are quite literally modern-day heroes for the sacrifices they make by working hard abroad, away from family and friends, while sending money back to support their communities.

Failing to build stronger ties with the diaspora is a huge missed opportunity, and the Mexico News Daily team is certain that we can and must play an important role in further engaging this community. I personally have been working very hard to actively find ways for us to do so, including attending the national conferences of the U.S.-Mexico Chamber of Commerce in Washington, D.C., and the U.S. Hispanic Chamber of Commerce in Fort Worth, Texas, in just the past few months. I have also met with Ana Valdez of the Latino Donor Collaborative to explore collaboration with her organization, and I just recently met with the newly formed American Mexican Leadership Council to find out how we can work with them.

The following is a summary of what the MND team has been working on, as well as a preview of what is coming soon:

Preparing a bi-weekly business newsletter for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in Mexico – Active Preparing a monthly business newsletter for the U.S.-Mexico Chamber of Commerce chapters of California, Houston and Miami, with more chapters to come – Active Creating more business newsletters with other U.S.-Mexico organizations – Coming soon Publishing weekly MND Intelligence reports that educate and inform about Mexico with data, not opinions – Active Publishing MND Kids as a tool to educate, inform and engage Mexican American kids in the U.S. about Mexico. – Active Launching MND en Español to reach a broader audience of Mexican Americans who might prefer to read in Spanish – Coming soon Engaging with the Mexican government to inspire them to leverage our platform to connect with both Mexican American communities and foreign commuities in Mexico – Coming soon Launching a new podcast targeting the Mexican American community – Coming soon Publishing a deep-dive series on Education in Mexico to highlight problem areas, as well as opportunities for engagement and improvement – Coming soon

We are certain that both countries can achieve massive benefits from a more actively engaged Mexican American diaspora. The team at MND will do our part to educate and inform the Mexican American community, and to inspire leaders to increase the engagement between the two countries. We have no doubt that a more actively engaged diaspora can accomplish great things.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: New episode: ‘Confidently Wrong’ breaks down the state of public education in Mexico
World.content:
Many foreigners have a positive impression of the private education system in Mexico. I have written about it several times, and we even did an entire season of our Confidently Wrong podcast on what it is like for foreign kids to go to school in Mexico. We interviewed kids, parents, teachers, and administrators about what they have experienced and what they would recommend to families considering making the move.

In this new episode of Confidently Wrong, we focus on the public education system in Mexico. Several weeks ago, the international standardized testing results of PISA were released for 15-year-olds across the globe. The results were troubling in most countries, but especially bad in Mexico, which saw its results continue to deteriorate across the board. I reviewed the disastrous results in a recent article here: Mexico fails the 2025 PISA evaluation: A perspective from our CEO.

The test results show that nearly half of Mexican 15-year-olds cannot read at the most basic level. This means that they cannot even read at a level that permits them to learn. Imagine what awaits these kids in an economy that increasingly requires knowledge of AI and robotics for what used to be entry-level manufacturing jobs.

Mexico News Daily recently wrote a deep-dive report into the Mexican public education system. We looked at key metrics across the educational spectrum, and looked at the country’s progress (or lack of) in each. You can check it out here: The MND Mexico Well-being Series, Part 2: Education.

Tune into this week’s episode of Confidently Wrong as we break down the problems and implications of the public education system in Mexico.

World.title: Antonelli Takes Austin Pole, Eyes F1 Title
World.content:
The Circuit of the Americas seen from a passing airliner in November 2024; the 5.513 km track winds around the paddock and observation tower. Photo: Spheroidite / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

Key Facts Who: Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes) took pole; Verstappen and Isack Hadjar (both Red Bull) follow.

Lap: Antonelli’s 1:34.035 beat Verstappen by 0.179 seconds and Hadjar by 0.215.

Race: Sunday, 25 October, 3 p.m. CDT (4 p.m. ET), 56 laps, 308.432 kilometres.

Title: Antonelli led Mercedes teammate George Russell by 102 points before Austin.

Prediction markets: Kalshi gives Verstappen 45% and Antonelli 43% to win the race (25 October, 00:25 ET).

This story is part of our coverage of the us grand prix 2026. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Formula 1 Qualifying in Austin Is Saturday

Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli will start Sunday’s US Grand Prix 2026 from pole position at Circuit of The Americas in Austin, Texas. He set a 1:34.035 lap in Saturday’s qualifying, 0.179 seconds ahead of Red Bull’s Max Verstappen.

Antonelli leads the drivers’ championship, and a win on Sunday could make him champion with five rounds still to run. The race starts at 3 p.m. Austin time (4 p.m. ET, 20:00 UTC).

How Qualifying Finished

Antonelli topped Q3 on Saturday, 24 October. Verstappen took second with 1:34.214, and Hadjar was third with 1:34.250.

Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton qualified fourth and fifth, at 1:34.267 and 1:34.311. Russell was sixth (1:34.476), ahead of McLaren’s Oscar Piastri (1:34.803) and Lando Norris (1:35.049).

What Antonelli Needs on Sunday

Five rounds remain after Austin, with 125 points available. To be champion in Texas, Antonelli must leave the race at least 125 points clear of every rival.

According to GrandPrix.com, that means winning the race while Russell finishes ninth or lower and Hamilton fifth or lower. A second place would not be enough, even if Russell scored nothing.

Grid Penalties Reshuffle the Back

Audi’s Nico Hülkenberg qualified 12th but starts 11th. Racing Bulls driver Arvid Lindblad, who qualified ninth, drops to 14th after a new combustion engine.

Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto qualified 13th but takes a back-of-the-grid penalty for new power-unit parts. Franco Colapinto also takes a 10-place penalty and starts 21st.

What Prediction Markets Say

Kalshi’s market for the race winner, with 663,168 contracts traded, priced Verstappen at 45% and Antonelli at 43% on 25 October at 00:25 ET. Polymarket’s market on the season’s drivers’ champion, with US$204.7 million traded, put Antonelli at 98.7%.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Prices are bets, not forecasts or polls. Kalshi is regulated in the US by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

What It Means for US Readers

Austin is one of three US rounds on the 2026 calendar, alongside Miami and Las Vegas (19–21 November). COTA has hosted the US Grand Prix since 2012, so a title decided here would be settled on home soil for American fans.

With the race at 4 p.m. ET on a Sunday, a possible championship celebration falls in prime US viewing time. Our earlier piece on how Antonelli can clinch the title and the qualifying preview give the background.

What Is Not Known

The race result, podium and final points were not known when this was written. Penalties, incidents or technical investigations after the start could still change the classification.

Whether Verstappen, Ferrari or McLaren can match Mercedes over 56 laps is also open. Exact penalty sizes for Bortoleto differ between early reports.

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS

Published Sunday, 25 October, 12:07 a.m. ET · Source: Futura Inteligência

Key Facts The country Brazil, Latin America’s largest country, elects its president in a runoff on Sunday 25 October between President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

What happened On Saturday 24 October, the Brazilian polling firm Futura Inteligência published a final runoff survey that shows a technical tie.

The numbers Flávio Bolsonaro has 50.1% of valid votes and Lula 49.9%, a gap of 0.2 points with a 2.2-point margin of error.

The change Futura’s survey of 13 October had Flávio at 51.8% and Lula at 48.2% of valid votes, so the gap has narrowed since.
