World.title: Hungary’s opposition marks 1956 revolution with warnings over freedom and political repression
World.content:
Hungary’s opposition parties used the 70th anniversary of the 1956 revolution to warn about threats to national freedom, criticise Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government and call for political resistance. At the Fidesz–Christian Democrat commemoration in Budapest, former President János Áder recalled how the anti-Soviet uprising shook the world, while Fidesz parliamentary leader János Bóka accused the government of undermining democratic freedoms. At a separate event, Our Homeland leader László Toroczkai announced a new campaign of “national resistance”.

The commemorations took place on Friday, 23 October 2026, as Hungary marked seven decades since the uprising against communist dictatorship and Soviet domination.

While official ceremonies focused on the revolution’s historical legacy and Hungary’s European future, opposition speakers drew parallels between the events of 1956 and present-day political disputes.

Fidesz supporters gather in Budapest to commemorate the 1956 revolution

The opposition Fidesz party and its Christian Democrat ally, KDNP, held their main anniversary event in Bem József Square, a historically significant location on the Buda side of the Danube.

The square was one of the starting points of the demonstrations on 23 October 1956, when thousands gathered near the statue of Polish general Józef Bem before the protests developed into a nationwide uprising.

According to Hungarian news agency MTI, participants filled the square, with some arriving in a procession from the Budapest University of Technology and Economics.

The march, organised by the Flame of ’56 Foundation, featured a 1,848-metre-long Hungarian tricolour banner and a Székely flag.

The event opened with the national anthem and an address by Fidesz MP Gábor Szűcs.

János Áder: The 1956 uprising shook the entire world

Former Hungarian President János Áder focused on the historical significance of the revolution and the sacrifices made by those who resisted Soviet rule.

He recalled that by 1956, Hungarian society had become increasingly disillusioned with the communist system established after the Second World War.

Áder said the uprising had shaken the Soviet empire and demonstrated the strength of Hungarians’ desire for independence.

He emphasised that remembrance remained a collective responsibility, calling on people to honour the revolution’s victims through quiet acts of respect, including visits to Plot 301 of Budapest’s New Public Cemetery.

The burial site became a symbol of communist repression after several leading figures of the revolution, including executed Prime Minister Imre Nagy, were buried there in unmarked graves.

For Áder, the international impact of the revolution remained central to its significance, even though Soviet military intervention ultimately crushed the uprising.

If you missed it – Hungarian Revolution of 1956: Why does its legacy still divide Hungary?

Fidesz accuses government of threatening political freedom

Other speakers adopted a more confrontational tone towards the current government.

Fidesz MP Gábor Szűcs compared the government’s National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office with the ÁVH, the communist-era secret police notorious for political persecution.

He alleged that the authorities were using similar methods against political opponents, claiming that Hungarians once again needed to regain their freedom.

The comparison was a political accusation made by the opposition politician, rather than an established equivalence between the two organisations.

Fidesz parliamentary group leader János Bóka also claimed that fundamental democratic freedoms were under threat.

“There is no political police in a free country,” Bóka said, arguing that authorities should not intimidate political opponents or use arrests as a form of political pressure.

He accused the government of attempting to weaken the opposition and warned against what he described as efforts to recreate a one-party political system.

Bóka argued that Hungary’s independence could not be separated from its freedom, presenting the 1956 uprising as a historical lesson for contemporary politics.

He also criticised the official commemorative session in Parliament, dismissing it as a “cheap farce”, and said Fidesz preferred to celebrate alongside Polish and Italian allies.

Looking ahead, Bóka warned that difficult years awaited the opposition but urged supporters to remain organised.

He called for the creation of “circles of freedom”, presenting continued political mobilisation as a central task for Fidesz.

Former minister’s family reads letter from detention

One of the more personal moments at the Bem Square gathering came when the wife of former culture minister Balázs Hankó appeared on stage with their children.

She read a letter from her husband, who is being held in connection with the National Cultural Fund corruption investigation.

In the letter, Hankó described himself and others detained in the case as “political prisoners”, rejecting the allegations against them.

He asked supporters to spread the message that those under investigation were innocent and appealed for solidarity.

His claims of political persecution were presented as his own position; they do not in themselves establish that the criminal proceedings are politically motivated.

The episode reflected how ongoing disputes over corruption investigations have become part of the wider confrontation between the new government and the former governing parties.

Mária Schmidt opposes changes to House of Terror Museum

Historian Mária Schmidt, the former director-general of Budapest’s House of Terror Museum, strongly criticised government plans to reorganise the institution.

The museum, located on Andrássy Avenue, documents political persecution under Hungary’s Nazi-aligned Arrow Cross regime and the subsequent communist dictatorship.

The Tisza government has presented the proposed changes as an attempt to create a more balanced and impartial exhibition.

Schmidt, however, warned that the reorganisation could alter the presentation of communist-era crimes and the memory of their victims.

She criticised proposals to reconsider the museum’s Gallery of Victimisers, which displays photographs of individuals associated with political repression.

“We will not allow it,” she declared, calling on supporters to resist the changes.

Schmidt also argued that the heroes of 1956 remained important symbols of historical justice and warned against what she regarded as attempts to reinterpret the revolution’s legacy.

Our Homeland announces ‘national resistance’ at separate 1956 commemoration

The opposition Our Homeland Movement (Mi Hazánk) held its own anniversary gathering at Corvin Passage, another landmark of the 1956 revolution.

The passage was the scene of some of the fiercest fighting between Hungarian insurgents and Soviet forces during the uprising.

Party leader László Toroczkai announced plans to establish “national resistance circles”, which he said would oppose government decisions the party regarded as contrary to Hungary’s national interests.

Hungary’s opposition marks 1956 revolution with warnings over freedom and political repression. Photo: MTI

According to MTI’s report published by Infostart, Toroczkai said the groups would use civil and political means to organise resistance.

Their first announced campaign would target amendments to Hungary’s child protection legislation.

Toroczkai called on parents to submit written declarations opposing sessions delivered by representatives of LGBTQ organisations to their children.

He also criticised the government’s decision to honour writer and Nobel laureate László Krasznahorkai and pianist András Schiff with state decorations.

In his speech, the party leader objected to the invitations extended to several international figures for the anniversary events, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, French President Emmanuel Macron and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

He accused European leaders of pursuing policies that threatened national sovereignty, presenting his party’s planned resistance campaign as a continuation of Hungary’s historical struggle for self-determination.

Our Homeland deputy leader Máté Tóth also emphasised the importance of protecting Hungary’s national identity and independence.

What’s next? EU funds return to Hungary as von der Leyen and Costa hail democratic renewal on 1956 anniversary

The legacy of 1956 remains central to Hungary’s political divisions

The opposition commemorations illustrated how differently Hungary’s political parties interpret the contemporary meaning of the 1956 revolution.

While Áder concentrated on the uprising’s historical importance, Fidesz politicians used the anniversary to challenge the current government’s conduct, particularly over corruption investigations, political freedoms and the planned reorganisation of the House of Terror Museum.

Our Homeland, meanwhile, focused on national sovereignty and announced a new grassroots political initiative.

The gatherings also took place against the backdrop of the official commemorations organised by Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government, which emphasised democratic renewal, national unity and Hungary’s place in Europe.

Seventy years after Soviet troops crushed the uprising, the anniversary remains an important occasion for honouring the revolution’s victims. At the same time, the speeches in Budapest demonstrated that the meaning of freedom, independence and the legacy of 1956 continues to be debated across Hungary’s political spectrum.

World.title: PM Péter Magyar marks 1956 revolution with powerful message on freedom, unity and Hungary’s future
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar described the 1956 revolution as “possibly the most important revolution of the 20th century” in a major speech marking its 70th anniversary in Budapest on Friday. Addressing crowds in Kossuth Square outside Parliament, Magyar paid tribute to the heroes who resisted Soviet oppression, reaffirmed Hungary’s place in a free and democratic Europe, and pledged to build a country where political differences would no longer divide the nation.

The prime minister delivered his address on 23 October 2026, exactly 70 years after the outbreak of the anti-communist uprising and 37 years after the proclamation of the Hungarian Republic in 1989.

According to the Hungarian news agency MTI, Magyar said that the revolutionaries of 1956 had changed the course of history despite ultimately being overwhelmed by Soviet military force.

The 1956 revolution that shook the world

“On October 23, 1956, a few hundred thousand Hungarians and the millions joining them wrote world history,” Magyar declared.

He described the revolution’s 13 days as a unique period in Hungarian history, when ordinary people confronted one of the world’s most powerful military forces and demanded national independence.

“In those 13 glorious days, the Hungarian people said, shouted, screamed as one: Russkies go home!” he recalled, referring to the famous revolutionary slogan demanding the withdrawal of Soviet troops.

For international readers, the 1956 Hungarian Revolution began with student demonstrations in Budapest that developed into a nationwide uprising against communist dictatorship and Soviet control. Soviet forces launched a massive military intervention on 4 November, crushing the resistance. Thousands were killed, many more suffered reprisals, and approximately 200,000 Hungarians fled the country.

Magyar argued that although the revolution was defeated militarily, its political and moral significance endured.

He said Hungarians had driven “the first and perhaps most important nail into the coffin of communism”, exposing the contradiction between the regime’s promises of freedom and its violent suppression of popular demands.

The prime minister also recalled the executions of former Prime Minister Imre Nagy, Defence Minister Pál Maléter and journalist Miklós Gimes in June 1958, presenting their sacrifices as symbols of the struggle for an independent and democratic Hungary.

Magyar: No leader’s power can outweigh Hungary’s freedom

One of the strongest political messages of Magyar’s speech concerned the relationship between national sovereignty and foreign influence.

He insisted that every Hungarian leader must recognise that remaining in power can never be more important than protecting the country’s freedom.

“No Hungarian leader may back-seat the blood sacrifice of 1956 for the sake of momentary economic bargains or dubious alliances,” he warned.

“Anyone who makes excuses for an aggressor after 1956, or subordinates the nation to foreign imperial interests, has understood nothing of the message of 1956.”

Magyar argued that the uprising demonstrated that a government might preserve its authority temporarily through foreign support, but could never permanently suppress the Hungarian people’s desire for freedom.

His remarks connected the historical experience of Soviet domination with broader questions about sovereignty, international alliances and the responsibilities of political leaders today.

If you missed it – Hungarian Revolution of 1956: Why does its legacy still divide Hungary?

Hungary belongs to a free and democratic Europe

Magyar also used the anniversary to underline Hungary’s European identity, rejecting the idea that the country should continually balance between East and West.

He argued that Hungarians had already made their choice in 1956: they wanted to belong to a free and democratic Europe.

According to the prime minister, Hungary should be a reliable partner that participates confidently in international cooperation rather than isolating itself through confrontation.

Hungarians wanted to be allies who could sit at the common table with their heads held high, he said, “not adventurers isolating themselves through blackmail and go-it-alone paths”.

He presented a strong, independent and forward-looking Hungary as one capable of meeting emerging challenges through knowledge, courage and cooperation.

The European message was particularly significant given the change of government following the April 2026 election and the renewed emphasis on rebuilding Hungary’s relationships with its European partners.

The legacy of 1956 belongs to every Hungarian

Another central theme was the need to overcome political divisions within Hungarian society.

Magyar rejected the notion that national symbols, patriotic identity or the memory of the revolution could belong exclusively to any single political movement.

“For long years, we were told the lie that the nation and everything national can belong to only one side,” he said.

He criticised the practice of treating fellow citizens with different political opinions as enemies, arguing that the Hungarian flag, national coat of arms, tricolour cockade and historical memory of 1956 belonged to everyone.

The prime minister recalled the diverse backgrounds of those who participated in the revolution, including students, workers, intellectuals, soldiers and religious figures.

He named several prominent participants and victims, among them Ilona Tóth, István Angyal, Mária Wittner, István Bibó and Cardinal József Mindszenty.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar described the 1956 revolution as “possibly the most important revolution of the 20th century” in a major speech marking its 70th anniversary in Budapest on Friday.

Their differences, Magyar argued, demonstrated that the revolution had united people across ideological and social boundaries.

He called on Hungarians to make room for people who think differently and warned against dividing citizens into supposedly worthy and unworthy members of the nation.

Read more news about the Hungarian Revolution of 1956

From the sacrifice of 1956 to the responsibilities of government

Magyar pledged that his government would carry forward the revolution’s legacy not only through remembrance but also through concrete principles of governance.

He argued that the freedom demanded in 1956 also included the dignity of work, economic security and the possibility of planning a future at home.

“We carry this legacy forward when we build a country where freedom comes with a decent livelihood, respect and opportunity,” he said.

The prime minister promised to regard government as a public service rather than a means of exercising power over citizens.

He also pledged that public money would once again be treated as the community’s property, that the law would apply equally to everyone and that political leadership would be based on accountability.

Magyar said his Tisza government would not create new enemies or deepen divisions between Hungarians.

Instead, he described its responsibility as turning political freedom into security, dignity and opportunity for every citizen.

These statements were commitments outlined in his anniversary address rather than announcements of specific new legislative measures.

The light of 1956 must guide future generations

Towards the end of his speech, Magyar described the revolution as a “fixed star shining beyond the decades of the dictatorship”.

He said its example had reached beyond Budapest, throughout Hungary and across the Iron Curtain, inspiring people who had previously known little about the country.

The memory of the revolution, he argued, continued to pass from one generation to another, carrying lessons about courage, solidarity and the defence of freedom.

Magyar also thanked the countries that welcomed Hungarians fleeing persecution after the Soviet crackdown, expressing gratitude for their solidarity and for the presence of foreign representatives at the anniversary commemorations.

The prime minister concluded by stressing that freedom was not simply the achievement of a historical moment, but a responsibility requiring constant attention.

“Freedom is not the celebration of a single day but responsibility to be shouldered every day,” he said.

His speech brought together remembrance of the victims of Soviet repression and a vision of contemporary Hungary built around democracy, national unity and European cooperation.

For Magyar, the most important tribute to the revolutionaries of 1956 was not merely to honour their memory, but to ensure that their struggle continued to shape the country’s future.

“It would be good to leave our children a country they can be proud of, a country we can be proud of,” he concluded.

What’s next? EU funds return to Hungary as von der Leyen and Costa hail democratic renewal on 1956 anniversary

World.title: EU funds return to Hungary as von der Leyen and Costa hail democratic renewal on 1956 anniversary
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced that EU funds are once again accessible to Hungary, while European Council President António Costa emphasised the importance of democracy, national sovereignty and European unity. Both leaders addressed a commemorative session of the Hungarian Parliament in Budapest on Friday, marking the 70th anniversary of the 1956 anti-Soviet revolution.

Von der Leyen: EU funds are returning to Hungary

Speaking at the Hungarian Parliament on 23 October, Ursula von der Leyen praised the reforms introduced by Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government, saying they were already delivering tangible results.

According to the European Commission president, Hungary has strengthened legislation against fraud and corruption, improved transparency in public spending and is joining the European Public Prosecutor’s Office.

“European funding is back,” von der Leyen declared, confirming that access to the Horizon Europe research programme had been restored and Hungarian students could once again participate fully in Erasmus.

She also indicated that further progress was expected before the end of 2026, including developments concerning NextGenerationEU recovery funding and financial resources linked to academic freedom.

“So, your hard work is paying off. Investor confidence is returning,” she said, adding that Hungary’s renewed commitment to the European project was strengthening the EU as a whole.

Her remarks signal an important development in Hungary’s relationship with Brussels following years of disputes over rule-of-law concerns and the suspension of substantial EU funding. However, the announcement did not specify the precise amount of additional funding to be released by the end of the year.

Hungary’s democratic renewal sends a message to Europe

In her full address published by the European Commission, von der Leyen drew parallels between the courage of the 1956 revolutionaries and Hungary’s recent political transformation.

Referring to the April 2026 parliamentary election, she highlighted the exceptionally high voter turnout and described the result as the beginning of a new chapter for the country.

She argued that Hungary had demonstrated that democratic decline could be reversed and that disinformation and fearmongering could be overcome through democratic participation.

Von der Leyen also recalled the bravery of the students and workers who confronted Soviet oppression seven decades earlier. Their struggle, she stressed, illustrated why democracy and freedom could never be taken for granted.

She concluded by invoking French writer Albert Camus, who had called for European solidarity following the Hungarian uprising, underlining the responsibility of today’s Europeans to preserve unity.

If you missed it: Hungary ranks among Europe’s worst for rule of law in new global index

Costa: Democracies must never give way to tyranny

European Council President António Costa likewise placed the historical significance of 1956 at the centre of his address.

“The memory of the 1956 Revolution is also a reminder that democracies must not be complacent in the face of tyranny and imperialism,” Costa said.

He described the uprising as an expression of the Hungarian people’s determination to defend independence and self-determination, linking it to other decisive moments in the country’s history, including the revolutions of 1848 and the democratic transition of 1989.

Costa also emphasised that European integration should not come at the expense of national identity. Rather, the EU’s diversity of languages, cultures, histories and traditions strengthens cooperation among its members.

EU membership has transformed Hungary’s economy

In his official speech published by the European Council, Costa highlighted the economic benefits of Hungary’s accession to the EU in 2004.

He noted that Hungary’s economy had nearly tripled in size over the past 22 years, while average salaries had increased fivefold.

According to Costa, almost 80% of Hungarian exports go to EU countries, while nearly 70% of imports originate from other member states, illustrating Hungary’s integration into the European single market.

However, he argued that economic prosperity was inseparable from democratic institutions, transparent governance, freedom of expression and academic freedom.

Costa also cited figures suggesting that 80% of Hungarians regard the European Union as a source of stability and consider membership highly beneficial.

The legacy of 1956 and Hungary’s European future

The speeches came exactly seven decades after the outbreak of the Hungarian Revolution on 23 October 1956, when demonstrators demanded political freedom and an end to Soviet domination. The uprising was subsequently crushed by Soviet military intervention, forcing approximately 200,000 Hungarians to flee their homeland.

Although von der Leyen focused more heavily on Hungary’s reforms and the restoration of access to EU funds, both European leaders presented the anniversary as a reminder of the connection between democracy, prosperity and European cooperation.

Their messages also reflected a broader shift in relations between Budapest and Brussels following Hungary’s change of government earlier this year.

For Hungary, the immediate significance lies in renewed opportunities for European funding, education and research. For the EU, the anniversary offered an opportunity to reaffirm the shared democratic values that both leaders identified as central to Europe’s future.

World.title: Hungary could gain billions from defence industry expansion, Budapest conference hears
World.content:
Europe’s growing defence budgets will not automatically translate into stronger military capabilities without new financing mechanisms, industry investment and greater cooperation between governments and financial institutions. This was the central message of the International Defence Finance Conference held in Budapest on 21 October, where Canadian and Hungarian officials, international banking executives and defence finance experts discussed the proposed Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB).

The conference, entitled Financing Defence, Security and Resilience in Hungary and Central & Eastern Europe, was convened by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Hungary and Halftermayer & Partners, with Baker McKenzie, PwC and ING among its sponsors.

The event brought together representatives of government, commercial banks, international financial institutions and the defence industry to examine how rising European and NATO defence commitments could be translated into industrial investment, stronger supply chains and sustainable economic growth.

A particular focus was the proposed DSRB, a new international financing institution intended to address longstanding barriers to investment in defence and security.

Canadian businesses see opportunities in Europe’s defence industry

Opening the conference, Nicholas Sarvari, the president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Hungary highlighted the considerable potential for cooperation between Canadian companies and European defence manufacturers.

He noted that Ontario alone had approximately 400 companies licensed to operate in the relevant sector, with additional industrial capabilities in provinces including Quebec and Alberta.

According ige l chamber president, smaller companies are increasingly interested in entering the defence industry, developing international partnerships and expanding their production capabilities. However, access to finance remains a major obstacle.

Financing Defence, Security and Resilience in Hungary and Central & Eastern Europe. Photo by Alpár Kató

„What’s missing in all of it? Finance. That’s a ige lement of it,” he told participants.

Sarvari explained that traditional commercial banks have often been reluctant to support military technology projects, creating difficulties for innovative businesses seeking to develop new products or expand production.

The chamber president also emphasised the organisation’s ambition to move beyond its traditional networking role and facilitate practical business cooperation between Canadian and European partners.

Financing Defence, Security and Resilience in Hungary and Central & Eastern Europe. Photo by CCCH/Gréta Sánta

If you missed it – Deterrence needs a balance sheet: The rise of Europe’s defence finance ecosystem

Canadian ambassador highlights proposed international defence bank

Canada’s ambassador to Hungary, Her Excellency Judith Gelbman, underlined the importance of financial institutions in strengthening the industrial and technological foundations of collective security.

She argued that increasing defence expenditure was only one part of the challenge. Governments and industry must also ensure that manufacturers have sufficient capital to expand production and meet growing demand.

“Increased defense spending doesn’t automatically translate into increased industrial output if companies are lacking the financing to scale up,” the ambassador said.

She outlined Canada’s cooperation with international allies and partners on the proposed Defence, Security and Resilience Bank.

Modelled on existing multilateral financial institutions, including the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the proposed DSRB is intended to provide multi-year investment financing on favourable terms throughout the defence and security supply chain.

Small and medium-sized enterprises would be among its intended beneficiaries, particularly those facing difficulties obtaining conventional bank financing despite their strategic importance.

HE Gelbman stressed that the proposed institution would complement rather than replace existing European mechanisms, including the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) initiative, the European Investment Bank and national defence financing programmes.

Canada’s ambassador to Hungary, Her Excellency Judith Gelbman. Photo by CCCH Gréta Sánta

She also encouraged participants to use the conference to establish practical connections between defence companies, financial institutions and policymakers.

Hungarian state secretary: Finance must become part of defence strategy

Hungarian Deputy State Secretary János Szőnyegi offered a broader assessment of Europe’s changing defence financing requirements.

He argued that European governments had recognised the need for higher defence spending but had not yet fully addressed how the necessary industrial expansion should be financed.

For decades, defence capabilities were developed primarily through government procurement programmes. However, modern defence production depends on a much wider ecosystem encompassing manufacturers, smaller suppliers, dual-use technologies, research and development, infrastructure, logistics, energy, skilled workers and private investment.

Szőnyegi explained that companies often need substantial capital before they receive the government orders that would make their investments commercially viable.

This creates a financing gap between projects that are strategically necessary and those considered sufficiently attractive by conventional commercial lenders.

The deputy state secretary proposed three criteria for evaluating future defence financing mechanisms: speed, scale and strategic impact.

Hungarian Deputy State Secretary János Szőnyegi. Photo by CCCH/Gréta Sánta

Financing should be available more quickly than traditional procurement cycles allow, public resources should help mobilise private investment, and strategically essential projects should be able to obtain support even when their commercial risk profiles are challenging.

“Finance is becoming part of defense strategy itself,” Szőnyegi declared.

He also stressed the importance of strengthening Europe’s domestic manufacturing capacity rather than relying exclusively on purchases from external suppliers.

Concluding his address, he posed what he described as the central challenge facing policymakers and financial institutions: how to turn defence expenditure into actual defence capabilities.

Hungary’s defence investments could have a EUR 14 billion economic impact difference

One of the conference’s most significant economic assessments came from Dr Ferenc Antal, Managing Partner at Halftermayer & Partners.

In his keynote presentation on international defence finance, the geopolitical outlook and the proposed DSRB, Antal examined the economic implications of Europe’s growing defence commitments, with particular attention to Hungary.

He argued that European governments faced a difficult balancing act between financing defence requirements and maintaining economic competitiveness.

For Hungary, he suggested, the economic consequences would depend heavily on how much of the additional defence expenditure could be channelled into domestic production and industrial development.

“If we focus on 10% of local added value versus 40% of local added value, the difference in the next four years is 14 billion euros,” Antal said.

The figure compares two hypothetical scenarios presented by the speaker, rather than an already realised economic gain.

His calculations suggest that increasing domestic participation in defence-related production could have substantial implications for Hungary’s industrial development and economic performance.

Antal also examined the potential benefits of financing defence investments through a highly rated international institution.

According to calculations he presented, access to a financing facility with a AAA credit rating could potentially generate an annual financing cost benefit of approximately EUR 80 million.

Dr Ferenc Antal, Managing Partner at Halftermayer & Partners. Photo by CCCH/Gréta Sánta

However, he argued that cheaper borrowing would represent only part of the proposed DSRB’s potential contribution.

The greater opportunity, in his assessment, lies in establishing a financial ecosystem with specialised expertise, clearer regulatory frameworks, appropriate risk management practices and better cooperation between defence companies and commercial banks.

Antal noted that banks had traditionally faced two major obstacles when considering defence industry investments: reputational concerns and uncertainty surrounding financial risks.

The latter include limited visibility over future procurement contracts, cash flows and the commercial sustainability of individual projects.

He suggested that international cooperation and clearer financing frameworks could help make defence companies more bankable, particularly in Central and Eastern Europe.

What’s next? Billions at stake in NATO’s new pledge: how much of the defence spend stays in Hungary?

International banking executives discuss the emerging defence finance architecture

The conference continued with an executive panel examining the proposed DSRB and the emerging international defence finance architecture.

The discussion, entitled DSRB and the Emerging International Defence Finance Architecture – International Lessons, Product Priorities and Market Expectations, brought together David Marks of the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank Development Group; Xavier Guzman, Country Managing Partner at DLA Piper Luxembourg; Julian Mömesheim, Corporate Bank Defence Coordinator at Deutsche Bank; and Michal Hubert Mrozek, Executive Vice President and Head of Wholesale Banking CEE Network at ING Bank. The panel was moderated by Dr Ferenc Antal.

DSRB and the Emerging International Defence Finance Architecture – International Lessons, Product Priorities and Market Expectations. Photo by CCCH/Gréta Sánta

The session focused on the international institutional framework surrounding defence finance, the types of financial products required by the sector and the expectations of commercial market participants.

The involvement of representatives from international banks, legal advisory services and the DSRB development initiative illustrated the range of expertise required to design financial mechanisms capable of supporting defence-related investment.

Hungarian and regional banks examine practical financing challenges

A second executive panel focused specifically on the needs of Hungarian and Central and Eastern European financial institutions.

Entitled What Hungarian and CEE Financiers Need from the DSRB: Bankability, Guarantees, Prudential Treatment and Project Pipeline, the session examined the financial and regulatory considerations relevant to expanding defence investment in the region.

Participants included Dr Ádám Banai, Executive Director and Chief Economist at the Hungarian National Bank; Andrew Giddings; József Vida of CAE; and Kamil Pruchnik, Senior Regional Representative for Hungary and Poland at the European Investment Fund. The discussion was moderated by Dr Sándor Kovács, Senior Counsel and Defence Lead at CMS Hungary.

What Hungarian and CEE Financiers Need from the DSRB: Bankability, Guarantees, Prudential Treatment and Project Pipeline. Photo by CCCH/Gréta Sánta

The panel’s agenda addressed several practical questions facing lenders and investors, including creditworthiness, guarantee structures, prudential treatment and the development of a pipeline of financeable projects.

Defence financing becomes an economic competitiveness issue

Across the keynote presentations and panel discussions, a common theme emerged: increasing defence budgets alone will not guarantee stronger industrial capacity.

For Hungary and other Central and Eastern European economies, the challenge extends beyond military procurement to questions of investment, domestic added value, industrial competitiveness and access to capital.

The proposed Defence, Security and Resilience Bank was presented as one possible instrument for addressing these challenges, alongside existing European initiatives, national financing programmes and private-sector investment.

The conference also highlighted the potential importance of international partnerships, particularly between Canadian and European companies, in developing defence technologies and expanding manufacturing capabilities.

While the proposed DSRB remains under development, the discussions in Budapest demonstrated the growing attention being paid to the financial structures needed to support Europe’s defence industry.

For Hungary, the central economic question is not simply how much additional money will be spent on defence, but how much of that expenditure can be converted into domestic production, investment and long-term industrial growth.

World.title: EU flight compensation rules: What changes from today, 23 October, and what must wait until 2027?
World.content:
New EU flight compensation rules promise faster refunds, simpler claims and stronger passenger protection across Europe. However, despite the attention surrounding the latest reforms, travellers should be aware of an important distinction: the newly approved reimbursement measures will not apply until 23 October 2027.

The European Parliament approved legislation strengthening passenger rights on 20 October 2026, with 652 votes in favour, two against and eight abstentions.

According to AIRportal.hu, the changes will introduce standardised refund and compensation procedures, clarify the responsibilities of online booking platforms and improve assistance for passengers with disabilities.

The legislation is part of a broader European effort to make passenger rights easier to enforce across different forms of transport.

EU flight compensation rules: What is changing?

One of the most important developments is the introduction of standardised EU forms for reimbursement and compensation claims.

Instead of navigating different procedures for individual airlines or transport companies, passengers will be able to use common European forms available in all official EU languages.

The European Commission will make these forms accessible online, while transport operators will also be able to provide equivalent alternatives.

According to the European Commission, the legislation is intended to make passenger rights more transparent and improve their enforcement.

The changes will cover several transport sectors, although some requirements differ depending on the mode of transport.

If you missed it: Flight diversion plans need a passenger plan too

Flight refunds within 14 days

The reforms also address a common difficulty faced by air passengers: recovering money for tickets purchased through travel agencies or online booking platforms.

Under the new arrangements, passengers will generally be entitled to a full refund within 14 days when reimbursement is handled through an intermediary.

The process will involve two stages:

First seven days: The airline transfers the refund to the intermediary.

The airline transfers the refund to the intermediary. Following seven days: The intermediary returns the money to the passenger.

The reimbursement will generally include the original airfare and applicable intermediary fees, although limited exceptions may apply.

Booking platforms will also have to explain the relevant refund arrangements before a passenger completes a purchase.

The new rules are designed to prevent situations in which passengers struggle to determine whether the airline or booking platform is responsible for returning their money.

What compensation can passengers claim for delayed or cancelled flights?

It is important to distinguish between ticket refunds and financial compensation.

A refund allows passengers to recover the price of an unused ticket in qualifying circumstances. Compensation is an additional payment that may be available when flights are significantly delayed, cancelled at short notice or passengers are denied boarding.

Under the EU’s existing compensation framework, eligible passengers may receive:

€250 for flights of up to 1,500 kilometres.

for flights of up to 1,500 kilometres. €400 for longer flights within the EU and certain flights between 1,500 and 3,500 kilometres.

for longer flights within the EU and certain flights between 1,500 and 3,500 kilometres. €600 for other flights exceeding 3,500 kilometres.

These amounts have been maintained under the revised air passenger rights framework, as confirmed by the European Parliament’s legislative documentation.

However, airlines are not automatically required to pay compensation for every disruption. Extraordinary circumstances, including certain severe weather events, can affect eligibility.

Stronger protection for passengers with disabilities

The legislation introduces additional safeguards for passengers with disabilities or reduced mobility.

When an airline requires a passenger to travel with an accompanying person for safety reasons, the companion will be entitled to travel free of charge.

The aim is to bring air travel protections more closely into line with arrangements already available in other European transport sectors.

National enforcement authorities will also receive stronger powers to investigate potential violations of passenger rights, including launching checks without waiting for individual complaints.

The Council of the European Union has described these measures as part of efforts to strengthen the enforcement of passenger rights throughout the EU.

What do the changes mean for travellers flying from Hungary?

The reforms will also be relevant to travellers using Budapest’s Ferenc Liszt International Airport and other Hungarian airports.

For international visitors, EU air passenger rights generally apply to flights departing from airports within the European Union, regardless of the passenger’s nationality.

They also cover flights arriving in the EU from non-EU countries when operated by qualifying European airlines.

For example, a British, American or Canadian tourist departing from Budapest may benefit from EU passenger protection even if they do not hold EU citizenship.

Passengers booking flights through third-party travel websites should particularly benefit from clearer responsibilities and more predictable reimbursement procedures once the new legislation becomes applicable.

When will the new rules actually apply?

Although the broader EU air passenger rights reform has already progressed through the legislative process, the latest measures concerning enforcement and refunds are not applicable on 23 October 2026.

The enforcement legislation still requires formal approval by the Council of the European Union before publication in the EU’s Official Journal.

The new provisions are scheduled to apply from 23 October 2027, alongside the revised air passenger rights framework.

Until then, travellers affected by cancellations, long delays or denied boarding should continue to rely on the applicable EU passenger rights rules.

For passengers flying to and from Hungary, the reforms should eventually mean clearer information, simpler procedures and stronger safeguards when seeking refunds or compensation. The key point for travellers today is that existing rights remain enforceable, while the latest improvements are still awaiting implementation.

World.title: ‘Collective Fear’: Pressure on Serbians with Disabilities to Vote for Ruling Party
World.content:
According to Serbia’s 2022 census, more than 356,000 people with disabilities in Serbia, or roughly 5.5 per cent of the population over the age of two.

For years, Serbian election authorities have been criticised for failing to ensure voting privacy for people with disabilities, such as those living with blindness or vision impairment who are not provided with braille ballot papers; international election observers have previously cited the inaccessibility of polling stations for people with disabilities.

Political pressure on socially vulnerable voters in Serbia has been documented before.

In a 2023 report, election watchdog CRTA identified networks of political influence within social welfare centres and collected accounts from employees describing the use of social assistance to secure political support, including votes and participation in party activities.

CRTA’s monitoring of the 2023 elections also documented a case in which beneficiaries of social welfare support were denied that support for supporting an opposition party.

According to 2021 data from the association Creative-educational centre, people with disabilities and their families are among those at highest risk of poverty, with over 70 per cent of families living below the poverty line and only 13 per cent of people with disabilities in work.

Many people with disabilities are dependent on state welfare support – financial as well as in healthcare support and services – and on associations that usually provide help with access to assistive devices, education, training and employment.

Out of a dozen people interviewed by BIRN for this story, five reported witnessing statements from representatives of these associations that could be interpreted as pressure to vote for the SNS.

A person from a disability organisation in southern Serbia said the recently appointed head of the organisation had asked others within the organisation to pledge their vote for the ruling party and its candidate for prime minister, ex-President Aleksandar Vucic.

“I was present at the assembly when she was elected president,” the person said. “Afterwards, she told several people to stay because she wanted to ask them something. She then took each of them outside individually, including my neighbour. When my neighbour returned, I asked her what she had been asked. She told me she had immediately realised what it was about – whether she was willing to pledge her support to Vucic and the SNS as a secure vote.”

Many of these organisations are dependent on funding from public coffers.

Another person from a Belgrade-based organisation said such pressure is commonplace.

“We receive threats that our funding will be cut,” the person said.

Associations linked to politics

World.title: Week in Review: Polls and Storms
World.content:
A two-year-long political and societal crisis is set to culminate in parliamentary elections set for October 25 in Serbia. But will the elections put an end to the crisis, or make it worse? In his opinion piece for Balkan Insight, Djorjde Trikos looks at how and why the tide in Serbia may be turning against the Serbian Progressive Party and its de facto leader, Aleksandar Vucic.

Our investigations and analyses also look into how the ruling party is pulling out all the stops to ensure a favourable outcome, from pressuring public sector employees to obstructing an audit of the country’s electoral roll.

World.title: Proposed Law to Curb Powers of Hague-Based Court Returned to Kosovo Assembly
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Supporters of former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leader and former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci take part in a march in support of him in Pristina, Kosovo, prior to the verdict, September 12, 2026. EPA/GEORGI LICOVSKI

Kosovo President Justina Shiroka Pula sent the amended Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC) bill back to parliament on Thursday for review on the request of the Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) which had proposed the bill, less than three weeks after its controversial approval.

The law, which aims to curtail the jurisdiction of the Hague-based court, came after weeks of street protests led by Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) veterans, who rallied under the slogan “Not in my name” – a reference to the KSC judge’s choice of words, “In the name of the people of Kosovo”, when he read the verdict.

“The president received a formal proposal from the parliamentary group of the Democratic Party of Kosovo – the sponsor of the legislation – to allow the assembly to reconsider the law, specifically the provisions concerning the jurisdiction and mandate of the Specialist Chambers,” read a statement from the president’s office on Thursday.

“The president has reiterated her opposition to any attempt to distort the historical truth of Kosovo, to cast doubt on the liberationist nature of the war, or to equate the people who fought for freedom and survival with the regime that oppressed them,” the statement read.

The initial bill was passed after four former KLA leaders were convicted by the KSC for the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder, committed between April 1998 and June 1999.

Hashim Thaci and Jakup Krasniqi were sentenced to 25 years in prison each and Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi received 18 and 13 years, respectively, with credit for time served in detention from November 2020. The verdict can be appealed and their lawyers are working to challenge the conviction.

Given the uncertainty over whether the KSC will indict anyone else, the effect of the bill is uncertain, but the message it sent was clear, and the European Union was unhappy.

“The Law […] goes against Kosovo’s international obligations towards the EU,” read a statement from the EU after the law was initially approved. The EU finances most of the court’s operations.

In a speech at the Berlin Process Summit in Montenegro on Thursday, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said that “weeks and months of defining moments” lie ahead for the Western Balkans and reminded Kosovo of its obligations under international law.

On Thursday, Perparim Gruda, a MP from PDK who was involved in drafting the recent KSC bill wrote on Facebook that “there is no error in the law amending the Law on the Specialist Chambers.”

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers is a hybrid court, part of Kosovo’s judiciary but located in The Hague and staffed by internationals. The court was established in 2015 under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies. Hashim Thaci was one of the main Kosovar supporters of the establishment of the court.

Since the conviction of the former KLA leaders over a month ago, criticism of the KSC has continued unabated in Kosovo. On October 14, Kosovo’s Ombudsperson, Naim Qelaj, held an event in Pristina to demand external oversight of the KSC.

Qelaj claimed that the court “has not been subject to democratic monitoring and control by the institutions of the Republic of Kosovo, creating a lack of transparency and accountability towards the citizens and institutions of Kosovo”.

He said it should report to the Kosovo authorities and that the Ombudsperson institution should be able to have access to its work.

KSC spokesperson Angela Griep told BIRN that “according to the legal framework of the Specialist Chambers, the Kosovo Ombudsperson does not have any responsibility with respect to the Specialist Chambers. This responsibility falls exclusively with the Ombudsperson of the Specialist Chambers in accordance with the Kosovo Constitution”.

World.title: One Dead, Crew Members Missing After Ship Sinks off Romania
World.content:
A Romanian navy squad during NATO naval drill ‘Sea Shield 24’ on the Black Sea, off the coast of Constanta, Romania, 16 April 2024. Photo: EPA/ROBERT GHEMENT

Romanian maritime authorities launched a rescue operation on Friday morning about 24 kilometres off the coast after a vessel was reportedly struck by a drone.

Rescuers are continuing to search for three missing crew members, according to preliminary reports.

The circumstances of the incident remain unclear, including the origin of the drone and whether the vessel was deliberately targeted.

President Nicusor Dan reacted swiftly to the incident, saying that it “is another event in the process of escalation that Russia is pursuing in the Black Sea region.”

The sinking follows an incident on October 15 when two other commercial ships were hit overnight while anchored in the Black Sea near the mouth of the Danube-Black Sea Canal, a major shipping route used to transport Ukrainian goods. Ukraine’s Black Sea ports have been a frequent target of Russian attacks.

Similar incidents have also occurred in Bulgarian territorial waters, where drone strikes have reportedly left at least 23 sailors dead or missing.

The escalating tensions in the Black Sea have prompted NATO to announce increased surveillance in the region following recent attacks on commercial vessels.

Meanwhile, Romania has proposed that it join Bulgaria and Turkey, the other two NATO member states bordering the Black Sea, in establishing a joint military command to be led by the three countries on a rotational basis.

World.title: Alleged Police Violence Against Minors Alarms Albania
World.content:
In a video shared on Monday evening, a group of police officers can be seen rushing towards several young people and beating them with batons. Amid the blows, one of them can be heard shouting that he is only 13 years old.

BIRN was unable to independently verify the ages of the young people in the video, but similar footage showing police in Tirana using violence against protesters, including minors, has circulated widely in the media and on social media over the past week.

The footage has raised concerns about how the State Police is treating children and teenagers involved in the wave of protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government.

World.title: Serbia Braces for Most Uncertain Elections in 14 Years
World.content:
On Sunday, Serbia is bracing for what could be its most uncertain and high-stakes elections in 14 years, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, facing a challenge that has emerged out of a two-year student-led protest movement.

Since 2012, Aleksandar Vucic and his party SNS have largely dominated the political and electoral landscape. This time, however, the election outcome is far less predictable, political analysts say, as the student movement has reshaped the opposition landscape and mobilised supporters well beyond the established parties.

“These are the first elections in a long time whose outcome is entirely uncertain,” Nebojsa Vladisavljevic, a professor at the Faculty of Political Sciences in Belgrade, told BIRN.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czech Culture Ministry Cuts Funding for Velvet Revolution Anniversary
World.content:
Former Hungarian central bank chief detained; govt tries to solve budget dilemma

Hungary’s former central bank governor, Gyorgy Matolcsy, was detained on Wednesday on suspicion of economic fraud causing substantial financial losses and the use of forged documents. Under Matolcsy, the Hungarian National Bank spent lavishly on refurbishment projects and established several foundations that channelled money into dubious foreign investments and projects that seemed to benefit family and friends. Several hundred billion forints are alleged to have been diverted from the central bank during his tenure or lost through investments. Media estimates put the total losses at 400-500 billion forints (1.0-1.4 billion euros). The current governor, Mihaly Varga, a former finance minister, and his team had submitted more than 30,000 pages of documents to the special investigative committee on central bank affairs by the end of September. Matolcsy’s detention signals the new government and prosecutors are getting serious about making key figures in the previous administration accountable for financial losses incurred during their 16 years in power. Matolcsy, once former PM Viktor Orban’s cherished economy guru, became governor of the central bank in 2013 after serving as economy minister in 2010-2014. Matolcsy’s term ended in 2025. His son and people in his business circle were reportedly among the main beneficiaries of lavish renovations to the central bank building.

Hungary’s new government tabled its first draft budget, causing disappointment in various quarters. The finance minister warned that budget discipline is necessary to prepare the country for joining the euro, planned for 2030-2032. In the draft budget for 2027, the government has pledged to cut the deficit from the current 7.0 per cent of GDP to 4.9 per cent by the end of next year and to 2.9 per cent for the end of its term in office in 2030. Inflation is forecast at 3.0 per cent and GDP growth at 2.4 per cent. Both Finance Minister Andras Karman and PM Peter Magyar acknowledged that there is a need for further wage increases in several sectors, but those could only happen “step by step”. As for immediate measures, the government fulfilled its electoral promise of doubling childcare to 24,000 forints (66 euros) a month per child and raising the minimum pension from January 2027. The draft budget would increase corporate taxes for multinationals, aligning with the global minimum tax regulations, from the current 9 per cent to 11.25 per cent. The government is introducing a special wealth tax for assets over 1 billion forints, and will further tax energy companies and banks. Major investments are pledged for health care, transport and energy, mostly funded by the unblocking of frozen EU funds. Magyar argued in his two-hour speech to parliament that cutting the deficit is essential, pointing to France and Romania as examples of governments unable to halt the spiral in spending. “Powerful, major economies – including European economies – are struggling in a debt trap, with the burden of interest payments choking their economies,” he said. Most controversial is the promised 1.5-trillion-forint cut in public sector funding. The police said they were disappointed by the 15 per cent wage increase and teachers voiced concerns about the 25 per cent increase pledged by the government from 2027. Workers in the cultural sector staged a small protest against their 10 per cent rise. “There are also sectors where there are no wages increases at all,” Magyar pointed out to those complaining, while asking for more societal solidarity.

World.title: He Survived a Shipwreck and Built a Church – 900 Years Later, Croatia Officially Protected it
World.content:
October the 25th, 2026 – A merchant surviving a shipwreck and then building a church in gratitude that Croatia officially chose to protect almost 1,000 years later is the story behind a construction on an island few know about.

It’s believed that the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian (Crvka sv. Kuzme i Damjana) on the island of Ugljan dates from the 11th or 12th century. It is located in a peaceful cove, right by the sea, not far from the hamlet of Guduće. Olive groves, dense pine forests, beautiful coves, old fishing villages, crystal-clear sea and views of the Zadar archipelago are what await visitors to Ugljan.

As Ivana Vasarevic writes for Putni Kofer, it’s widely known as one of Croatia’s greenest islands, which also carries the flattering nickname “the garden of Zadar.” It’s just 22 kilometres long, has a little over 5,600 inhabitants, is separated from the mainland by the Zadar Channel, and is connected to the neighbouring island of Pašman by a bridge across the Ždrelac passage. Among Ugljan’s main attractions is the fortress of St. Michael above Preko; nearby is also the islet of Galevac, known for its Franciscan monastery, while in Muline you can visit the remains of an ancient oil mill where the Liburnian olive oil was once produced.

TODAY IT IS CONSIDERED THE OLDEST PRESERVED CHURCH IN THE SETTLEMENT OF UGLJAN

The island’s special charm comes from its small stone churches. One of them was recently declared a cultural asset by the Ministry of Culture and Media of the Republic of Croatia. It is the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, located in Ljokine Cove, not far from the hamlet of Guduće, on the southwestern side of the island. This modest stone building stands right on the shore and is the oldest preserved church in the settlement of Ugljan: it is believed to date from the 11th or 12th century.

Besides its exceptional historical value, the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian is also interesting because of the unusual legend that has accompanied it for centuries. According to the story, a merchant and sailor named Toricella was shipwrecked in the waters around Ugljan. He managed to save himself and swim to the shore in Ljokine Cove, and on that spot he decided to build a votive church. He dedicated it to Saints Cosmas and Damian, early Christian martyrs and physicians, in gratitude for his rescue.

THE ROOF OF THE SIMPLE LITTLE CHURCH WAS COVERED WITH BROKEN STONE SLABS

Although the shipwreck story cannot be historically confirmed, the name Toricella also appears in old documents. The little church is first mentioned on 6 August 1512 in the will of F. Toricella from Bergamo in Italy. In it he stipulated that a piece of land should be given for use to the priest who celebrates a sung Mass in the little church on the feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian. According to the interpretation of don Marko Dokoza, a priest who for years led tours of Ugljan’s little churches as part of Open Doors Days, Toricella was only later identified with the seafarer from the shipwreck legend.

The original church was a very simple, square stone building, 4.8 metres long and 2.8 metres wide. Its walls were about 80 centimetres thick, and at the rear it had a lowered semicircular apse. The roof was covered with broken stone slabs, and there were two small windows in the side walls. The interior had a half-barrel vault, while the simple architectural details reflected the modesty and age of the building.

PAINTINGS DEPICTING SAINTS COSMAS AND DAMIAN AND THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY WITH THE CHILD

At the beginning of the 20th century the little church was significantly enlarged. A new nave, ten metres long and 3.8 metres wide, intended for gatherings of the faithful, was added to its front part. Today its interior contains an altar, pews and paintings depicting Saints Cosmas and Damian as well as the Blessed Virgin Mary with the Child. On the façade a small round window stands out, and above it a stone bell-gable with a bell made in the workshop of Jakov Cukrov in Split.

Saints Cosmas and Damian, to whom the church is dedicated, were twin brothers and physicians who helped the sick free of charge. Their feast day is celebrated on the 26th of September. For centuries that date held special significance for the inhabitants of Ugljan: according to records in the parish chronicle, numerous pilgrims from all the settlements on the island, as well as from the neighbouring areas, used to come to the little church on that day.

IN THE NEARBY HAMLET OF GUDUĆE YOU CAN ALSO SEE A UNIQUE MOSAIC BENCH

The tradition, of course, lives on today. Mass is still celebrated in the little church, during which blessings are invoked upon Ugljan sailors and ships all over the world. Thus this small place of worship has remained connected with the sea and seafarers, just as in the legend of its origin. The Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian on the island of Ugljan is also interesting as an excursion destination.

It is located in a peaceful cove, and a gravel road through a pine forest leads to it. In the nearby hamlet of Guduće you can also see an unusual mosaic bench created back in 2019 by the retired Božica Kliman, known as Boška. On its front side is a depiction of the Church of Saints Cosmas and Damian itself, along with a magical sunset, a squid and a lighthouse — colourful reminders of the islanders’ unbreakable connection with the sea and fishing.

World.title: The 3,500 Year Old Settlement Found Near Split
World.content:
October the 25th, 2026 – There is a fascinating 3,500 year old settlement in the suburbs of Split, with archaeologists coming upon the remains of houses, ovens and ancient graves.

Split is well known as the second largest city in Croatia and one of the best-known tourist destinations. It boasts an exceptionally long and proud history, but many don’t know that in its suburbs lies a settlement that is even older than this Dalmatian gem. As Lana Mindoljevic writes for Putni Kofer, over more recent years, archaeologists visiting the settlement of Stobreč have been discovering remains of life from the Bronze Age, long before the arrival of the Greeks and the Romans. Stobreč is formally a suburban settlement of Split and a popular tourist area, but it has its own exciting history that many people simply overlook.

the remains of an ancient epetium

Stobreč has long been known to archaeologists as the site of ancient Epetium, or Epetion. However, extensive protective research that began back in 2024, the largest so far conducted at this site, has also opened a much older chapter of its history. According to the information available so far, the earliest finds date approximately to 1500 BC, and detailed processing of the material is still ongoing.

over 10,000 fragments have been found

In a scientific paper written by Marina Ugarković and Niko Romac, published on the Hrčak website, parts of Hellenistic defensive walls and a tower, a Roman road and drainage system, and late antique buildings are described. Among these layers, the remains of an earlier prehistoric settlement have for the first time been unequivocally confirmed. Already in the research covered by that paper, more than 100,000 fragments of objects and other movable finds from different periods were documented. The soil under Stobreč has proven to be a vast archive of life that changed and built upon itself here for centuries.

ancient homes and grave sites

Archaeologist Niko Romac also described finds of ovens, possibly intended for food preparation, and complete ceramic vessels: trays, cups and jugs. Precisely such objects bring the ancient inhabitants of Stobreč closer to us. Someone made them, took them in their hands and used them in everyday life. Based on traces of burning and the arrangement of the remains, researchers assume that the house was destroyed by fire. Among the particularly sensitive finds, the grave of a newborn in its floor was also recorded.

an archaeological park is being considered

These remarkable discoveries have also opened the question of the future of the very special site. According to the response of the Ministry of Culture and Media, a zone of approximately 3,000 square metres is currently being planned for the presentation of the archaeological heritage. On an additional around 2,500 square metres construction is possible, but it depends on the results of further research. The sensitive Bronze Age finds require special protection. The Ministry states that the ovens and the find interpreted as a threshing floor should be moved to the Archaeological Museum in Split, while the appearance of the settlement could be presented with three-dimensional models and virtual reconstructions. An archaeological park currently exists only as an idea, and time will show whether it will be realised.

Stobreč is located on a peninsula east of Split, near the mouth of the Žrnovnica. In the central part of the place there are sandy and pebble beaches, while towards the southwest the coast becomes rockier. Because of the beautiful beaches and the proximity of Split it is a popular summer destination, and the proximity of Perun and Mosor also opens possibilities for trips into nature. Interestingly, even the name of Stobreč itself preserves the memory of its long past. As the Croatian Encyclopaedia notes, archaeologist Frane Bulić etymologically linked the present-day name of the place with the name of Saint Lawrence, i.e. the Roman martyr Laurentius, to whom the local early Christian basilica was dedicated. In its apse a small church of Saint Lawrence was later arranged, later dedicated to Our Lady of Carmel. Along with the preserved remains of the ancient walls, this is another reminder that in Stobreč different periods of history can be encountered during a completely ordinary walk.

World.title: Croatia is Introducing a New Digital Customs System
World.content:
October the 25th, 2026 – Croatia is set to introduce a brand new digital customs system as of November the 1st this year, with the hope of making crossing the border more efficient.

As of the 1st of November 2026, the Customs Administration is introducing a new digital service called eObračun of customs duties in passenger traffic (eODPP). Index reports that this brand new service is intended for passengers who bring goods into Croatia, i.e. the EU, on which import duties are payable, and its aim is to facilitate and speed up border crossing.

how it works…

Via the new application, passengers will be able to check in advance whether there is an obligation to pay duties on the goods they are bringing in their personal luggage. The service also enables them to declare goods whose value or quantity exceeds the permitted limits and to pay online the customs duties and taxes calculated on the basis of the declaration. Goods can be declared up to five days, i.e. 120 hours, before the planned arrival at one of the international border crossings within the territory of Croatia.

Upon arrival at the border, a customs officer will check the declaration and the goods in a short procedure. If no irregularities are found, the import procedure will be quickly completed. The Customs Administration states that the application is designed to be intuitive, and the data-entry procedure for calculating duties has five steps.

no registration required

The brand new Croatian digital customs service will be available to all passengers entering the EU via Croatian road, railway, air and maritime border crossings. No registration is required to use it. The system is adapted for computers, smartphones and tablets, and will be available from the 1st of November 2026 here.

World.title: Croatia is at Back of EU When it Comes to Electric Car Purchases
World.content:
October the 25th, 2026 – Despite the global climb in people buying electric vehicles, Croatia ranked at the very back of the EU when it comes to electric car purchases.

The share of fully electric cars among new cars is growing around the world, and in many countries it has reached record levels. Vedran Salvia reports for Index that this is clearly shown by the latest data from the international energy organisation Ember, which analysed car sales on global markets. Croatia is significantly lagging behind the other EU countries.

croatia is at the very back of the eu

According to Ember’s analysis, which tracks the share of fully electric cars (BEVs) among newly registered cars, Croatia recorded its own record during 2026, but despite that remained in last place in the European Union. From March to August such cars accounted for around 4.3 percent of all new registrations in Croatia. The data are based on rolling six-month periods because this presentation allows clearer tracking of trends.

The research covered 56 countries, while 49 of them are shown on the interactive chart, i.e. only those that achieved record shares during 2026. The difference between Croatia and the European leaders is extremely large. In Norway, which is not a member of the European Union, the share of fully electric cars reached as much as 97.8 percent, in Denmark 79.8 percent, in Finland 49.7 percent, in the Netherlands 42.8 percent and in Sweden 40.8 percent. The European Union average was 22.5 percent, more than five times higher than in Croatia. As for the EU members that are not shown on the chart, these are Poland and Romania, which did not achieve record shares of electric cars during 2026. However, both are ahead of Croatia. From March to August the share of fully electric cars among new registrations was 4.8 percent in Poland and 7.4 percent in Romania.

why is croatia lagging so much?

One of the reasons for the weaker sales of electric cars across Croatia could be their high price, especially in relation to average local purchasing power. That Croatian buyers are largely turning to used vehicles is also shown by data from the Croatian Vehicle Centre, according to which more used cars are imported into Croatia than new ones are registered, while the average age of passenger cars is more than 13 years. The European Commission in its 2026 report on Croatia also warns of the high costs of public charging of electric vehicles, problems with different charging systems and limited possibilities for home charging, especially for citizens who live in apartment buildings.

State incentives also play an important role; they are not awarded continuously but through occasional tenders. Available funds can sometimes be used up in just a few hours. Thus in 2024 citizens reserved all 15 million euros earmarked for subsidies in only four hours, after which the Environmental Protection Fund closed the tender. Such a system makes purchase planning more difficult because citizens cannot count on the constant availability of incentives.

large market differences

There are also significant differences among the large European markets. In France the share of fully electric cars was 30.6 percent, in Germany 27.5 percent and in Italy 8.3 percent. Germany and France have in recent years been moving towards an ever higher share of electric cars, while their penetration in Italy is considerably slower. Nevertheless, the Italian market is also recording growth, especially during 2026. Looking at absolute numbers, China is by far the world’s largest market for electric cars by the number of vehicles sold and is in a category of its own. According to Ember’s data, from January to August 2026 almost 4.46 million fully electric cars were registered there, which is almost half of the total of 9.33 million registered worldwide. In the EU in the same period around 1.65 million such cars were registered.

electric cars are conquering even emerging markets

The data show that the growth in the share of electric cars is no longer limited to developed European countries and China. Among the countries with high shares, Uruguay stands out with 40.2 percent, while in Thailand the share reached 28.8 percent and in Indonesia 24.2 percent. “Strong growth outside the USA and China was key to the continued growth in electric vehicle sales. Excluding the USA and China, global BEV sales rose by an estimated 45% in the period from January to August 2026 compared with the same period of the previous year,” the research states. At the same time, electric cars in some large countries still occupy a relatively small part of the market. In India their share is 7.4 percent, in Japan 3.3 percent and in Mexico only 2.1 percent.

the usa didn’t even make it on the chart

Ember particularly highlights the example of the United States of America, which did not even make it among the 49 countries with record shares of electric cars shown on the chart. After last year’s abolition of federal support for electric vehicles, their share among new vehicles fell to only six percent in the first eight months of 2026. Looking at everything in absolute numbers of electric cars sold the USA stands considerably better. From January to August around 640 thousand such vehicles were registered there, which puts it in second place in the world, immediately behind China. However, the American car market is so large that electric cars still make up a small part of total sales. According to Ember’s analysis, as many as 49 of the 56 observed countries now have a higher share of electric cars than the USA, and during this year alone 15 countries overtook it, among them Brazil, India, Italy, Malaysia and New Zealand.

electric cars and energy security

Ember emphasises in its analysis that the spread of electric cars affects not only the car market but also the energy security of states. According to the organisation’s estimates, electric cars in oil-importing countries from March to August this year replaced oil consumption worth around 20 billion dollars.

The authors of the research conclude that the electrification of transport can reduce states’ exposure to disruptions on the oil market and sudden changes in fuel prices. “Countries that invested in electric cars before this crisis are now better protected, and their example is being followed by an increasing number of other countries. Every electric car on the road reduces exposure to volatile oil markets, and as their number grows, so does protection against future supply disruptions,” the research states.
