-And second, that was due to open external support to Armenia. We did not start the war, we just responded and we do it based on the United Nations Charter. United Nations charter provides the right of every country for self-defense. What we are doing? We are defending ourselves, and we are liberating internationally recognized territories of Azerbaijan from Armenian occupation. Nothing more than that. And with respect to Armenian people I have said many times that Armenian people who live in Nagorno-Karabakh are our citizens. We will take care of them. They will live in dignity, in peace, side by side with Azerbaijanis who will return there.

-Mr president, why are you resisting calls from the UN as you mentioned Russia, Iran the United States, the EU, NATO, why are you resisting calls for a ceasefire? And in fact, breaking to the terms to create a ceasefire. And I know today, that’s what Secretary of State Pompeo will be asking for a ceasefire to exchange bodies, to exchange the wounded. Isn’t this a good time for a ceasefire?

-We were ready for a ceasefire and on the 10th of October, in Moscow, our foreign minister, Armenian foreign minister and Russian foreign minister issued a joint declaration about the ceasefire. But the next day, the next day, Armenians from the territory of Armenia launched an attack on the second largest city of Azerbaijan-Ganja, situated far away from the area of clashes with ballistic missiles killing 10 civilians and wounding more than 30. Then, there was a second ballistic attack on Ganja, killing 15 people. So it was Armenia…

-But you violated ceasefire as well.

-No, we just responded, because we agreed about ceasefire two times, the first time Armenians at night, at 1 am at night, launched a ballistic missile on a sleeping city. Second time, ceasefire lasted only for two minutes and Armenia violated it. There are no evidence that Azerbaijan violated the ceasefire.

-But let me put it this way, if Secretary of State Pompeo today puts it to your foreign minister, the US really wants a ceasefire another try. Will you give it another try?

-Yes, we are ready. I said many times publicly. We are ready to agree on ceasefire today, but at the same time Armenia, its prime minister should say that they are committed to the basic principles elaborated by the United States, Russia and France. Armenian prime minister two days ago said that there is no diplomatic solution to the conflict of Nagorno-Karabakh.

-So, this has got strings attached. Is there a ceasefire with no strings attached.

-We want a ceasefire, we want our territories back. Armenia should commit that they will liberate the territories. According to the United Nations Security Council resolutions and according to the peace plan presented by US, France and Russia. But he does not say this.

-Mr president, how do you respond to charges that your military is inordinately targeting civilian areas, homes, residences, stores even a very important church has been hit by your high tech weaponry. Thousands others have been killed or injured just in the past four weeks.

-We do not attack civilians. After Armenian brutal attack, an act of terror against the city of Ganja with ballistic missiles where dozens of people have been killed, we publicly said that we will take revenge but on the battlefield. We do not attack civilians, we do not attack religious sights. What happened to the church in Shusha was either a mistake, and I already publicly commented on that, or it was done by Armenians themselves in order to put a blame on us.

-Again, Mr. president, we are seeing video scenes of the capital of Nagorno-Karabakh, all the population there has to live in basements. They are hearing artillery every twenty minutes. Their city where civilians are living is wrecked. You can’t call the entire city a military target.

-There have been military targets in the capital of the so-called "Nagorno-Karabakh republic" Khankandi and our attacks there were only before 9th of October. We didn’t attack any civilians or cities, in the Nagorno-Karabakh after that, but they attacked. Have you seen the images of what they have done to Ganja? What they done

-Were you targeting civilians from September 27 to October 19?

-No, no, no. we were targeting military infrastructure in the so-called "capital of Nagorno Karabakh" Khankandi, because

military basis, military infrastructure is situated in the city.

-You have drones from Turkey, you have military gear from Israel, you have high-tech equipment from Russia. How can you use that and not also hit civilians?

-No, no. Our drones and these images, a lot of them are on the internet. You can look, how our drones destroy Armenian tanks and other weapons. So far, our drones destroyed more than 230 tanks. We destroyed 6 S-300 anti-air missile system. We destroyed hundreds of their armed vehicles. We do not use drones for civilians this is false information.

-Let’s talk about the soldiers, the troops that are in action. From multiple sources, from France, from Russia from independent respected journalists at the New-York Times for example, they absolutely assert that Syrians, militias gathered and transported by Turkey in a hundreds are now fighting your war. Why do you have Turkish backed Syrian militias fighting your war in Azerbaijan?

-This is another fake news. I regret that Russia and France, the only countries by the way, which publicly commented on that made such an irresponsible statement. And I demanded and still demand proofs, evidences. It is more than 20 days after the war has started again. So far, not a single evidence or proof was presented to us neither by Russia nor from France.

-The evidence was in the New-York Times. I direct you to the story five days ago that says that 57 Syrian fighters killed in Azerbaijan, were brought back across the border from Turkey and buried in Syria. Their families all attest that they went to Azerbaijan, to fight alongside your army.

-Do you know do you remember how President Trump calls New-York times? Fake news. This is fake news. No evidence, no proof. Give us evidence not only New-York Times.

-I’m just curious, you have a 100 thousand soldiers. Why do you need some scrappy mercenaries?

-Yes. Exactly. We don’t need them.

-That’s a good question. Why?

-We don’t need them. That was what I was talking about. A 100 thousand soldiers in the regular army, plus maybe couple or three times more soldiers we can recruit within couple of days plus more than equipment. We don’t need any mercenaries at all. This is fake news, just in order to damage the image of our country, and in order to diminish the bravery of our soldiers on the battlefield.

-Mr president, let’s get back to the timing of this. Why we are seeing military action now? Why we are seeing clashes? Critics of your government, of your presidency say that you are using this war as a smokescreen to deflect the tension from problems in your own country, social issues, economic stagnation, corruption, COVID-19. Are you using this just to overattention in a public maybe dissatisfied on a lot of different accounts towards the patriotic battle.

-No, no. This is absolutely wrong. First, our economic performance is one of the best in the world. Economic decline in Azerbaijan in the ten months is less than 4 percent. You can compare it with your own country, or with European countries. Level of unemployment in Azerbaijan is 7 percent, compare it with your own country. Level of poverty in Azerbaijan is five percent, compare it again. We don’t have serious social problems. On COVID-19, Azerbaijan is considered as an example by World Health Organization. We provided support to more than 30 countries, financial support, humanitarian support. Our economy is stable. Our economy is sustainable. And there was no need as you say to launch the war in order to cover some of internal problems. It was on the other side, Armenia which is completely now in economic and social problems. They need to distract attention. It is Armenian prime minister who puts leading opposition party leader to jail. He is pursuing two former presidents.

-We know that there are some accusations of human rights abuses with your own government and suppression of freedom of speech and specifically talking about the corruption and the family rule of both your government and many of the corporate structures. So this is not to pull the attention of your public or some members of your public away from those considered misdeeds by some people.

-No, no, no. Corruption is here and we are fighting against it. We have introduced a broad economic reforms program. Many people, many governmental officials and high ranking officials have been arrested recently for charges of corruption. Corruption is everywhere and we are fighting against it. With respect to the family rule, again, I would like to refer you to your own country, where important positions were held by father and son. Just Bush family, Clinton family, husband and wife, Kennedy family, and in many other countries. So, it’s nothing different from what is happening in the United States.

-They were all elected democratically and transparently.

-Yes, especially President Bush who was elected by the decision of the US Supreme Court.

-You know the American politics Mr President.

-I know yes. I am well prepared for that.

-Let’s go to the United States now. What would you like to see today and in the future Secretary of State Pompeo do? There has been some criticism of Secretary Pompeo and the US that they haven’t been enough engaged. I know, Russia is quite involved, Turkey in various ways involved, even Iran is offering help. What would you like? Has the US done enough would you like to see the US do more? What would you like Washington to do?

-I think that the US as one of the three co-chairs of the Minsk group has a mandate from OSCE to help parties to come to an agreement. And agreement must be based on international law it should not be based on what I want or what Armenian prime minister wants. It should be based on international law. Nagorno-Karabakh is recognized by the United States and all other countries as integral part of Azerbaijan. So what I can expect from Secretary Pompeo first? To tell prime minister Pashinyan’s envoy that statements like "there is no diplomatic solution" is wrong and dangerous. Second, statements by Armenian prime minister that "Karabakh is Armenia" is dangerous and wrong and they should be reasonable. They should give us a timetable for withdrawal from the occupied territories. They should agree for peaceful coexistence between the Armenians and Azerbaijanis in the territory of Nagorno-Karabakh. And they should stop trying to internationalize the conflict. They should stop asking Russia for direct military involvement. This is counter-productive. All the efforts of Armenian prime minister during these times is to ask Russia to send troops to fight against Azerbaijan. And this is very dangerous.

-What’s your deadpoint, I mean another criticism of Secretary of State Pompeo, and he directly says, and certainly, the US and Turkey has as many areas of commonality but he says Turkey’s assistance of your effort is actually causing problems, it’s fueling the flames. How do you react to that?

-Turkey provides political support to Azerbaijan. It is our closest ally and friend. And we are proud and happy that we have such a great country as our partner. Every country has a right to have friends and allies. Armenia has its allies.

-Turkey has been pushing for war. Turkey says there is a military way to go.

-No, not at all. Not at all. Not a single evidence about that. Turkey only provides political support and this is enough, because when Turkey says that they stand side by side with Azerbaijan, and Azerbaijan is not alone, this is a message to all those who want to penetrate and provide their interests with respect to the conflict.

-You did offered an important line when we were speaking just a short while ago. You said in our discussions in your discussions with the Secretary of State Pompeo that there is a diplomatic solution. Do you believe there is a diplomatic solution to this crisis?

-Yes, I believe, otherwise I wouldn not have been in the negotiations for 17 years. You were trying to say that I launched the war. But if I launched the war why should I wait for 17 years? Azerbaijani army is well-prepared already for at least ten years already. Therefore, the diplomatic solution is on the table. Armenia must liberate territories surrounding Nagorno-Karabakh. Azerbaijanis must return to those territories and then live in peace and dignity with Armenians. That’s our position.

-So, you are saying diplomatic solution but with a military overlay.

-I said that I wish the military solutions stop today and we move on negotiation table. This military factor is causing a lot of damage and a lot of victims,unfortunately. Therefore, the sooner we start substantive negotiations, not imitation like Armenia wanted to do all these years but substantive negotiations, the sooner the resolution will be found. And if resolution is based on territorial integrity of Azerbaijan.

-The worry of some outside of your country, outside of your region and perhaps what should be the worries of yours as well is that this contained conflict becomes a wider regional problem. You have Turkey, with a real interest, you have Russia with a real interest, you have Iran with a real interest. Are you risking your own standing as a country of stature, both economic and politically get lost in some kind of a regional maelstrom that you could have a part in starting?

-All our efforts during the conflict aimed to stop active phase as soon as possible. And we are completely against any form of internationalization of the conflict so that conflict spread over. That's what Armenia wants to do. And as I said, they asked Russia to send military personnel to the area of conflict which is absolutely counterproductive, and which is completely in violation of international law. We don’t want other countries to interfere.

-Well, there are Russian bases in Armenia already.

-Exactly, in Armenia, yes.

-They are not illegal.

-Yes, it is in Armenia but not in Nagorno-Karabakh. What they are asking Russians is to send troops to Nagorno-Karabakh and we know about that. Therefore, our position is all the regional countries, and all the countries should stay away from direct involvement in the conflict. Those who want to help and those who have a mandate, OSCE Minsk Group co-chairs must persuade Armenia. I hope it will happen today in Washington, to stop aggression, to commit to ceasefire, and to make commitment that they will leave the territories. They don’t do it.

-There was an expression during the Gulf War that it was all about the oil, okay? You got oil pipelines, energy pipelines, within, I don’t know, 50-60 miles of the fighting. Are you concerned that your very important energy pipelines and connections could be disrupted by fighting one side or another? And in fact maybe that is helping to drive your military to conduct this war.

-Actually, we are concerned because we heard the statements from high-ranking Armenian officials that they will attack our strategic oil infrastructure, including pipelines and one of the biggest oil and gas terminal in Sangachal district of Baku. And the July clashes where Armenia attacked us, took place 15 kilometers from the gas pipeline which is supposed to provide energy security to Europe. So, it was Armenian plans to disrupt oil and gas supplies from Azerbaijan to Europe and to the world.

-So, were part of motivational what you’re doing right now is to defend your economic interest against any threat like that?

-No, we are defending ourselves. You know, our oil pipeline from Baku to Mediterranean was commissioned in 2006 and it works without any disruption. Our gas pipeline from Azerbaijan to Turkey was commissioned in 2007. A big pipeline to connect Azerbaijan with European consumers is going to be opened in a couple of months probably, maybe even less. Therefore, why should we launch a war in order to protect the pipeline when the pipeline is already protected. It is Armenia which wants to disrupt the pipeline and to make economic damage to Azerbaijan.

-Are you satisfied with what President Trump and his administration has been saying about the conflict? He has been critical of Turkey. But frankly, he has been critical of both sides. He is outweighing very large Armenian diaspora in the United States. So there are political elements in this too. Do you think the United States is handling its role well?

-I think what President Trump does with respect to the conflict resolution is fully in line with international relations. We fully support his position, his personal comments on that. And we see that the position of the United States is balanced and as it should be, because United States is a mediator. President Trump’s comments on criticism on Turkey, I did not see it, by the way, in the press. But his comments were constructive. The United States does not take sides as other co-chairs should also don’t take sides. We understand internal politics not only in America, but also, in France and Russia. With a very large Armenian community which influences which has a lot of lobbying activity and which is now in full operation against Azerbaijan. And we understand the level of pressure which they can impose. But at the same time, very straight forward position of President Trump is highly supported here in Azerbaijan not only by me, but also our people.

-Mr president, you know politics. And I bet you know American politics too. We are ten days away from a major presidential election, in figuring out this move towards diplomacy in Washington. Do you think the idea of maybe a diplomatic success might be figuring in the minds of my Washington politicians and having said that do you find that’s okay any motivation to get things going?

-Any motivation in order to put an end to the hostility is supported by us. And I think that today’s meeting in Washington can have a very good result only if Armenia will commit to peaceful settlement, will stop attacking us and will make commitment that they will withdraw the troops.

-Do you think it is driven by US presidential politics this diplomatic effort today?

-Well, I don’t know, I think that the American voters will make the vote based on their approach and their assumption of what is the best for America. I don’t think that Karabakh conflict is something which American people are concerned about. Maybe most of them even do not know. But of course, America as a superpower has a very important say in this conflict resolution. And our position is that America as a mediator should continue to be neutral, and should try again and more and more to bring both sides closer to the common decision.

-But let me pick up on that point as we conclude this in the next two minutes. Why should the United States care? I think you probably are right. Most Americans could not find Nagorno-Karabakh on a map. But there were strategic issues you are dealing with, political, cultural, demographic. If you were talking to the United States people now, and said excuse me, I know you have got the presidential. I know you have got the world series baseball, but you should pay attention to this too. What would you tell a typical American. Why it is important for us to care and look at this?

-I would say that Azerbaijan has always been a very true partner to the United States. We are together on the fight against international terrorism, we are together in Afghanistan and we keep our military servicemen in Afghanistan, thus, providing the cause of our peacekeeping operations. We have an important topic on our agenda of energy security. The United States has always strongly supported Azerbaijan’s efforts to diversify its energy supply routes. And with a strong support of the United States we managed to complete important projects. Azerbaijan and the United States have a very strong partnership relations. And the United States considers Azerbaijan as a friend. And we are really friends. Therefore, it is in the interests of the United States that there is peace here. Azerbaijan continues its path on the route of independence, strengthening the independence. We are situated just between Europe and Asia, on the crossroads of transportation, energy. Our political importance is growing. Therefore, Azerbaijan is an important partner to the United States and the United States to Azerbaijan.

-So, stability in your country, in your region, politically, economically et cetera could be good for us as well 3000-5000 miles away.

-Yes. America is a superpower. The distance does not make any difference. And I think that the modern, secular, friendly Muslim country is also a big asset for our friends. And the United States from the very first years of independence, always supported Azerbaijan. Today I can tell you we have maybe the highest ever level of our bilateral cooperation and we hope that today’s meeting in Washington will be important to persuade Armenia to stop aggression, stop occupation and then peace will come to our land.

-There is a lot of support for Armenia as you know that earlier in the interview in the United States.

-Yes.

-The support for the Christian religion there, for the church is there. For the diaspora the punishment that they incurred many years ago by Turkey. So, you know that there is a warm emotional feeling towards Armenians as well in the United States

-Yes, I know that, I said before that we understand the internal politics, and the Armenian lobby organization. But when we look at the issues related to international relations, there must be principles. Emotions, feelings, some other expression of good will is different. It can be in the family, it can be at the dinner. But in international relations, there is an internationally recognized territory of Azerbaijan, which is occupied by Armenia. So, the occupation must come to an end. And those Armenians who live in America, who live in France, who live in Russia, the rich people don’t care about those Armenians in Nagorno-Karabakh. How they live in poverty.

-They will probably disagree with you on that one. But okay. Two final questions. Back to presidential politics. Former vice president Joe Biden might be the president-elect in ten days time. Have you ever had any contact with him maybe in his vice-presidential role? And how do you take a Biden administration would deal with this conflict right there in your region?

-Yes, I met with vice-president Biden four years ago in Washington at the Nuclear Summit which was organized by President Obama. I had bilateral meeting with Mr. Biden and I saw that he was deeply involved in regional issues. We discussed many issues of our bilateral relations, of course, including Nagorno-Karabakh settlement. I can tell you that Obama’s administration was very active on the Nagorno-Karabakh track. Therefore, Mr. Biden and I am sure the people who support him there are well aware about that. So, I have very good memory of our meeting with him.

-Do you think he will be favorable to your position? Will he be favorable to Armenia? Well, he probably will talk against war. I mean he probably will also push for a ceasefire, push for a diplomacy. Do you think that would be an okay approach?

-I think, taking into account what we have just discussed, the Armenian lobbying organizations in America, in France and Russia, for Azerbaijan the most favorable situation will be that the leaders of these three countries stay neutral on the conflict and don’t take sides. Actually, that’s what their mandate dictates them. If they take sides, they cannot be mediators. And we expect from the US foreign policy team in the future also, to be neutral, and to be objective.

-Finally Mr. President, your prediction for the future. I mean your region, your country, Armenia. Such horror late 80s and early 90s. Tens of thousands of people were killed. What are we looking now? Tens of thousands of people more killed? More destructions? How do you see this going forward?

-It is difficult to predict now what will happen. It not only depends on us, because the war is not held by one country. It is not a unilateral process. But how I want to see the region I can tell you. I want the region of the Southern Caucasus to be deeply integrated. I want that the strategic relations which we have with another South Caucasian country, Georgia, can be to certain degree a model of relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia once in the future. Because all wars stop and peace comes. We know how...

-You think there can be a peaceful resolution of this conflict?

-Definitely.

-Fine, a diplomatic answer.

-I am absolutely confident. But it depends on the will from Armenian side. What happened after the second World War? Germany and the United States were killing each other. Soviet Union and Germany were killing each other. Tens of millions were killed. But look now. It is not any longer in the memory. It is not provoking hostility. Why Armenians and Azerbaijanis cannot live together in the region of Nagorno-Karabakh, while they live together in Georgia, in Russia, in Ukraine, in many other countries? I think that the Southern Caucasus…

-Can be peace at the same time recognizing the rights of both sides?

-Yes, exactly. It must be based on the reasonable background, within the framework of territorial integrity of Azerbaijan, with full protection of rights and concerns of Armenian population of Azerbaijan. That’s I think, that is doable.

-Mr president, thank you very much for this lengthy interview and I am sure, we will inform not just me, but our American public.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan customs revenue exceeds target by 4.6% in nine months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 25. Kyrgyzstan’s State Customs Service collected 139 billion soms ($1.6 billion) in revenues in January–September 2026, exceeding its target by 4.6%, according to the country’s Cabinet of Ministers.

Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers and Head of the Presidential Administration Adylbek Kasymaliev announced the figures at a government meeting on October 7, following which he issued a series of instructions to government agencies.

"Revenues collected by the State Customs Service amounted to 139 billion soms, with the target fulfilled by 104.6%. By the end of the year, while maintaining the positive trend, it is necessary to ensure the fulfillment of the budget revenue target, as well as the timely and efficient use of allocated funds," he said.

Kasymaliev noted that the revenue side of the republican budget had performed well in the first nine months of 2026.

He also said that Moody’s upgrade of Kyrgyzstan’s sovereign credit rating from B3 to B2, with a stable outlook, represented an important assessment of the country’s economic and financial policies.

"Moody’s noted the sustained growth and diversification of our economy, an increase in GDP per capita, large-scale infrastructure investment, stronger public finances, and a decline in public debt relative to GDP. The rating upgrade strengthens international investors’ confidence in Kyrgyzstan and creates broader opportunities for attracting long-term financing to the country," he said.

According to Trend’s calculations, Kyrgyzstan’s State Customs Service could collect around 185.3 billion soms ($2.13 billion) in revenues in 2026 if the average monthly collection rate recorded in January–September continues through December.

This projection assumes that monthly collections in the final three months remain at the average recorded during the first nine months. It does not indicate year-on-year revenue growth.

World.title: Uzbekneftegaz produces $3.47B in industrial goods in nine months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 25. Uzbekistan’s state-owned oil and gas company Uzbekneftegaz produced industrial goods worth 41.8 trillion soums (about $3.47 billion) in January–September 2026, exceeding its production plan by 3.5%, while its industrial output growth index reached 105.9%.

This was reported by Uzbekneftegaz.

According to Trend’s calculations, the company’s industrial output increased by approximately 5.9% year over year, implying production value of around 39.5 trillion soums (around $3.28 billion) in the first nine months of 2025.

During the reporting period, Uzbekneftegaz produced 773,500 tons of gasoline, 759,700 tons of diesel fuel and 210,600 tons of aviation kerosene, helping supply the domestic market and strategic sectors.

The company also produced 452,700 tons of liquefied petroleum gas, 135,100 tons of sulfur and 101,300 tons of polyethylene.

The production figures come as President Shavkat Mirziyoyev emphasizes the importance of processing natural gas into higher-value products rather than using it solely for electricity generation.

Speaking during an open dialogue, Mirziyoyev highlighted the need to deepen gas processing and create greater added value. The synthetic liquid fuel complex in the Kashkadarya region produces up to 1.5 million tons of fuel and other products annually.

Uzbekistan also plans to implement a methanol-to-olefins (MTO) project in the Bukhara region to produce polyethylene, polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate (PET). Modernization of the Bukhara and Fergana oil refineries is also planned.

Mirziyoyev said the country welcomes investor proposals for economically viable projects that use new technologies and meet environmental requirements. Uzbekneftegaz’s development strategy similarly prioritizes extending the value chain and expanding the production of higher-value goods.

World.title: Iranian banks increase startup lending by 92.2% in August–September
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Iranian state-owned and private banks increased lending to startup companies by 92.2% year-on-year to 1.56 quadrillion rials (about $864 million) during the period from August 23 through September 22, 2026.

According to Trend's analysis of statistics from the Central Bank of Iran, the banks extended approximately 814 trillion rials (about $449 million) in loans to startup companies during the same period in 2025.

Private banks provided 1.42 quadrillion rials (about $785 million) in loans to startup companies during the period from August 23 through September 22, 2026, up 94.3% compared with the corresponding period in 2025. In the same period last year, private banks extended approximately 732 trillion rials (about $404 million) in loans to startups.

State-owned banks provided 142 trillion rials (about $78.7 million) in loans to startup companies during the period, an increase of 73.4% year-on-year. During the corresponding period in 2025, lending by state-owned banks totaled approximately 82.2 trillion rials (about $45.4 million).

During the preceding period, from July 23 through August 22, 2026, state-owned and private banks provided approximately 1.32 quadrillion rials (about $727 million) in loans to startup companies.

World.title: Fishermen racing crocs for crabs in Wadeye as new industry emerges
World.content:
Before dawn, the sea farmers are already on the water.

As the fishermen steer their boat along the mangrove-lined banks, they know they must move fast so they can load their catch onto a light plane bound for the Darwin Fish Market by the afternoon.

For Theo Dooling, these waters feel familiar. He has fond memories of catching crabs from mud holes with his family as a child.

Loading

"You can put in a stick and just take the crab out," he says.

Back then, the biggest challenge was avoiding a pinch on the finger.

Now, the sea farmers compete with crocodiles for their bounty. Mr Dooling says the reptiles have crushed five of his crab pots in their jaws, desperately trying to poach the fleshy crustaceans.

In Wadeye, a small mud crab venture has grown into a full commercial operation. (ABC News: James Elton)

As the pots are hauled in, it is easy to see why. Nearly all contain mud crabs, with the biggest weighing two kilograms.

A remote community

Sitting on the west coast of Australia's Top End, Wadeye is one of the NT's most unique Aboriginal communities.

Traditional culture thrives here through music and dance, and both adults and children speak the Aboriginal language Murrinh-patha fluently.

Wadeye's main ceremonial groups performed traditional dances during the 2025 Yidiyi Festival. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Its approximately 2,500 residents are cut off for half the year when the rugged Port Keats Road washes out.

But in recent years, the community has also been one of the NT's most troubled.

Wadeye is one of the largest Aboriginal communities in the Northern Territory. (ABC News: James Elton)

It has made headlines for large-scale street fights involving weapons such as spears and crossbows.

Standard three-bedroom houses have as many as 20 people living in them, and black-market liquor is widely available but cripplingly expensive.

Desmond Longmair says a group torched his car using a Coke bottle filled with petrol in a recent round of fighting. (ABC News: James Elton)

Yet, nearly everyone in town points to the lack of jobs as the biggest problem.

At the 2021 census, only about one in five adults had a job.

The lack of jobs is a major issue for the residents in Wadeye. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

It is against this backdrop that the Thamarrurr Sea Farmers have used Aboriginal coastal licences to grow their modest operation into a larger commercial venture that could change outcomes for the Wadeye community.

The acquisition of a full commercial licence means the fishermen can have up to 60 crab pots in the water, and they have expanded their team from three to nine workers within a year.

On average, they send 35 to 50 kilograms of mud crabs to Darwin each week.

Sea farmer Maurice Bitting with freshly caught crabs. (ABC News: James Elton)

"The people we brought on to the team, they are really very good," says Johnson Katuura, the sea farmers coordinator.

"They're people who have fished all their lives."

Joel Martin, one of the team's youngest members, said the sea farmers had already inspired local schoolkids.

Joel Martin is one of the youngest members of the Thamarrurr Sea Farmers. (ABC News: James Elton)

"We go out to school sometimes, talk to the students, let them know that they're going to have to graduate, then they can find a good job," Mr Martin says.

" We want more young boys to come in so they can have a good life, good job. "

Sustainability a top priority

The NT's largest crab licence holder, the Aboriginal Sea Company, says Wadeye is the only "community-run" commercial fishing operation in the NT.

The operation is getting mentoring and training from Humpty Doo Barramundi, one of Australia's biggest aquaculture players.

The Thamarrurr Sea Farmers have grown to a workforce of nine. (ABC News: James Elton)

Elsewhere in the NT, concerns about mud crab numbers led to a pause on commercial licences so stocks could recover.

It came at a bad time for the sea farmers, who were about to begin commercial operations.

But once they negotiated with authorities, the licences were temporarily converted back to Aboriginal coastal licences, then returned to commercial when the pause ended.

Tracey Leo, the deputy CEO of Thamarrurr Development Corporation, backed the way the sea farmers do business.

Tracey Leo is the deputy CEO of the Thamarrurr Development Corporation. (ABC News: James Elton)

"We fully support sustainable harvest strategies," Ms Leo says.

She says the crew keeps detailed records of where they fish and how many crabs they take, "so that we're not over-harvesting in one … location".

The corporation is also lobbying for the Territory's fishery management zones to be reviewed, arguing that rules designed for more heavily fished areas don't necessarily make sense in the relatively "un-fished" waters around Wadeye.

Mr Katuura says the industry's sustainability is the top priority.

Johnson Katuura hopes the commercial operation will be sustainable and long-lasting. (ABC News: James Elton)

"We want it to be long-living," he says.

" We are focused on making a stronger foundation [rather] than rushing to numbers. And I believe that will be the game changer. "

Slow and steady investment

Ms Leo previously worked with Humpty Doo Barramundi and helped establish a two-way training relationship between the operators.

She believes a fully-fledged seafood industry could emerge in Wadeye within a decade, employing about 100 people across mud crabs, a black-lip oyster farm, and some other fisheries.

The black-lip oysters are yet to reach commercial production. (ABC News: James Elton)

"When we first invested in the Sea Farmers, there was a lot of capital infrastructure required, with a big shed and the boats and crab pots and oyster cages, but that's not going to translate to 100 jobs in a short period of time," Ms Leo says.

"We need government to recognise … those employment outcomes [are] going to take a long time.

"[Humpty Doo] were [running] 14 or 15 years before they were even profitable. And they've been going 30 years or whatever it is now … extremely successful."

The impact of 100 jobs to Wadeye would be significant, boosting family incomes in a town where only about 300 adults are currently employed.

But it's also about the type of work. Ms Leo says most of the existing jobs in Wadeye are "very service-based", staffing places such as the local supermarket or the family centre.

"Client-focused jobs, they don't meet the aspirations of local people … there's a lot of kinship complexities, and you might not be able to serve someone if there's relationships in the kinship system," Ms Leo says.

" Working on Country is what everyone wants to do. "

Mr Katuura says it is important to grow the industry sustainably and carefully.

There are hopes the crabbing operation could go on to provide 100 jobs for the local community. (ABC News: James Elton)

"We talk to the people who run [Humpty Doo] all the time," Mr Katuura tells 7.30.

" They train us. They inspire us. And what they tell us is 'take baby steps'. "

While most of the mud crabs go to the market in Darwin, some are going direct to seafood restaurants. (ABC News: James Elton)

Mr Dooling says working with his hands on his traditional Country has given him peace and purpose.

He also wants customers to know where the mud crabs came from, and that they were caught with pride.

"It makes me feel happy when I go out where my sea Country is," he says.

"I'm not an inlander. I'm a seaman."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Another Perth beach closed as more whale remains found
World.content:
Whale remains have closed another Perth beach today, as authorities warned of possible shark activity in Sorrento after removing the tail of a carcass found just off the shore.

This is the second whale carcass to wash up on the city's beaches this week, and the third in the past month, raising concerns about a further increase in shark activity just as beaches are about to become more crowded ahead of summer.

Sorrento Beach was closed about five weeks ago when Perth father Greg O'Neill was attacked and killed by a large great white shark as he was swimming close to the shoreline.

Sorrento Beach was closed last month after the fatal shark attack. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

He was the third person killed by a shark in Western Australia this year.

Greg O'Neill, left, was killed by a shark while swimming at Sorrento Beach. (Supplied)

The City of Joondalup removed the whale remains from Sorrento Beach a few hours after surf lifesavers reported seeing them, but said the beaches in the area remained closed as "residue from where the whale carcass was beached may attract sharks to the area".

AI-powered drones on cards for WA shark monitoring Western Australia's shark-tagging program will be expanded and the use of AI-powered drones investigated as new funding is announced.

The Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD), along with staff from other agencies, is monitoring the situation, according to the government's SharkSmart app.

On Thursday, a 3-metre, significantly decomposed partial whale carcass washed up at South Cottesloe beach, triggering the closure of all beaches in the area.

Council staff remove the whale carcass from South Cottesloe. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

The remains were buried at the Red Hill Waste Management Facility.

On September 27, a 13-metre, 72-tonne humpback whale carcass washed up on South City Beach, requiring an excavator to remove it.

The state government is expanding its shark-tagging program and may use AI-powered drones as part of a suite of measures aimed at keeping beachgoers safe.

World.title: Darwin patients' medical information posted to Instagram in privacy breach
World.content:
Royal Darwin Hospital has issued an apology for a privacy breach that led to confidential medical information belonging to about a dozen pregnant patients being shared to 28,000 followers on Instagram by a "medical observer" associated with the hospital.

In the letter sent to affected patients, RDH management said NT Health had been informed an overseas trained doctor attached to the hospital's obstetrics and gynaecology unit had posted to social media images and videos where "patient details were visible".

The information exposed included patient names, their presenting condition or any diagnoses they had. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"The information visible about you from our handover sheet included your name, your hospital record number, the ward and bed number, the name of the consultant, the presenting problem, medical history, investigations, and plan of management," the letter said.

"I recognise that learning of this incident may cause distress, embarrassment or concern about your privacy and your trust in our service.

" You should not have had to experience this and we are deeply sorry. "

The content, which has been seen by the ABC, was posted to the Instagram account of Dr Neda Mogharehabed and also included a video from a staff meeting, where health professionals can be heard discussing a woman's care.

Screenshots of the posts featured on the Instagram account @dr.neda.mogharehabed (Supplied)

In a statement to the ABC, Dr Mogharehabed said she "cannot confirm how these images were posted" or "whether they originated from the account I currently control", noting "there may be other accounts using my name".

Dr Mogharehabed added she "did not intend to disclose any patient information" and that she takes "patient privacy seriously".

"I am sorry for the concern this situation has caused. At this stage, however, I cannot verify the origin or circumstances of the images," she said.

In their statement, RDH management noted the doctor as a "medical observer" who was not permitted to undertake any patient management and that her attachment to NT Health had since been terminated.

Dr Neda Mogharehabed is no longer associated with NT Health. (Supplied)

'Shocking' and a 'violation'

One of the women whose information was exposed was ABC Radio Darwin producer, Shanelle Tobin, who is 17-weeks pregnant with her second child.

Ms Tobin said when she went for her appointment at RDH two weeks ago she was asked if she consented to a "medical observer" being present.

"I didn't give it a second thought, I was like 'yep, they're here to learn, to get exposure, whatever it is, I'm comfortable', and now I guess I'm reflecting on that [choice]," Ms Tobin said.

Shanelle Tobin is expecting her second child in April-May next year. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

The expectant mother said the information shared in these medical appointments was detailed and highly sensitive.

"You go through everything from previous pregnancies, whether or not you've had terminations, they talk through your mental health generally and how it was with your last pregnancy," she said.

"Every facet of physical health, so that goes into STIs [sexually transmitted diseases], any issues with your reproductive organs ... your fertility journey, whether that's with IVF or not, and your experience of domestic violence.

" So, yeah it is a very vulnerable space ... and you're just putting your trust in them that this is the cone of silence. "

When Shanelle Tobin saw the screenshots of the images posted showing private informaiton she was shocked. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

Ms Tobin said she discovered her personal information had been shared online when a member of the public reached out to her saying they had seen the post and her name featured.

"It was obviously shocking," she said.

"I then received a phone call from Royal Darwin Hospital from the head of obstetrics who outlined that this breach had happened."

Ms Tobin said when she realised the account had 28,000 followers the "feeling of violation really set in".

Shanelle Tobin says the exposure of her information made her feel "violated". (ABC News: Grace Atta)

'Major wake-up call' for RDH

In a statement, the vice president of the NT Branch of the Australian Medical Association Dr Dayna Duncan said "any breach of patient confidentiality is unacceptable in all situations".

"There are very clear laws and guidelines about patient privacy in Australia, including social media," Dr Duncan said.

"All patients should expect that everyone in their treating team keeps their personal information confidential, with no exceptions."

Dayna Duncan says all patients should expect confidentiality from their treating medical professionals. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Ms Tobin said she hoped the incident would be a "major wake-up call" for RDH about how it manages patient privacy and educates its staff, including international medical observers, about this principle.

The ABC asked Dr Mogharehabed if she had received any training from RDH about expectations around social media use and patient confidentiality.

Dr Mogharehabed said did not receive any specific training about "photography, video recording or posting content on social media" and that she was "not specifically informed during my observership that posting such content on social media was prohibited".

She added: "To my knowledge, the content I became aware of did not tag or mention Royal Darwin Hospital by name."

NT Health was contacted for comment.

Shanelle Tobin gave birth to her toddler at Royal Darwin Hospital almost three years ago. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

Despite her recent bad experience, Ms Tobin said she still planned to access care and give birth at RDH.

"My birth at RDH with my first baby was a really amazing experience, thanks to the people that work there.

"They are some of the hardest workers you could ever imagine and ... I will put my trust back into those people because I know this is one individual who's decided to act in a certain way."

World.title: Final MotoGP race at Phillip Island washed out
World.content:
The MotoGP race at Phillip Island has been cancelled as heavy rain and poor visibility washed out what was the final race at the island circuit.

All races at the track, including the Australian Superbikes race three and both the Moto2 and Moto3 races, were cancelled earlier on Sunday, with hopes that fans would see the MotoGP take a final turn around the iconic circuit fading as the day passed.

The race will move to a street circuit in Adelaide, South Australia in 2027, after three decades at the circuit on the Bass Coast.

The wet weather derailed plans for a final lap of the Ventnor circuit, with the announcement made at 3:30pm that the MotoGP race had been called off after motoring fans sat in the stands for hours in the rain.

Jack Miller farewells fans after the race was cancelled. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

The race had been delayed from its original 2pm start time, with hopes it would begin at 4:30pm.

A MotoGP riders farewell lap was being held at 3:45pm.

Racing fans braved the wet and windy conditions at the track before the race was cancelled. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

In a statement, the Australian Grand Prix Corporation said poor visibility that prevented the medical helicopter from flying was behind the cancellation.

"We know this is an incredibly disappointing outcome for fans, teams and everyone who has contributed to the event," it said.

"Safety must always come first, and racing cannot take place without the medical helicopter able to operate."

The corporation said it would provide full refunds for Sunday ticketholders and partial refunds for multi-day ticketholders.

The official morning warm up was also cancelled, along with track side entertainment such as the monster trucks and a celebratory legends lap with world champions Mick Doohan, Casey Stoner and Wayne Gardner.

World.title: Measles-stricken Amish hit hard amid US vaccine misinformation fight
World.content:
In a rural corner of the US state of Pennsylvania, crop fields, maple trees and colonial-era barn farmhouses dot a patchwork landscape of rolling grassy hills.

At the foot of the Appalachian Mountains, Lancaster County is less than 300 kilometres from New York City and home to the country's oldest and largest Amish community.

But it has also become the focus of a heated political row amid a scramble to contain one of the US's worst measles outbreaks in recent history.

Amish communities are caught in the state's fight to curb rising measles cases. (Reuters: Mark Makela)

The most vulnerable infiltrated

Measles is a highly contagious illness that can lead to the hospitalisation or death of a person, with up to nine out of 10 people who are not vaccinated likely to fall sick, the Australian Centre for Disease Control says.

Authorities in Pennsylvania say the outbreak there began in late April, west of one of the state's largest cities, Philadelphia.

Cases have since ballooned above 1,300 in what has become Pennsylvania's largest spread of the disease in more than three decades.

At least six people have died, including two infants — one of which was a newborn — and a 20-year-old from Lancaster County, an 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County, a 40-year-old woman from Jefferson County and a 39-year-old female from Franklin County.

The Pennsylvania Health Department said none of the victims was vaccinated, and Franklin County officials reported the 39-year-old had a previous measles diagnosis and "several underlying conditions".

Authorities say the disease has mostly impacted people aged between 18 and 49, who account for about 800 of the state's cases, and at least 251 people — or about one in every five — have been hospitalised.

Low vaccination rates, mostly in vulnerable Amish communities, remain the biggest challenge according to officials.

At least five who died were from Amish communities, local media reported.

The Amish traditionally reject modern-day medicine and technologies in favour of communal living. (Reuters: Mark Makela)

The Amish are insular, religious people who associate piety with surrendering to strict rules for the greater good of their community, and reject modern-day technologies.

They came to the US from Europe in the 1700s, and more than 410,000 still live across the country, including at least 40,000 in Lancaster County.

Braxton Mitchell, co-director of the University of Maryland's Amish research program, says their communal way of life creates a unique risk of rapid virus spread.

"Amish are very social. The Amish families have a lot of kids — the average [has] seven or eight, so a lot of people in the household," he said.

"The Amish get together with their neighbours, with their relatives; they have church services on Sundays which tend to be at somebody's house and the whole church district shows up."

The measles outbreak has also impacted Amish children in parts of Pennsylvania, including some infants who died as a result of their illnesses. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

He said they were sceptical of government intervention and do not see the need to engage with modern medicine.

"They don't like governments telling them what to do … Amish don't subscribe to the national health insurance," Professor Mitchell said.

" With some diseases, the Amish [believe] 'if we get sick, if God's will is that we're meant to survive, we'll survive'. "

Steve Nolt, a professor at Elizabethtown College, has lived in Lancaster County for most of his life and said he loves the area's reputation for diversity, manufacturing, picturesque nature and pleasantness of local life.

"There's a strong sense of Lancaster heritage and Lancaster identity … [The county] is special, especially in the minds of people with deep roots here," he said.

Steve Nolt (left) says Lancaster County boasts a lifestyle and nature that make it attractive as a potential place to retire. (Supplied: Steve Nolt)

But he said while the majority of the non-Amish population live with them harmoniously, there is still concern about the spread of measles.

That worry has extended to non-Amish residents warily monitoring transmission alerts naming schools, stores or other popular locations where the virus has spread outside of Amish areas, Mr Nolt said.

Fears of deadly under-reporting

In the neighbouring Chester County, 93 cases have been reported this year, but there is concern around unreported infections.

Jeanne Franklin, the county's public health director, said officials were aware of people who fell ill and did not feel the need to access medical care or alert authorities.

She said by the time some patients present to hospitals or other medical clinics, they were significantly ill.

"What we're seeing is the worst of the worst," she told the ABC.

" It is definitely bigger than we are able to report because it is moving very quickly … Statistically speaking, we're likely going to see more deaths. "

In Chester County, and parts of the neighbouring Lancaster County, door-to-door and community outreach efforts are underway to spread vaccination awareness. (AP: Matt Rourke)

Ms Franklin described the Amish as "vaccine hesitant", but does not treat them as unique from the non-Amish who choose not to be vaccinated according to political or religious beliefs.

"What we want to remind people is, regardless of whether you're Amish or an anti-vaxxer … reassess the decision in the light of today," she said.

"Thirty years ago you may have said: 'Why do I need that? Measles isn't an issue.' Well, guess what, it's an issue."

Measles and other diseases are making a comeback A recent outbreak of measles in Adelaide has sparked concern from health authorities, but it's not the only infectious illness where cases are rising once again.

She said Chester County adopted a word-of-mouth approach to promoting vaccination and dispelling common myths about measles.

"We have a whole team … painting the picture [of the disease's spread]. Where is it? Is it in our adults? Is it in our youth?" she said.

"We're a health department; we can't be everywhere, but we know the church on Main Street, the food pantry on South Street, and the hardware store are trusted business owners and community members.

"We are going out to meet them, educate them, so if they get questions, they know how to direct to us … Some of them are like, 'give me 100 [flyers], I'm going to put it in everyone's grocery bag.'"

Pennsylvania health authorities say more than 6,000 MMR vaccines have been administered at 212 pop-up clinics in affected communities since April. (AP: Matt Rourke)

White House clash clouds vaccine efforts

With more than 4,500 reported cases, the US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said.

Rural Pennsylvania is not the only area under strain — large outbreaks have been reported in Texas, Utah, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Florida.

In New York, Governor Kathy Hochul this month declared a disaster emergency because of rising cases in neighbouring states.

The US eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates.

But the CDC said rates have fallen recently to below the 95 per cent coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.

Following Pennsylvania's first two deaths, a political clash erupted between the state's vaccine-promoting Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro and the Trump Administration's Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr — known for raising alarms about vaccines.

Can anyone Make America Healthy Again? Robert F Kennedy Jr vowed to Make America Healthy Again, but his alliance with Donald Trump has left some true believers jaded.

Mr Kennedy suggested Mr Shapiro's office may have "altogether fabricated" the deaths and accused the governor of "fearmongering, misinformation, finger-pointing, and the weaponisation of infectious disease fears for political gain."

For weeks, the CDC did not record the measles-related deaths on its public disease-tracking dashboard, saying it was seeking more information to prove their validity.

Mr Shapiro condemned Mr Kennedy for those comments, and other claims he made that the US's MMR vaccine — which protects people against measles, mumps and rubella — included traces of fetal tissue.

Josh Shapiro accuses Trump administration authorities of allowing misinformation to spread, hampering his state's efforts to fight off measles. (Reuters: Hannah Beier)

"Unfortunately at a time where I needed the top 'health expert' in the nation to responsibly work with us to deal with this outbreak, he instead chose to go down a rabbit hole of conspiracy theories and false claims," Mr Shapiro said in a post on X.

" The correlation is clear: Secretary Kennedy has stoked confusion amongst parents and others — and the result has been less protection from measles and more cases. "

Robert F Kennedy Jr has routinely questioned the efficacy and safety of medically proven vaccines. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

The Pennsylvania Health Department said at least 6,500 MMR vaccines have been administered at 226 pop-up clinics in affected communities since April.

Paul Griffin, the director of infectious diseases at Mater Health Services, said that while the vaccine was "incredibly effective", Mr Kennedy's comments undermine public health efforts.

"We need the advice to come from people that have a very good understanding of what [measles] is and what we need to do to address it," he said.

Loading...

Ms Franklin said she had seen no evidence of Mr Kennedy's comments impacting how frontline CDC health staff, who were aware of the urgency of addressing the outbreak, operate.

"They are still core passionate public health professionals … They're not misleading; they're being told what they can and cannot publish [and] how they define things," she said.

She says the outbreak is now a race against time.

"It's either how many people can get vaccinated and protected, or how many people are going to get the disease," she said.

" Pennsylvania is too far into this, by the numbers only, to outrace it. Now it's, how do we stay the course with as many people as we can in the hopes of minimising the impact and deaths? "

ABC/AP

World.title: Man dies after being crushed by ramp in northern Victoria
World.content:
A man has died in a workplace incident on a rural property near Shepparton in Victoria's north-east.

Emergency services were called to Evans Road, Waggarandall, about 40 kilometres north-east of Shepparton, to reports a man was trapped under a loading ramp about 10:20am on Sunday.

Advanced life support paramedics attended the property, but the man died at the scene.

The scene of the incident at Waggarandall today. (ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf)

Police and SES also attended the scene.

The death is not being treat as suspicious and WorkSafe has been notified.

Police will prepare a report for the coroner.

World.title: Man dies on Tasmania's west coast while waiting for ambulance
World.content:
A man on Tasmania's west coast has died while waiting for an ambulance which took nearly 80 minutes to arrive because of staffing issues.

The ABC understands the man, aged in his 60s, called Triple Zero (000) from the Zeehan area on Saturday, complaining of chest pains and issues breathing.

Health and Community Services Union state secretary Robbie Moore said this would be a "priority one" case, meaning an ambulance would try to get there "as soon as possible".

However, the ambulance in Zeehan was unstaffed on the day due to an unfilled gap in the roster, and the nearby crews in Strahan and Queenstown were responding to other calls.

An ambulance in Burnie, about 140 kilometres north of Zeehan, was dispatched and arrived about 78 minutes after the Triple Zero call — however the man was dead when it arrived.

Mr Moore said a crewed ambulance in Zeehan would have been able to arrive at the scene a "fair bit quicker than that".

"This is a very tragic situation that just highlights the need for the government to resource ambulance properly and to put on more permanent paramedics," Mr Moore said.

"Seventy-eight minutes is way too long to wait for somebody with chest pain — that's an emergency situation and it's likely to be a heart attack.

"You need an ambulance within 10 minutes to be able to give the best chance of survival and we weren't able to provide that due to a series of situations."

Robbie Moore says more permanent paramedics are needed. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

In a statement, a spokesperson from the Department of Health said it expressed its "heartfelt condolences to the patient's family, friends and loved ones".

"Attempts were made to fill the vacant shift through the usual backfilling arrangements, including overtime and the use of volunteers," they said.

"There are ongoing efforts to recruit more paramedics to the region, however the remoteness of the area does provide challenges."

They said a "comprehensive investigation" would be held into the circumstances surrounding the incident, to "identify any immediate actions required".

Labor MP Ella Haddad said it was "absolutely unthinkable" that another person had died "because of cuts to the health budget".

"This really shines a light on the absolute dire need for investment in regional healthcare in Tasmania," Ms Haddad said.

The incident comes less than two weeks after an investigation was launched into the death of a man in Hobart, whose family had to transport him to hospital due to ambulance delays.

Tasmania's Health Minister, Bridget Archer, said this morning that she was not aware of any similar incidents involving ambulance delays.

"Any death that occurs is a tragedy and our hearts go out to any family and friends that are involved in that situation," Ms Archer said.

World.title: ‘Petrol’s paid for’: Carroll kicks off re-election campaign in Geelong
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election ‘Petrol’s paid for’: Carroll kicks off re-election campaign in Geelong Patrick Hatch and Bridget McArthur October 25, 2026 — 4:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Premier Ben Carroll has launched his re-election campaign in earnest by promising to spend $750 million a year to fund 250 more emergency department beds at 12 hospitals across the state. Dodging torrential rain in North Melbourne and dogged by dire opinion polls that show Labor heading for defeat on November 28, Carroll boarded his election campaign bus for the first time on Sunday morning and fired the starting pistol on a five-week campaign. Premier Ben Carroll began his 2026 election campaign on a trip to Geelong University Hospital on Sunday. Photograph by Chris Hopkins The slogan printed on its rear – “New Premier, New Direction” – is about as subtle as the bright red coach itself, as Carroll attempts to distance himself from his predecessors Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan, who he successfully challenged for the leadership just three months ago. “Petrol’s paid for,” he joked while boarding the bus, referencing a bungle earlier this week when he inadvertently drove off from a service station without paying. The premier blamed the lapse on a busy and stressful day, and has since paid the $90 outstanding.



The first stop in trying to win over voters was Geelong’s University Hospital, where Carroll, flanked by Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams and Health Minister Ingrid Stitt, announced Labor would spend $1.5 billion over four years to tackle chronic emergency department wait times. Related Article Healthcare Inside the storm: On the front line of Victoria’s stretched emergency departments The funding would pay for 1500 extra health workers, including 750 nurses, and allow 250 more beds to operate across 12 hospitals: the Alfred, Austin, Ballarat Base, Bendigo, Footscray, Latrobe Regional, Royal Children’s, Shepparton, Swan Hill, Werribee Mercy, Wonthaggi, and University Hospital Geelong. Carroll said the funding would expand the hospitals’ emergency capacity by 25 per cent on average, to treat an extra 210,000 patients a year and cut wait times by 20 per cent. As The Age reported on Sunday, hospital emergency departments are struggling to treat a record number of acutely unwell and injured Victorians presenting for treatment every day.



Victorian Agency for Health Information data shows more that half of emergency department patients are now waiting more than four hours to be treated, and the Australasian College of Emergency Medicine has warned the situation will deteriorate without urgent action. Carroll said investing in public hospitals was “in Labor’s DNA” and took aim at Opposition Leader Jess Wilson, alleging she would “Americanise” the health system in partnership with One Nation if elected. Ben Carroll’s ‘big red bus’ is set to tour the state ahead of the Victorian election on November 28. Chris Hopkins “It is so critically important that every Victorian knows there’s a real choice this election: a party and a movement that is fighting for working people, or a Liberal-One-Nation coalition that will hurt working people,” he said. Speaking at a press conference in Melbourne’s outer east this morning, accompanied by federal Liberal Senator James Paterson, Wilson described Carroll’s announcement as just another hollow promise – citing languishing hospital projects in West Gippsland, Torquay, Eltham, Wonthaggi and Maroondah.



The Coalition’s health policy includes building new “transit lounge” waiting areas in up to 10 hospitals, incentives for healthcare workers to move to the regions, and spending $1.27 billion for public patients to have elective surgeries in private hospitals to clear waitlists. Wilson said her party was looking at upgrading the Maroondah Hospital – something the community has campaigned for – but would not commit to it or other specific projects. Jess Wilson rejected Ben Carroll’s assertion on Sunday, saying she had no plans to “Americanise” the state’s health system if elected. Bridget McArthur She also rejected Labor’s accusation that she was seeking to “Americanise” the state’s healthcare system by sending public patients into private hospitals. “We have private capacity right here, right now. And my priority … is making sure that the nearly 70,000 Victorians waiting on the elective surgery waitlist get surgery sooner,” she said. “That is what a government should be doing. Not making big promises before an election, failing to deliver after.”



While Wilson has ruled out a partnership with One Nation, she was forced to concede on Sunday that the Liberal Party’s candidate for Sunbury, Simmone Cottom, “made a mistake” after being caught on a recording encouraging people to vote for One Nation. “I’m encouraging people to change the government. In the lower house, vote Liberals and in the upper house, vote One Nation,” Cottom said in the recording, obtained by The Age. Wilson said she had not discussed the incident directly with Cottom, but said campaign staff had. “Simmone has said that she made a mistake and mistakes happen in campaigns. She’s apologised,” Wilson said. Labor seized on the incident to bolster its attacks that the Liberals will govern in partnership with the populist right-wing party.



“It is clear: a Liberal and One Nation coalition will come together,” Carroll said. Related Article Victorian election Deal or no deal? How the major parties are tackling the minority government risk The Age’s latest Resolve opinion poll has the Coalition with a primary vote of 28 per cent, Labor on 25 per cent and One Nation on 23 per cent. Those numbers point to a likely change of government, but it is unclear whether the Liberals and Nationals will be able to form a majority government in their own right. Carroll’s election bus stopped en route back to Melbourne at the Werribee Centrals Cricket Club to meet about 50 Labor volunteers working on local candidate John Lister’s campaign. Lister, a local school teacher, narrowly retained the seat of Werribee during last year’s byelection, despite a 16 per cent swing against it, following the resignation of former treasurer Tim Pallas.



Carroll said that despite being in office for 12 years, the byelection victory was proof Labor’s fight for a historic fourth term was far from over. “You are going to help us make a very historic victory come November, just like we did in this room at the Werribee byelection,” he told supporters on Sunday afternoon. “We’re going to defy the pundits. We’re going to make sure Labor wins – because we have to.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: What would you cut? Chalmers challenges critics of government spending
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalAustralian economy What would you cut? Chalmers challenges critics of government spending Paul Sakkal and Shane Wright October 25, 2026 — 4:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has refused to put a cap on near-record government spending that economists and the opposition insist must be reduced to tame inflation while admitting his ambitious budget is causing his colleagues to worry about Labor’s electoral fortunes. Chalmers told this masthead’s Inside Politics podcast he was “not prepared to put a specific number on the optimal spending as a share of GDP” despite calls from leading policy thinkers such as Ken Henry and Saul Eslake for rules to impose fiscal discipline. Jim Chalmers has pushed back demands to set a level of government spending. Alex Ellinghausen The level of government spending, the state of the budget and its heavy dependence on personal income tax are becoming more powerful headaches for Chalmers who, with Finance Minister Katy Gallagher, say they are working on savings in the mid-year budget update due in early December. In the just-completed financial year, spending as a share of the economy reached 26.9 per cent. Outside the pandemic, it was the highest share since 1986-87. The budget recorded a deficit of $22.2 billion which is expected to grow to $31.5 billion this financial year.



Chalmers said those advocating more cuts in spending should nominate what they would slash, arguing that pressures on the government were growing rather than receding. Related Article Political leadership In a funk: How economic pain is straining the PM and treasurer’s relationship “People will have different views about what the optimal level is. From our point of view, it needs to recognise some of these pressures in the care economy and elsewhere … defence spending and the like,” he said. Financial markets put the chance of a fifth interest rate rise this year, at the Reserve Bank’s early November meeting, at 60 per cent. But that has prompted concerns about the state of the economy with the chief economists of the Commonwealth Bank and BetaShares warning the country could tip into a recession. A growing problem is the surge in oil prices. At the weekend, Brent crude hit $US117 a barrel, its highest level since the war against Iran started.



Chalmers would not be drawn on the RBA’s next move but noted he and the Reserve had to balance the financial fallout from the war on the jobs market and the entire economy. “Whether it’s the independent Reserve Bank weighing up all of those things or the government weighing up all of those things ... we’ve all got balances to strike,” he said. The Coalition has declared the next election to be a referendum on the economy. A growing group of Labor-aligned figures, including backbencher Ed Husic last week, joined conservatives such as Mattias Cormann and Josh Frydenberg in making urgent warnings on the need for pro-growth reforms. Several leading policy voices say Labor’s budget should be in surplus at a time when tax receipts were strong and welfare payments low due to strong employment. Many are driving for deep personal income taxes on top of those put in place by the government this year and in mid-2027. Chalmers said the pressures on the economy and budget were complicating the timings for a round of larger tax cuts, expected to be promised in next year’s budget or before the election due in 2028.



“We will look to cut taxes again, but it’s not clear yet what the best way to go about that would be, or the most appropriate time to do that would be given the really substantial fiscal pressures,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

RBA 150,000 words, zero guarantees: Bullock’s high-stakes interest rate revolution Chalmers admitted the suite of tax changes contained in the budget in May “makes life tougher” for Labor MPs who have recently spoken out about the government’s handling of inflation and productivity. The treasurer, who has come under the sharpest criticism of his four-and-a-half years in the job, argued Labor had “lost some paint over the course of not just the last six months or so but over a longer period”, suggesting Labor’s midterm turbulence was caused by factors outside the budget. “I think it’s only right and only fair that I put my hand up and take responsibility for my share of that,” he said. “It’s up to other ministers and the prime ministers how they describe their part in that.”



The relationship between Chalmers and Albanese has come under the spotlight given the strong political reaction to key budget measures. Chalmers has been more explicit than Albanese in taking responsibility for the government’s drop in the polls, which still has Labor in a winning position against a fractured right flank. The treasurer, 48, said he and Albanese, 63, “actually work really closely together”, adding “treasurers are lightning rods when the government is under pressure”. Responding to observations from colleagues that he had become an isolated figure in the cabinet, Chalmers said: “If you’re asking me about my kind of internal political or factional management style, it is a fair criticism of me to say that I spend a lot of time locked in windowless rooms working very hard on some of these difficult economic challenges.” Chalmers said he took very seriously the suggestion he was not open to feedback, also insisting the economic agenda was a top priority for a prime minister who critics say is not as personally interested in economic policy as previous leaders. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said inflation had been a problem since July last year when it moved above the RBA’s target band.



“Inflation won’t be tamed until the government kicks its spending addiction,” Wilson said. Chalmers came under heavy fire last term when he declared the RBA’s higher interest rates were “smashing the economy”, which the opposition said was an attempt to turn the monetary policy setting body into an economic bogeyman. He said the remark was a “a self-evident piece of economic analysis”. He rejected the notion that Labor should have waited for clearer economic skies to pursue such an ambitious tax agenda. “If you wait for calm in the world, you’ll be waiting forever,” he said. “The relative calm of the post-Cold War period has been replaced by chaos, and these rolling economic shocks mean that we are in a very substantial period of global economic uncertainty, volatility, risk and flux.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis.
