World.title: Pay war threatens to get ugly as deadline looms
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Pay war threatens to get ugly as deadline looms Iain Payten October 25, 2026 — 4:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s been mostly fought out behind closed doors so far, but standby for the pay dispute between Australia’s professional players and Rugby Australia to go public – and get ugly – this week, with the deadline for a new collective bargaining agreement only days away. And if you want to know what might unfold if the tense negotiations can’t produce a deal, the playbook of NRL players in their bitter CBA dispute in 2023 is a good starting point. Loading The Rugby Union Players’ Association (RUPA) and Rugby Australia have been at the table for months trying to strike a deal for a new five-year CBA, with the current agreement expiring on Saturday, October 31. Based on dispatches from both trenches, it’s fair to say the talks have grown tetchy and relations have strained.





Players in a league of their own The stink between RUPA and RA comes after much smoother CBA deals in 2020 and 2022, when the existential financial threat to the game of COVID was a backdrop. But now the game is back on its feet, the players’ union has adopted a more combative stance and there’s a clear rugby league flavour to the RUPA camp. New RUPA boss Adrian Turner, who took over in April, was formerly the head of legal at the Rugby League Players Association and he brought in another long-time RLPA figure, former Roosters and Manly player Tom Symonds, to become RUPA chief operating officer. RUPA boss Adrian Turner (middle) and new COO Tom Symonds (front left) with the Wallabies in camp recently. RUPA



What happens if a deal can’t be reached by Saturday? A strike by the Wallabies or the Aussie sevens players is not on the cards, given players are under contract. But with no CBA in place, other action could be taken to put pressure on RA, such as refusing to participate in RA’s commercial events and wearing protest shirts at training. In 2023, when the RLPA and the NRL couldn’t be reach a CBA deal by deadline, NRL stars then refused to do interviews with host broadcasters on match days, delayed kick-off times and even taped over the NRL logo on their jerseys. There were threats to repeat their pay dispute boycott of the 2003 Dally M Awards, but that didn’t eventuate, with a deal finally struck after a month-long, mid-season standoff. Daniel Tupou wearing a Roosters jersey with the NRL logo taped over in 2023. Getty The John Eales Medal night will be held on Friday – a night before the CBA deadline expires – so a boycott of that won’t happen either. Some other NRL’s squeeze points may also not translate to rugby, with players either playing overseas or just starting pre-season training. The Wallabies fly out for a spring tour to London on Saturday. However it plays out, a public stoush about money will likely take skin off, for both sides. The clock ticks.



Basic tunes gets the job done in Nashville Australia A had more than enough power to overwhelm a disappointing USA side in Nashville on Sunday, overcoming a red card to cruise to a 61-12 victory. With only a week’s training in “Music City”, Australia’s second XV stuck to playing pretty basic chords but dominance at set-piece and in the contact zones was enough to run up a score. David Feliuai was sent off for a high shot in the opening half, but it barely affected the Stephen Larkham-coached side. The Aussie A back row were strong, with No.8 Joe Brial winning man of the match, and Will Harris and Rory Scott both busy. Nick Frost also turned in a good 80-minute shift, as he tries to earn his way back into the Wallabies.



In that same boat, Dylan Pietsch scored twice and defended like a back-rower in the middle of the field. Force halfback and former Highlander Nathan Hastie added to the growing list of Wallaby contenders at No.9, with a classy effort. The sides will go at it again on Saturday in New Jersey, where the likes of Zac Lomax, Corey Toole and Luke Reimer will all likely get a start. Young stars stand up as Wallaroos finish strong The Wallaroos finished the year with a third straight win over Scotland on Friday night in Canberra, and further highlighted some positive shifts already made under the new Tim Walsh regime. Skills look sharper, and so too the Wallaroos’ ability to retain the ball and build pressure. The tendency to drop out of games for a 10-15 minute stretch is still a big work-on for Walsh, however.



Teenage playmaker Waiaria Ellis steps through the Scotland defence in Canberra. Getty Images The big takeaways of 2026? The impressive young halves partnership of Samantha Wood (22) and Waiaria Ellis (19) only gets better and better, and throw in Faitala Moleka (21) at No.12, and you have a long-term trio to take to the 2029 World Cup. There are now good headaches in picking a back three, too, with Amelia Whitaker taking every chance she gets. Up front, powerhouse prop Falaki Pohiva is arguably the most important Wallaroos forward, but she’s closely followed by back-rower Piper Duck, who has put years of bad luck and injury behind her and been outstanding this year.

World.title: The other Bolsonaro who could become Brazil’s next president
World.content:
WorldSouth AmericaBrazil The other Bolsonaro who could become Brazil’s next president Ana Ionova October 25, 2026 — 4:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Rio de Janeiro: Clad in a yellow-and-green shirt over a bulletproof vest, Flávio Bolsonaro danced on a carnival float as thousands of euphoric supporters cheered below. “Brazil already chose change!” he shouted, pumping his fist in the air. Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator whose father was president not long ago, is heading into Sunday’s presidential race as the front-runner, having edged out leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in a first-round election this month. Cometh the hour, cometh the son: A victory for Bolsonaro Jnr would mark another big swing to the right in South America. AFP A victory for Bolsonaro would deliver the biggest win yet for an ascendant right-wing movement sweeping Latin America. Right-wing leaders, propelled in part by voter discontent over security, have won seven straight elections in the region over the past 18 months. If Brazil elects Bolsonaro, it would put an enthusiastic ally of Washington in power in the region’s largest nation and leave Mexico as the only big country still in the hands of the left.



Related Article US midterms ‘Like Saddam opened a Cheesecake Factory’: Obama hits out at Trump in campaign trail comeback Bolsonaro, 45, has aligned himself with President Donald Trump on using lethal force to fight drug gangs and has offered Brazil’s vast critical mineral deposits as a way to reduce America’s reliance on China. Trump has not formally backed Bolsonaro, but his administration has telegraphed its support in other ways, including by labelling Brazilian gangs as terror groups. The move shone a spotlight on crime, a concern for many Brazilian voters and a vulnerability for Lula. A right-wing victory would also mark the Bolsonaro family’s stunning return to power, less than four years after the senator’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, tried to stage a coup and inspired his supporters to storm Brazil’s capital, in an episode echoing the attack on the US Capitol. He was convicted of plotting a coup and sentenced to 27 years in prison. Flavio Bolsonaro and incumbent President Luiz Igacio Lula da Silva (right) are neck and neck in the polls heading into Sunday’s final round of voting. AP Photo/Andre Penner



Flávio Bolsonaro and his family may now be on the cusp of gaining sweeping new powers to rewrite Brazil’s history, reshape its future and target their perceived enemies. If elected, Bolsonaro has promised to seek amnesty for his father and the rioters, impeach the Supreme Court justices who jailed them and change Brazil’s Constitution. Related Article Updated

World politics Ex-Brazilian president Bolsonaro sentenced to 27 years in jail over coup plot Just months ago, Bolsonaro’s candidacy seemed like a long shot, with many sceptical that he could overcome a string of scandals and ignite the kind of enthusiasm that catapulted his father to office in 2018. And with the elder Bolsonaro jailed for trying to subvert democracy after losing the last election to Lula, his movement appeared to be in tatters. Then the younger Bolsonaro shocked many when he nearly won outright in the first round of voting this month, drawing more ballots than Lula, though the margin was the narrowest ever in Brazil. “Bolsonarismo is winning the battle for the hearts and minds of a large portion of the population,” said Rosana Pinheiro-Machado, a professor at University College Dublin who studies Brazil’s populist movements.



Bolsonaro’s success has largely been rooted in sweeping, if vague, promises to tackle crime, high grocery bills and a stagnating economy – issues at the top of the list of concerns for Brazilian voters. Taking a page out of the playbook of right-wing allies in Latin America, Bolsonaro has vowed to “declare war” on drug traffickers by building more prisons, labelling gangs as terrorist groups and lowering the age of criminal responsibility. Bolsonaro supporters hold a campaign rally one week ahead of the presidential election runoff. AP Photo/Andre Penner While violent crime has fallen to a 14-year low, many working-class Brazilians live side by side with drug gangs that have expanded their control over neighbourhoods through fear and extortion. “I will reclaim every metre, I will reclaim every street, every neighbourhood, every city, every territory that these scoundrels have taken from the Brazilian people,” Bolsonaro said during a debate days before Sunday’s run-off.



Inspired by the chainsaw used by Argentine President Javier Milei to symbolise a leaner state, Bolsonaro has adopted a pair of giant scissors as his symbol, vowing to cut about $US40 billion in public spending and privatise public companies. Speaking to a growing number of Brazilian workers who have migrated to the gig economy, he also pledged to lower taxes and decrease red tape for entrepreneurs. Even as experts have questioned the economics of Bolsonaro’s promises, including how he can cut taxes without reducing welfare benefits, many voters have responded to his agenda with excitement. Bolsonaro is eager to channel Argentina’s Javier Milei (left) in making heavy cuts to state institutions. AP Photo/Ettore Chiereguini Bolsonaro has also drawn overwhelming support in Brazil’s agricultural belt and in regions of the Amazon, where farmers and cattle ranchers have cheered his promises to make it easier to explore the riches of the rainforest. Crucially, Bolsonaro has also tapped into a deep fatigue many voters feel toward Lula, painting him as a corrupt symbol of the political establishment.



Between 2003 and 2010, during his first two terms, Lula helped lift millions out of poverty through generous social programs financed by a commodities boom. When he left office, his approval ratings topped 80 per cent, but his legacy was later tainted when a sprawling corruption scandal landed him in prison. Related Article Trump diplomacy ‘Brazil belongs to Brazilians’: The world leader who refuses to bow to Donald Trump In 2021, his convictions were tossed out by the Supreme Court amid evidence that the judge who convicted him was biased. This paved the way for Lula’s resurrection and return to the presidency in 2022, though he has struggled to clean up his image among voters who still link him to graft. In Lula’s third term, Brazil’s economy has posted modest growth and largely escaped US tariffs, while unemployment has fallen to record lows. Still, rising household debt and eroding affordability have dampened his approval and fuelled Bolsonaro’s popularity. Lula has also been saddled with the political fallout of a crisis engulfing Brazil’s Supreme Court. Against this backdrop, Bolsonaro’s attacks on the judiciary have grown more alluring to many Brazilians who have lost trust in institutions.



Lula scored points with many Brazilians by standing up to Trump last year when he tried to force the nation into dropping the coup charges against the elder Bolsonaro. Those efforts, the fruits of lobbying by a brother of Flávio Bolsonaro who lives in the United States, ultimately failed. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. World.title: Soggy streets, icy winds: Melbourne shivers through spring cold snap
World.content:
NationalVictoriaWeather Soggy streets, icy winds: Melbourne shivers through spring cold snap Ashleigh McMillan, Hannah Kennelly and Roy Ward Updated October 25, 2026 — 4:33pm ,first published 2:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Victorians face below-average spring temperatures and alpine snow flurries before conditions improve ahead of Melbourne Cup Day. On Sunday, organisers cancelled the Australian MotoGP on Phillip Island after wild weather and poor visibility grounded the medical helicopter, making track conditions unsafe for racing.

Pedestrians attempt to shield themselves from the rain. Arsineh Houspian In Melbourne, it was a soggy start to the day, with more than 22mm of rain falling across the 12 hours to midday on Sunday. In the city’s south-west, Altona recorded heavier totals of 40mm of rain across 24 hours. Health authorities remain on high alert for a thunderstorm asthma emergency, due to a combination of high grass pollen counts and likely strong winds and thunderstorm activity over East Gippsland.



People try to shield themselves from the rain as they cross Collins Street in the Melbourne CBD. Arsineh Houspian A severe thunderstorm warning is in place for the state’s north-east across into the afternoon on Sunday, as damaging wind moves across Wodonga, Corryong, Bright, Falls Creek, Mount Hotham and Omeo. View post on X While Melbourne is expected to reach a top of 19 degrees on Sunday, the Bureau of Meteorology’s senior forecaster Michael Efron said the city would feel much colder due to the breezy conditions. “It’s going to feel a lot colder as we get into this afternoon as those winds pick up,” he said. “It will be quite a shock to the system, compared to the conditions that we’ve seen over the last week with those temperatures pushing into the low 30s.”



Fans waiting for the rain to clear at the 2026 Australian Motorcycle Grand Prix in Phillip Island. Joe Armao Across the first half of the week, Melbourne temperatures will be three to six degrees below average for this time of year, with a high of 16 degrees on Monday as rainfall eases, and a high of 17 degrees on Tuesday. The cold front crossing the state will also bring minor snowfall across the Alpine region on Monday and Tuesday. “There will be some flurries, especially at resorts like Mount Baw Baw, with all this cold air pushing through, and even the risk of some small hail along the coast overnight tonight and into the early hours of Monday,” Efron said on Sunday.



“These cold conditions are quite a typical weather system for spring – it’s when we do tend to see the largest swings between hot and cold weather for Victoria. “Those really dramatic shifts in conditions are driven by the interior of the continent really heating up with the more intense sunlight at this time of year, whereas the oceans to our south are still quite cold.” The 2026 MotoGP was also cancelled due to poor weather conditions, leaving thousands of fans unable to say goodbye to the last race at the iconic Phillip Island circuit. Race organisers battled set back after set back due to the weather on Sunday, postponing track action until after 1pm after poor visibility around Phillip Island and Melbourne impacted the medical helicopter’s ability to fly. Fans wait for the rain to clear during the MotoGP Joe Armao



Organisers said if a crash occurred during the race, the medical helicopter needed to be able to land and also navigate to the nearest trauma centre in Melbourne. Both the MotoGP warm-up session and the Australian Superbikes Race 3 were cancelled in the morning and the Motor3 race was cancelled in the early afternoon. Just after 3.30pm , race organisers announced the event had been cancelled. People with asthma and spring hayfever in East Gippsland are being warned of an increased risk of developing asthma symptoms if large amounts of pollen are whipped into the air on Sunday.



Acting chief health officer Dr Clare Looker said people in the region needed to be prepared while the high-risk forecast was in place across Sunday. Those who had never had asthma could also experience shortness of breath and wheezing, she said. View post on X “Asthma can become serious very quickly, so make sure you have your reliever medication with you and call Triple Zero if someone is struggling to breathe or their asthma is not improving,” Looker said. “The safest place to be during the strong wind gusts before and during a thunderstorm is indoors, with windows and doors closed.” Temperatures are likely to bounce back by late next week, with a forecast top of 25 on Saturday in Melbourne. Reasonable spring weather is expected for the Melbourne Cup.

World.title: When tragedy demands women be treated better, men twist it into an excuse to treat them worse
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack Opinion When tragedy demands women be treated better, men twist it into an excuse to treat them worse Sean Kelly Columnist October 25, 2026 — 4:30pm

October 25, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In his new history of Wikipedia, journalist Richard Cooke writes that we may be witnessing the “beginning of the end of the encyclopaedic age”. This was an age marked not only by a belief in the importance of knowledge, but in its civilising function. If we could just assemble enough facts and give them to enough people, we could create a better society. Two weeks ago, Cooke offered this bleak verdict to Crikey: “Wikipedia is the closest thing that’s ever existed to that universal encyclopaedia, and its effect on making things like public discourse more reasonable or more reason-driven is undetectable.” Don’t assume the attack on Helen Haines will change anything. That’s the quickest way to ensure it doesn’t. Marija Ercegovac I helped launch that book last week, two days after Helen Haines was brutally attacked. That is an event on which there is not yet agreement about facts, though this has not stopped widespread discussion of the political environment in which it took place. And nor should it have. Such sudden, passionate, ubiquitous discussion is always worth paying attention to. A similar phenomenon occurred in the aftermath of the Sydney Swans Pullman Hotel allegations, and in relation to the allegations about the students at Scots College who are accused of sexual assault. Occasionally, you will hear the argument that this means we should refrain from such discussions until more is known. On the specifics of those cases, that is reasonable.



But such sudden eruptions of debate can point us to something important, something worth noticing for its own sake: a deep well of anger, frustration, fear. Such events command national attention not only because of their intrinsic horror but because of the way they unearth such feelings, caused by significant problems in our society. These feelings are all the stronger for the way they are usually pushed down. The passion with which such events are met is a reaction to the complacency with which the topic areas into which they fall are usually met. To many women, in particular, it can seem as though there is a conspiracy to avoid significant discussion of violence against women. It seems that way because, for all intents and purposes, there is. Related Article Opinion

Haines attack What do Jacqui Lambie, Helen Haines and Queen Victoria have in common? Far too much Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author If this sounds like overreach, recall the absolute outpouring of the #metoo movement, those many, many voices: so powerful, so passionate, in part because they had been silenced for years. But this was only a temporary shattering of the status quo before great efforts resumed to return those voices to silence. Consider the hideous media campaign waged against Brittany Higgins. Recall the way defamation is increasingly used to silence women who have spoken up – an international phenomenon portrayed in the recent documentary Silenced. And think, too, of the ways both media campaigns and lawsuits act not only to silence those individual women but all the other women who might consider speaking in the future. Because, of course, this is the broadest danger of the attack on Haines: that women, who already face high barriers to participation in public life, will be further put off. That there are other voices that will be silenced before they even begin to speak.



As a political staffer, I witnessed both these strands in Parliament House – the repressed rage finally surfacing and the way such rage was immediately turned against the person feeling it – on the day when Julia Gillard stood and delivered what would become known as the misogyny speech. The prime minister’s sincere and cutting words, full of fury at the way her gender had been turned against her for so long, resonated with so many. Immediately, though, many journalists rejected those words as unimportant – and went further, too, using them as another piece of evidence in their catalogue of Gillard’s failings. Related Article Opinion

Matthew Canavan Canavan’s bizarre manosphere comments show he should check his own algorithm Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist Or take Nationals leader Matt Canavan’s recent comments about boys being driven to interact with toxic masculinity by a curriculum focused on respectful relationships and consent. Again and again we see that if women demand respect, it is not long before men will find a way to blame men’s failure to show respect on the fact it was asked for in the first place – as experts such as Monash University’s professor Steven Roberts point out, a common manosphere manoeuvre. There is no way out of this catch-22 logic: no action that women might take that will not later be twisted into an excuse for treating them worse. We should be wary, then, of assuming the attack on Helen Haines will change much. If we assume that open discussion and debate will improve the situation, we can look to Cooke’s conclusion: the situation has only worsened. If we assume that a high-profile attack on a woman, universally decried, will shift things, we need only look at the history of violence against women. Even the more fundamental idea that violence is sufficiently shocking that it might act as an alarm that will wake up society is doubtful. German historian Philipp Ruch recently explained the Nazis’ success at the 1930 elections. At first, he said, people were repelled by violence – until the opposite occurred. “It’s hard to admit this from a modern perspective, but historical Fascism’s lust for violence didn’t make it repulsive but extremely attractive to a lot of German voters.”



It is possible that an attack like the one against Helen Haines will make us change our ways. But it is also possible that we live in a society in which violence is increasingly permissible, and in which violence only brings more violence. Taken together, all this does not offer as bleak a prognosis as it might seem. A realistic appraisal of the barriers to change can be depressing, but it is also necessary. In fact, any genuine shift is only likely to begin with a recognition of the immense strength of the forces that work to keep us stuck where we are now. Those forces will never be beaten once and for all. But they can be resisted, and each bit of resistance – be it open debate or pushing back against social media or acting against both violence against and abuse of women – is worthwhile for two reasons. First, because that act may help change things. Second, because each act signals to everyone else that nothing is inevitable – neither change nor the status quo. Sean Kelly is author of The Game: A Portrait of Scott Morrison, a regular columnist and a former adviser to Julia Gillard and Kevin Rudd.

World.title: Northcote triple-brick home passes in on a vendor bid of $1.7 million
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Northcote triple-brick home passes in on a vendor bid of $1.7 million Melissa Heagney-Bayliss October 25, 2026 — 4:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

Key points A Northcote house failed to sell under the hammer, passing in on a vendor bid of $1.7 million.

In Fitzroy, a four-bedroom home that had been newly renovated sold for $1,531,000.

Five bidders fought it out for the keys to an Essendon home, which sold under the hammer for $2,285,000.

A triple-brick character home in Northcote, with a separate apartment attached, didn’t receive a single offer from a buyer at auction on Saturday, passing in on a vendor bid of $1.7 million. The five-bedroom property at 173 Bastings Street had been advertised with a reserve of $1.8 million. Collings Real Estate’s Chris Vrantsis said though there had been a lot of interest in the property, buyers had stepped back after the reserve was revealed, which is required by law under new Victorian auction rules. “We had 30 to 35 people through the house and a few people came back quite a few times,” Vrantsis said. “But I think as soon as the reserve was shown they felt it was over the top.”



The property is now advertised for private sale with a $1,775,000 asking price. Related Article Melbourne house prices Melbourne set to drop out of the $1 million club as house prices fall The Northcote auction was one of 838 scheduled in Melbourne this week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 56 per cent from 612 reported results across the week, while 102 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Agents say market conditions in Melbourne, and the fear of another interest rate rise – with the Reserve Bank set to make its next decision on November 3 – were being talked about over the auction weekend.



Melbourne’s median house price is expected to fall below $1 million, after dropping 3.3 per cent in the September quarter, on Domain data. It only needs to fall another 1.5 per cent for prices to be in the high $900,000s. Meanwhile, banks including ANZ and Westpac are predicting another rate hike next month. Inside 173 Bastings Street, Northcote. Collings Real Estate Despite the challenges the current market was throwing up, Vrantsis was confident the property would sell. “We’ll just keep working through until we find the right buyer,” he said.



In Fitzroy, a fully renovated art deco home, at 74 Alexandra Parade, sold under the hammer for $1,531,000 above the $1.35 million reserve. Three bidders fought it out for the keys to the four-bedroom home – all were young first-home buyers. Nelson Alexander Fitzroy’s Mark Verrocchi said the auction went on for some time, as smaller bids of $5000 and then $1000 were being made throughout as a tactic to slow down proceedings. The young buyer, represented by a buyer’s advocate, will now make the property his family home.



Verrocchi said the property appealed to a lot of buyers as it had been newly renovated from top to bottom, and was on a larger parcel of land with a side driveway. However, it was in a tricky location being on such a busy road. “That area really is like an island in Fitzroy,” he said. “If this house was on any other street it would have cost $2 million plus.” Verrocchi said while higher interest rates were impacting the market, so was the upcoming Victorian State Election, with many prospective buyers and sellers waiting to see what the outcome would be in late November, before making any decisions. In Essendon, five bidders were sure of their decision, making offers for a four-bedroom home at 36 Washington Street. The home sold under the hammer for $2,285,000, above the $1.95 million reserve.



Bidding opened at $1.9 million, with $25,000 offers from bidders until the price reached $2 million. It then slowed to $10,000 and $5000 offers before the winning bid was made. The buyer is a young family from Pascoe Vale looking to move to Essendon. Jellis Craig Moonee Valley’s Jason Johnson said buyers had responded strongly to the reserves being advertised on properties listed for auction, as did vendors’ realistic pricing. “Price obviously had a lot to do with it,” Johnson said.



Another property at 15 Ferguson Street, Ascot Vale sold for $1.47 million, above the $1,385,000 reserve, after four bidders fought it out. The property sold to a young family who were upsizing from Tullamarine. Both were great results in a tough market, he said. “It was a bit out of the norm in terms of what’s happening in the market at the moment,” Johnson said. World.title: ‘Petrol’s paid for’: Carroll kicks off re-election campaign in Geelong
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election ‘Petrol’s paid for’: Carroll kicks off re-election campaign in Geelong Patrick Hatch and Bridget McArthur October 25, 2026 — 4:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Premier Ben Carroll has launched his re-election campaign in earnest by promising to spend $750 million a year to fund 250 more emergency department beds at 12 hospitals across the state. Dodging torrential rain in North Melbourne and dogged by dire opinion polls that show Labor heading for defeat on November 28, Carroll boarded his election campaign bus for the first time on Sunday morning and fired the starting pistol on a five-week campaign. Premier Ben Carroll began his 2026 election campaign on a trip to Geelong University Hospital on Sunday. Photograph by Chris Hopkins The slogan printed on its rear – “New Premier, New Direction” – is about as subtle as the bright red coach itself, as Carroll attempts to distance himself from his predecessors Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan, who he successfully challenged for the leadership just three months ago. “Petrol’s paid for,” he joked while boarding the bus, referencing a bungle earlier this week when he inadvertently drove off from a service station without paying. The premier blamed the lapse on a busy and stressful day, and has since paid the $90 outstanding.



The first stop in trying to win over voters was Geelong’s University Hospital, where Carroll, flanked by Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams and Health Minister Ingrid Stitt, announced Labor would spend $1.5 billion over four years to tackle chronic emergency department wait times. Related Article Healthcare Inside the storm: On the front line of Victoria’s stretched emergency departments The funding would pay for 1500 extra health workers, including 750 nurses, and allow 250 more beds to operate across 12 hospitals: the Alfred, Austin, Ballarat Base, Bendigo, Footscray, Latrobe Regional, Royal Children’s, Shepparton, Swan Hill, Werribee Mercy, Wonthaggi, and University Hospital Geelong. Carroll said the funding would expand the hospitals’ emergency capacity by 25 per cent on average, to treat an extra 210,000 patients a year and cut wait times by 20 per cent. As The Age reported on Sunday, hospital emergency departments are struggling to treat a record number of acutely unwell and injured Victorians presenting for treatment every day.



Victorian Agency for Health Information data shows more that half of emergency department patients are now waiting more than four hours to be treated, and the Australasian College of Emergency Medicine has warned the situation will deteriorate without urgent action. Carroll said investing in public hospitals was “in Labor’s DNA” and took aim at Opposition Leader Jess Wilson, alleging she would “Americanise” the health system in partnership with One Nation if elected. Ben Carroll’s ‘big red bus’ is set to tour the state ahead of the Victorian election on November 28. Chris Hopkins “It is so critically important that every Victorian knows there’s a real choice this election: a party and a movement that is fighting for working people, or a Liberal-One-Nation coalition that will hurt working people,” he said. Speaking at a press conference in Melbourne’s outer east this morning, accompanied by federal Liberal Senator James Paterson, Wilson described Carroll’s announcement as just another hollow promise – citing languishing hospital projects in West Gippsland, Torquay, Eltham, Wonthaggi and Maroondah.



The Coalition’s health policy includes building new “transit lounge” waiting areas in up to 10 hospitals, incentives for healthcare workers to move to the regions, and spending $1.27 billion for public patients to have elective surgeries in private hospitals to clear waitlists. Wilson said her party was looking at upgrading the Maroondah Hospital – something the community has campaigned for – but would not commit to it or other specific projects. Jess Wilson rejected Ben Carroll’s assertion on Sunday, saying she had no plans to “Americanise” the state’s health system if elected. Bridget McArthur She also rejected Labor’s accusation that she was seeking to “Americanise” the state’s healthcare system by sending public patients into private hospitals. “We have private capacity right here, right now. And my priority … is making sure that the nearly 70,000 Victorians waiting on the elective surgery waitlist get surgery sooner,” she said. “That is what a government should be doing. Not making big promises before an election, failing to deliver after.”



While Wilson has ruled out a partnership with One Nation, she was forced to concede on Sunday that the Liberal Party’s candidate for Sunbury, Simmone Cottom, “made a mistake” after being caught on a recording encouraging people to vote for One Nation. “I’m encouraging people to change the government. In the lower house, vote Liberals and in the upper house, vote One Nation,” Cottom said in the recording, obtained by The Age. Wilson said she had not discussed the incident directly with Cottom, but said campaign staff had. “Simmone has said that she made a mistake and mistakes happen in campaigns. She’s apologised,” Wilson said. Labor seized on the incident to bolster its attacks that the Liberals will govern in partnership with the populist right-wing party.



“It is clear: a Liberal and One Nation coalition will come together,” Carroll said. Related Article Victorian election Deal or no deal? How the major parties are tackling the minority government risk The Age’s latest Resolve opinion poll has the Coalition with a primary vote of 28 per cent, Labor on 25 per cent and One Nation on 23 per cent. Those numbers point to a likely change of government, but it is unclear whether the Liberals and Nationals will be able to form a majority government in their own right. Carroll’s election bus stopped en route back to Melbourne at the Werribee Centrals Cricket Club to meet about 50 Labor volunteers working on local candidate John Lister’s campaign. Lister, a local school teacher, narrowly retained the seat of Werribee during last year’s byelection, despite a 16 per cent swing against it, following the resignation of former treasurer Tim Pallas.



Carroll said that despite being in office for 12 years, the byelection victory was proof Labor’s fight for a historic fourth term was far from over. “You are going to help us make a very historic victory come November, just like we did in this room at the Werribee byelection,” he told supporters on Sunday afternoon. “We’re going to defy the pundits. We’re going to make sure Labor wins – because we have to.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: What would you cut? Chalmers challenges critics of government spending
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalAustralian economy What would you cut? Chalmers challenges critics of government spending Paul Sakkal and Shane Wright October 25, 2026 — 4:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has refused to put a cap on near-record government spending that economists and the opposition insist must be reduced to tame inflation while admitting his ambitious budget is causing his colleagues to worry about Labor’s electoral fortunes. Chalmers told this masthead’s Inside Politics podcast he was “not prepared to put a specific number on the optimal spending as a share of GDP” despite calls from leading policy thinkers such as Ken Henry and Saul Eslake for rules to impose fiscal discipline. Jim Chalmers has pushed back demands to set a level of government spending. Alex Ellinghausen The level of government spending, the state of the budget and its heavy dependence on personal income tax are becoming more powerful headaches for Chalmers who, with Finance Minister Katy Gallagher, say they are working on savings in the mid-year budget update due in early December. In the just-completed financial year, spending as a share of the economy reached 26.9 per cent. Outside the pandemic, it was the highest share since 1986-87. The budget recorded a deficit of $22.2 billion which is expected to grow to $31.5 billion this financial year.



Chalmers said those advocating more cuts in spending should nominate what they would slash, arguing that pressures on the government were growing rather than receding. Related Article Political leadership In a funk: How economic pain is straining the PM and treasurer’s relationship “People will have different views about what the optimal level is. From our point of view, it needs to recognise some of these pressures in the care economy and elsewhere … defence spending and the like,” he said. Financial markets put the chance of a fifth interest rate rise this year, at the Reserve Bank’s early November meeting, at 60 per cent. But that has prompted concerns about the state of the economy with the chief economists of the Commonwealth Bank and BetaShares warning the country could tip into a recession. A growing problem is the surge in oil prices. At the weekend, Brent crude hit $US117 a barrel, its highest level since the war against Iran started.



Chalmers would not be drawn on the RBA’s next move but noted he and the Reserve had to balance the financial fallout from the war on the jobs market and the entire economy. “Whether it’s the independent Reserve Bank weighing up all of those things or the government weighing up all of those things ... we’ve all got balances to strike,” he said. The Coalition has declared the next election to be a referendum on the economy. A growing group of Labor-aligned figures, including backbencher Ed Husic last week, joined conservatives such as Mattias Cormann and Josh Frydenberg in making urgent warnings on the need for pro-growth reforms. Several leading policy voices say Labor’s budget should be in surplus at a time when tax receipts were strong and welfare payments low due to strong employment. Many are driving for deep personal income taxes on top of those put in place by the government this year and in mid-2027. Chalmers said the pressures on the economy and budget were complicating the timings for a round of larger tax cuts, expected to be promised in next year’s budget or before the election due in 2028.



“We will look to cut taxes again, but it’s not clear yet what the best way to go about that would be, or the most appropriate time to do that would be given the really substantial fiscal pressures,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

RBA 150,000 words, zero guarantees: Bullock’s high-stakes interest rate revolution Chalmers admitted the suite of tax changes contained in the budget in May “makes life tougher” for Labor MPs who have recently spoken out about the government’s handling of inflation and productivity. The treasurer, who has come under the sharpest criticism of his four-and-a-half years in the job, argued Labor had “lost some paint over the course of not just the last six months or so but over a longer period”, suggesting Labor’s midterm turbulence was caused by factors outside the budget. “I think it’s only right and only fair that I put my hand up and take responsibility for my share of that,” he said. “It’s up to other ministers and the prime ministers how they describe their part in that.”



The relationship between Chalmers and Albanese has come under the spotlight given the strong political reaction to key budget measures. Chalmers has been more explicit than Albanese in taking responsibility for the government’s drop in the polls, which still has Labor in a winning position against a fractured right flank. The treasurer, 48, said he and Albanese, 63, “actually work really closely together”, adding “treasurers are lightning rods when the government is under pressure”. Responding to observations from colleagues that he had become an isolated figure in the cabinet, Chalmers said: “If you’re asking me about my kind of internal political or factional management style, it is a fair criticism of me to say that I spend a lot of time locked in windowless rooms working very hard on some of these difficult economic challenges.” Chalmers said he took very seriously the suggestion he was not open to feedback, also insisting the economic agenda was a top priority for a prime minister who critics say is not as personally interested in economic policy as previous leaders. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said inflation had been a problem since July last year when it moved above the RBA’s target band.



“Inflation won’t be tamed until the government kicks its spending addiction,” Wilson said. Chalmers came under heavy fire last term when he declared the RBA’s higher interest rates were “smashing the economy”, which the opposition said was an attempt to turn the monetary policy setting body into an economic bogeyman. He said the remark was a “a self-evident piece of economic analysis”. He rejected the notion that Labor should have waited for clearer economic skies to pursue such an ambitious tax agenda. “If you wait for calm in the world, you’ll be waiting forever,” he said. “The relative calm of the post-Cold War period has been replaced by chaos, and these rolling economic shocks mean that we are in a very substantial period of global economic uncertainty, volatility, risk and flux.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Pay war threatens to get ugly as deadline looms
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Pay war threatens to get ugly as deadline looms Iain Payten October 25, 2026 — 4:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It’s been mostly fought out behind closed doors so far, but standby for the pay dispute between Australia’s professional players and Rugby Australia to go public – and get ugly – this week, with the deadline for a new collective bargaining agreement only days away. And if you want to know what might unfold if the tense negotiations can’t produce a deal, the playbook of NRL players in their bitter CBA dispute in 2023 is a good starting point. Loading The Rugby Union Players’ Association (RUPA) and Rugby Australia have been at the table for months trying to strike a deal for a new five-year CBA, with the current agreement expiring on Saturday, October 31. Based on dispatches from both trenches, it’s fair to say the talks have grown tetchy and relations have strained.





Players in a league of their own The stink between RUPA and RA comes after much smoother CBA deals in 2020 and 2022, when the existential financial threat to the game of COVID was a backdrop. But now the game is back on its feet, the players’ union has adopted a more combative stance and there’s a clear rugby league flavour to the RUPA camp. New RUPA boss Adrian Turner, who took over in April, was formerly the head of legal at the Rugby League Players Association and he brought in another long-time RLPA figure, former Roosters and Manly player Tom Symonds, to become RUPA chief operating officer. RUPA boss Adrian Turner (middle) and new COO Tom Symonds (front left) with the Wallabies in camp recently. RUPA



What happens if a deal can’t be reached by Saturday? A strike by the Wallabies or the Aussie sevens players is not on the cards, given players are under contract. But with no CBA in place, other action could be taken to put pressure on RA, such as refusing to participate in RA’s commercial events and wearing protest shirts at training. In 2023, when the RLPA and the NRL couldn’t be reach a CBA deal by deadline, NRL stars then refused to do interviews with host broadcasters on match days, delayed kick-off times and even taped over the NRL logo on their jerseys. There were threats to repeat their pay dispute boycott of the 2003 Dally M Awards, but that didn’t eventuate, with a deal finally struck after a month-long, mid-season standoff. Daniel Tupou wearing a Roosters jersey with the NRL logo taped over in 2023. Getty The John Eales Medal night will be held on Friday – a night before the CBA deadline expires – so a boycott of that won’t happen either. Some other NRL’s squeeze points may also not translate to rugby, with players either playing overseas or just starting pre-season training. The Wallabies fly out for a spring tour to London on Saturday. However it plays out, a public stoush about money will likely take skin off, for both sides. The clock ticks.



Basic tunes gets the job done in Nashville Australia A had more than enough power to overwhelm a disappointing USA side in Nashville on Sunday, overcoming a red card to cruise to a 61-12 victory. With only a week’s training in “Music City”, Australia’s second XV stuck to playing pretty basic chords but dominance at set-piece and in the contact zones was enough to run up a score. David Feliuai was sent off for a high shot in the opening half, but it barely affected the Stephen Larkham-coached side. The Aussie A back row were strong, with No.8 Joe Brial winning man of the match, and Will Harris and Rory Scott both busy. Nick Frost also turned in a good 80-minute shift, as he tries to earn his way back into the Wallabies.



In that same boat, Dylan Pietsch scored twice and defended like a back-rower in the middle of the field. Force halfback and former Highlander Nathan Hastie added to the growing list of Wallaby contenders at No.9, with a classy effort. The sides will go at it again on Saturday in New Jersey, where the likes of Zac Lomax, Corey Toole and Luke Reimer will all likely get a start. Young stars stand up as Wallaroos finish strong The Wallaroos finished the year with a third straight win over Scotland on Friday night in Canberra, and further highlighted some positive shifts already made under the new Tim Walsh regime. Skills look sharper, and so too the Wallaroos’ ability to retain the ball and build pressure. The tendency to drop out of games for a 10-15 minute stretch is still a big work-on for Walsh, however.



Teenage playmaker Waiaria Ellis steps through the Scotland defence in Canberra. Getty Images The big takeaways of 2026? The impressive young halves partnership of Samantha Wood (22) and Waiaria Ellis (19) only gets better and better, and throw in Faitala Moleka (21) at No.12, and you have a long-term trio to take to the 2029 World Cup. There are now good headaches in picking a back three, too, with Amelia Whitaker taking every chance she gets. Up front, powerhouse prop Falaki Pohiva is arguably the most important Wallaroos forward, but she’s closely followed by back-rower Piper Duck, who has put years of bad luck and injury behind her and been outstanding this year.

World.title: The other Bolsonaro who could become Brazil’s next president
World.content:
WorldSouth AmericaBrazil The other Bolsonaro who could become Brazil’s next president Ana Ionova October 25, 2026 — 4:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Rio de Janeiro: Clad in a yellow-and-green shirt over a bulletproof vest, Flávio Bolsonaro danced on a carnival float as thousands of euphoric supporters cheered below. “Brazil already chose change!” he shouted, pumping his fist in the air. Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator whose father was president not long ago, is heading into Sunday’s presidential race as the front-runner, having edged out leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in a first-round election this month. Cometh the hour, cometh the son: A victory for Bolsonaro Jnr would mark another big swing to the right in South America. AFP A victory for Bolsonaro would deliver the biggest win yet for an ascendant right-wing movement sweeping Latin America. Right-wing leaders, propelled in part by voter discontent over security, have won seven straight elections in the region over the past 18 months. If Brazil elects Bolsonaro, it would put an enthusiastic ally of Washington in power in the region’s largest nation and leave Mexico as the only big country still in the hands of the left.



Related Article US midterms ‘Like Saddam opened a Cheesecake Factory’: Obama hits out at Trump in campaign trail comeback Bolsonaro, 45, has aligned himself with President Donald Trump on using lethal force to fight drug gangs and has offered Brazil’s vast critical mineral deposits as a way to reduce America’s reliance on China. Trump has not formally backed Bolsonaro, but his administration has telegraphed its support in other ways, including by labelling Brazilian gangs as terror groups. The move shone a spotlight on crime, a concern for many Brazilian voters and a vulnerability for Lula. A right-wing victory would also mark the Bolsonaro family’s stunning return to power, less than four years after the senator’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, tried to stage a coup and inspired his supporters to storm Brazil’s capital, in an episode echoing the attack on the US Capitol. He was convicted of plotting a coup and sentenced to 27 years in prison. Flavio Bolsonaro and incumbent President Luiz Igacio Lula da Silva (right) are neck and neck in the polls heading into Sunday’s final round of voting. AP Photo/Andre Penner



Flávio Bolsonaro and his family may now be on the cusp of gaining sweeping new powers to rewrite Brazil’s history, reshape its future and target their perceived enemies. If elected, Bolsonaro has promised to seek amnesty for his father and the rioters, impeach the Supreme Court justices who jailed them and change Brazil’s Constitution. Related Article Updated

World politics Ex-Brazilian president Bolsonaro sentenced to 27 years in jail over coup plot Just months ago, Bolsonaro’s candidacy seemed like a long shot, with many sceptical that he could overcome a string of scandals and ignite the kind of enthusiasm that catapulted his father to office in 2018. And with the elder Bolsonaro jailed for trying to subvert democracy after losing the last election to Lula, his movement appeared to be in tatters. Then the younger Bolsonaro shocked many when he nearly won outright in the first round of voting this month, drawing more ballots than Lula, though the margin was the narrowest ever in Brazil. “Bolsonarismo is winning the battle for the hearts and minds of a large portion of the population,” said Rosana Pinheiro-Machado, a professor at University College Dublin who studies Brazil’s populist movements.



Bolsonaro’s success has largely been rooted in sweeping, if vague, promises to tackle crime, high grocery bills and a stagnating economy – issues at the top of the list of concerns for Brazilian voters. Taking a page out of the playbook of right-wing allies in Latin America, Bolsonaro has vowed to “declare war” on drug traffickers by building more prisons, labelling gangs as terrorist groups and lowering the age of criminal responsibility. Bolsonaro supporters hold a campaign rally one week ahead of the presidential election runoff. AP Photo/Andre Penner While violent crime has fallen to a 14-year low, many working-class Brazilians live side by side with drug gangs that have expanded their control over neighbourhoods through fear and extortion. “I will reclaim every metre, I will reclaim every street, every neighbourhood, every city, every territory that these scoundrels have taken from the Brazilian people,” Bolsonaro said during a debate days before Sunday’s run-off.



Inspired by the chainsaw used by Argentine President Javier Milei to symbolise a leaner state, Bolsonaro has adopted a pair of giant scissors as his symbol, vowing to cut about $US40 billion in public spending and privatise public companies. Speaking to a growing number of Brazilian workers who have migrated to the gig economy, he also pledged to lower taxes and decrease red tape for entrepreneurs. Even as experts have questioned the economics of Bolsonaro’s promises, including how he can cut taxes without reducing welfare benefits, many voters have responded to his agenda with excitement. Bolsonaro is eager to channel Argentina’s Javier Milei (left) in making heavy cuts to state institutions. AP Photo/Ettore Chiereguini Bolsonaro has also drawn overwhelming support in Brazil’s agricultural belt and in regions of the Amazon, where farmers and cattle ranchers have cheered his promises to make it easier to explore the riches of the rainforest. Crucially, Bolsonaro has also tapped into a deep fatigue many voters feel toward Lula, painting him as a corrupt symbol of the political establishment.



Between 2003 and 2010, during his first two terms, Lula helped lift millions out of poverty through generous social programs financed by a commodities boom. When he left office, his approval ratings topped 80 per cent, but his legacy was later tainted when a sprawling corruption scandal landed him in prison. Related Article Trump diplomacy ‘Brazil belongs to Brazilians’: The world leader who refuses to bow to Donald Trump In 2021, his convictions were tossed out by the Supreme Court amid evidence that the judge who convicted him was biased. This paved the way for Lula’s resurrection and return to the presidency in 2022, though he has struggled to clean up his image among voters who still link him to graft. In Lula’s third term, Brazil’s economy has posted modest growth and largely escaped US tariffs, while unemployment has fallen to record lows. Still, rising household debt and eroding affordability have dampened his approval and fuelled Bolsonaro’s popularity. Lula has also been saddled with the political fallout of a crisis engulfing Brazil’s Supreme Court. Against this backdrop, Bolsonaro’s attacks on the judiciary have grown more alluring to many Brazilians who have lost trust in institutions.



Lula scored points with many Brazilians by standing up to Trump last year when he tried to force the nation into dropping the coup charges against the elder Bolsonaro. Those efforts, the fruits of lobbying by a brother of Flávio Bolsonaro who lives in the United States, ultimately failed. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. World.title: Soggy streets, icy winds: Melbourne shivers through spring cold snap
World.content:
NationalVictoriaWeather Soggy streets, icy winds: Melbourne shivers through spring cold snap Ashleigh McMillan, Hannah Kennelly and Roy Ward Updated October 25, 2026 — 4:33pm ,first published 2:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Victorians face below-average spring temperatures and alpine snow flurries before conditions improve ahead of Melbourne Cup Day. On Sunday, organisers cancelled the Australian MotoGP on Phillip Island after wild weather and poor visibility grounded the medical helicopter, making track conditions unsafe for racing.

Pedestrians attempt to shield themselves from the rain. Arsineh Houspian In Melbourne, it was a soggy start to the day, with more than 22mm of rain falling across the 12 hours to midday on Sunday. In the city’s south-west, Altona recorded heavier totals of 40mm of rain across 24 hours. Health authorities remain on high alert for a thunderstorm asthma emergency, due to a combination of high grass pollen counts and likely strong winds and thunderstorm activity over East Gippsland.



People try to shield themselves from the rain as they cross Collins Street in the Melbourne CBD. Arsineh Houspian A severe thunderstorm warning is in place for the state’s north-east across into the afternoon on Sunday, as damaging wind moves across Wodonga, Corryong, Bright, Falls Creek, Mount Hotham and Omeo. View post on X While Melbourne is expected to reach a top of 19 degrees on Sunday, the Bureau of Meteorology’s senior forecaster Michael Efron said the city would feel much colder due to the breezy conditions. “It’s going to feel a lot colder as we get into this afternoon as those winds pick up,” he said. “It will be quite a shock to the system, compared to the conditions that we’ve seen over the last week with those temperatures pushing into the low 30s.”



Fans waiting for the rain to clear at the 2026 Australian Motorcycle Grand Prix in Phillip Island. Joe Armao Across the first half of the week, Melbourne temperatures will be three to six degrees below average for this time of year, with a high of 16 degrees on Monday as rainfall eases, and a high of 17 degrees on Tuesday. The cold front crossing the state will also bring minor snowfall across the Alpine region on Monday and Tuesday. “There will be some flurries, especially at resorts like Mount Baw Baw, with all this cold air pushing through, and even the risk of some small hail along the coast overnight tonight and into the early hours of Monday,” Efron said on Sunday.



“These cold conditions are quite a typical weather system for spring – it’s when we do tend to see the largest swings between hot and cold weather for Victoria. “Those really dramatic shifts in conditions are driven by the interior of the continent really heating up with the more intense sunlight at this time of year, whereas the oceans to our south are still quite cold.” The 2026 MotoGP was also cancelled due to poor weather conditions, leaving thousands of fans unable to say goodbye to the last race at the iconic Phillip Island circuit. Race organisers battled set back after set back due to the weather on Sunday, postponing track action until after 1pm after poor visibility around Phillip Island and Melbourne impacted the medical helicopter’s ability to fly. Fans wait for the rain to clear during the MotoGP Joe Armao



Organisers said if a crash occurred during the race, the medical helicopter needed to be able to land and also navigate to the nearest trauma centre in Melbourne. Both the MotoGP warm-up session and the Australian Superbikes Race 3 were cancelled in the morning and the Motor3 race was cancelled in the early afternoon. Just after 3.30pm , race organisers announced the event had been cancelled. People with asthma and spring hayfever in East Gippsland are being warned of an increased risk of developing asthma symptoms if large amounts of pollen are whipped into the air on Sunday.



Acting chief health officer Dr Clare Looker said people in the region needed to be prepared while the high-risk forecast was in place across Sunday. Those who had never had asthma could also experience shortness of breath and wheezing, she said. View post on X “Asthma can become serious very quickly, so make sure you have your reliever medication with you and call Triple Zero if someone is struggling to breathe or their asthma is not improving,” Looker said. “The safest place to be during the strong wind gusts before and during a thunderstorm is indoors, with windows and doors closed.” Temperatures are likely to bounce back by late next week, with a forecast top of 25 on Saturday in Melbourne. Reasonable spring weather is expected for the Melbourne Cup.

World.title: When tragedy demands women be treated better, men twist it into an excuse to treat them worse
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack Opinion When tragedy demands women be treated better, men twist it into an excuse to treat them worse Sean Kelly Columnist October 25, 2026 — 4:30pm

October 25, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In his new history of Wikipedia, journalist Richard Cooke writes that we may be witnessing the “beginning of the end of the encyclopaedic age”. This was an age marked not only by a belief in the importance of knowledge, but in its civilising function. If we could just assemble enough facts and give them to enough people, we could create a better society. Two weeks ago, Cooke offered this bleak verdict to Crikey: “Wikipedia is the closest thing that’s ever existed to that universal encyclopaedia, and its effect on making things like public discourse more reasonable or more reason-driven is undetectable.” Don’t assume the attack on Helen Haines will change anything. That’s the quickest way to ensure it doesn’t. Marija Ercegovac I helped launch that book last week, two days after Helen Haines was brutally attacked. That is an event on which there is not yet agreement about facts, though this has not stopped widespread discussion of the political environment in which it took place. And nor should it have. Such sudden, passionate, ubiquitous discussion is always worth paying attention to. A similar phenomenon occurred in the aftermath of the Sydney Swans Pullman Hotel allegations, and in relation to the allegations about the students at Scots College who are accused of sexual assault. Occasionally, you will hear the argument that this means we should refrain from such discussions until more is known. On the specifics of those cases, that is reasonable.



But such sudden eruptions of debate can point us to something important, something worth noticing for its own sake: a deep well of anger, frustration, fear. Such events command national attention not only because of their intrinsic horror but because of the way they unearth such feelings, caused by significant problems in our society. These feelings are all the stronger for the way they are usually pushed down. The passion with which such events are met is a reaction to the complacency with which the topic areas into which they fall are usually met. To many women, in particular, it can seem as though there is a conspiracy to avoid significant discussion of violence against women. It seems that way because, for all intents and purposes, there is. Related Article Opinion

Haines attack What do Jacqui Lambie, Helen Haines and Queen Victoria have in common? Far too much Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author If this sounds like overreach, recall the absolute outpouring of the #metoo movement, those many, many voices: so powerful, so passionate, in part because they had been silenced for years. But this was only a temporary shattering of the status quo before great efforts resumed to return those voices to silence. Consider the hideous media campaign waged against Brittany Higgins. Recall the way defamation is increasingly used to silence women who have spoken up – an international phenomenon portrayed in the recent documentary Silenced. And think, too, of the ways both media campaigns and lawsuits act not only to silence those individual women but all the other women who might consider speaking in the future. Because, of course, this is the broadest danger of the attack on Haines: that women, who already face high barriers to participation in public life, will be further put off. That there are other voices that will be silenced before they even begin to speak.



As a political staffer, I witnessed both these strands in Parliament House – the repressed rage finally surfacing and the way such rage was immediately turned against the person feeling it – on the day when Julia Gillard stood and delivered what would become known as the misogyny speech. The prime minister’s sincere and cutting words, full of fury at the way her gender had been turned against her for so long, resonated with so many. Immediately, though, many journalists rejected those words as unimportant – and went further, too, using them as another piece of evidence in their catalogue of Gillard’s failings. Related Article Opinion

Matthew Canavan Canavan’s bizarre manosphere comments show he should check his own algorithm Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist Or take Nationals leader Matt Canavan’s recent comments about boys being driven to interact with toxic masculinity by a curriculum focused on respectful relationships and consent. Again and again we see that if women demand respect, it is not long before men will find a way to blame men’s failure to show respect on the fact it was asked for in the first place – as experts such as Monash University’s professor Steven Roberts point out, a common manosphere manoeuvre. There is no way out of this catch-22 logic: no action that women might take that will not later be twisted into an excuse for treating them worse. We should be wary, then, of assuming the attack on Helen Haines will change much. If we assume that open discussion and debate will improve the situation, we can look to Cooke’s conclusion: the situation has only worsened. If we assume that a high-profile attack on a woman, universally decried, will shift things, we need only look at the history of violence against women. Even the more fundamental idea that violence is sufficiently shocking that it might act as an alarm that will wake up society is doubtful. German historian Philipp Ruch recently explained the Nazis’ success at the 1930 elections. At first, he said, people were repelled by violence – until the opposite occurred. “It’s hard to admit this from a modern perspective, but historical Fascism’s lust for violence didn’t make it repulsive but extremely attractive to a lot of German voters.”



It is possible that an attack like the one against Helen Haines will make us change our ways. But it is also possible that we live in a society in which violence is increasingly permissible, and in which violence only brings more violence. Taken together, all this does not offer as bleak a prognosis as it might seem. A realistic appraisal of the barriers to change can be depressing, but it is also necessary. In fact, any genuine shift is only likely to begin with a recognition of the immense strength of the forces that work to keep us stuck where we are now. Those forces will never be beaten once and for all. But they can be resisted, and each bit of resistance – be it open debate or pushing back against social media or acting against both violence against and abuse of women – is worthwhile for two reasons. First, because that act may help change things. Second, because each act signals to everyone else that nothing is inevitable – neither change nor the status quo. Sean Kelly is author of The Game: A Portrait of Scott Morrison, a regular columnist and a former adviser to Julia Gillard and Kevin Rudd.

World.title: Northcote triple-brick home passes in on a vendor bid of $1.7 million
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Northcote triple-brick home passes in on a vendor bid of $1.7 million Melissa Heagney-Bayliss October 25, 2026 — 4:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

Key points A Northcote house failed to sell under the hammer, passing in on a vendor bid of $1.7 million.

In Fitzroy, a four-bedroom home that had been newly renovated sold for $1,531,000.

Five bidders fought it out for the keys to an Essendon home, which sold under the hammer for $2,285,000.

A triple-brick character home in Northcote, with a separate apartment attached, didn’t receive a single offer from a buyer at auction on Saturday, passing in on a vendor bid of $1.7 million. The five-bedroom property at 173 Bastings Street had been advertised with a reserve of $1.8 million. Collings Real Estate’s Chris Vrantsis said though there had been a lot of interest in the property, buyers had stepped back after the reserve was revealed, which is required by law under new Victorian auction rules. “We had 30 to 35 people through the house and a few people came back quite a few times,” Vrantsis said. “But I think as soon as the reserve was shown they felt it was over the top.”



The property is now advertised for private sale with a $1,775,000 asking price. Related Article Melbourne house prices Melbourne set to drop out of the $1 million club as house prices fall The Northcote auction was one of 838 scheduled in Melbourne this week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 56 per cent from 612 reported results across the week, while 102 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Agents say market conditions in Melbourne, and the fear of another interest rate rise – with the Reserve Bank set to make its next decision on November 3 – were being talked about over the auction weekend.



Melbourne’s median house price is expected to fall below $1 million, after dropping 3.3 per cent in the September quarter, on Domain data. It only needs to fall another 1.5 per cent for prices to be in the high $900,000s. Meanwhile, banks including ANZ and Westpac are predicting another rate hike next month. Inside 173 Bastings Street, Northcote. Collings Real Estate Despite the challenges the current market was throwing up, Vrantsis was confident the property would sell. “We’ll just keep working through until we find the right buyer,” he said.



In Fitzroy, a fully renovated art deco home, at 74 Alexandra Parade, sold under the hammer for $1,531,000 above the $1.35 million reserve. Three bidders fought it out for the keys to the four-bedroom home – all were young first-home buyers. Nelson Alexander Fitzroy’s Mark Verrocchi said the auction went on for some time, as smaller bids of $5000 and then $1000 were being made throughout as a tactic to slow down proceedings. The young buyer, represented by a buyer’s advocate, will now make the property his family home.



Verrocchi said the property appealed to a lot of buyers as it had been newly renovated from top to bottom, and was on a larger parcel of land with a side driveway. However, it was in a tricky location being on such a busy road. “That area really is like an island in Fitzroy,” he said. “If this house was on any other street it would have cost $2 million plus.” Verrocchi said while higher interest rates were impacting the market, so was the upcoming Victorian State Election, with many prospective buyers and sellers waiting to see what the outcome would be in late November, before making any decisions. In Essendon, five bidders were sure of their decision, making offers for a four-bedroom home at 36 Washington Street. The home sold under the hammer for $2,285,000, above the $1.95 million reserve.



Bidding opened at $1.9 million, with $25,000 offers from bidders until the price reached $2 million. It then slowed to $10,000 and $5000 offers before the winning bid was made. The buyer is a young family from Pascoe Vale looking to move to Essendon. Jellis Craig Moonee Valley’s Jason Johnson said buyers had responded strongly to the reserves being advertised on properties listed for auction, as did vendors’ realistic pricing. “Price obviously had a lot to do with it,” Johnson said.



Another property at 15 Ferguson Street, Ascot Vale sold for $1.47 million, above the $1,385,000 reserve, after four bidders fought it out. The property sold to a young family who were upsizing from Tullamarine. Both were great results in a tough market, he said. “It was a bit out of the norm in terms of what’s happening in the market at the moment,” Johnson said. World.title: Child critically injured in assault by unknown man at central Auckland park
World.content:
A child has been critically injured after an assault by an unknown man at a central Auckland park this afternoon.

Hato Hone St John said two people were taken to hospital after the incident in Myers Park at 4.45pm.

One has been taken to Starship Children's Hospital with critical injuries.

An area around the children's playground was cordoned off by multiple police officers.

Police said a 20-year-old man was taken into custody over the assault.

Inspector Jim Wilson said the man was not known to the victim.

Wilson said both the victim and offender required medical treatment.

"This was an isolated incident, and there is no ongoing risk to the public."

World.title: National removes volunteer after learning of sexual conduct with minor conviction
World.content:
National has removed one of its campaign volunteers after learning he had been convicted of sexual conduct with a minor five years ago.

In 2021, Stuff reported Roger Buchanan, who was a teacher, manipulated a student into an illicit sexual relationship.

Buchanan was a volunteer and member of National's Palmerston North electorate committee, and a National Party spokesperson confirmed it had removed him from those roles when it became aware of his history.

"The National Party stands with victims of sexual violence," a spokesperson said.

Leader Christopher Luxon said he'd only just become aware of the matter, and he was glad the party had acted swiftly.

"That's the entirely appropriate thing to do.

World.title: Ruthless Ferns flatten French at Women's Rugby League World Cup
World.content:
Ruthless. Merciless. Ominous.

The KIwi Ferns have put the Rugby League World Cup on notice with a 92-0 demolition of France.

It was nothing short of a 70-minute slaughter under the roof in Christchurch, as the Ferns ran riot against little French resistance.

Hat tricks for Stacey Waaka, Apii Nicolls, and Mele Hufanga were among the 18 tries scored, New Zealand delivering a rugby league lesson to utterly humiliate the French.

A late injury call-up to the squad, winger Mackenzie Wiki opened the scoring as the Ferns showcased some slick hands through the backline.

Eating up the metres at will through some damaging carries from Ivana Lauitiiti and Alexis Tauaneai, the Kiwi Ferns were in again through fullback Apii Nicholls.

Debutant Chantay Kiria-Ratu got her first test try as she pirouetted through some feeble French defence and slammed it on the chalk.

Nicolls stuck for her second on the next set, exploding onto a grubber through from her skipper Raecene McGregor.

The captain was next to get on the scoresheet with a beautiful show and go, McGregor far to quick for the cover as she dashed away for her side's fifth.

Mele Hufanga was at her dominant best with ball in hand. © Photosport Ltd 2026 www.photosport.nz

It was another of the big names scoring the sixth, Stacey Waaka showcasing her class with a fend and step and a swerve.

Out-scoring the clock, Mele Hufanga took a deft inside ball from Tenika Willison to notch her first try of the campaign, Waaka getting her second just moments later.

Hufanga got her double just before halftime with a display of pure power close to the line.

The rampaging centre kicked off the scoring in the second, set up by a clean Kaiyah Atai line break as the Ferns notched fifty.

They would continue to pile on the points, McGregor with another silky dummy and dart for her second.

After setting up several tries with some storming carries, Atai got her reward as she once again smashed her way through multiple French defenders.

There was no relief for the French, Willison getting a double on debut, first sent in by Hufanga, before McGregor sent a perfect cross kick, the former Olympian evading three would be tacklers on her way to score.

Waaka then decided to prove she can run over them as well as around them, bulldozing her way to a hat-trick and fifth World Cup try.

Further carnage was inflicted late with Wiki and Nicholls added to their tallys, NIcolls notching the ninety with her fourth to mercifully end the

massacre.

While rusty in their opening encounter against Fiji, it was a well-oiled Kiwi Ferns machine in Christchurch right from kick-off, sending a serious warning to the Jillaroos.

A woman's body has been found in a house during police enquiries into a crash involving a car and a train in the Bay of Plenty this morning.
